title: Falcons mock draft 2027: Who will Atlanta prioritize with a top-10 pick?
summary: It’s that time of year again. The Atlanta Falcons are 3-7 going into their Week 11 bye, and currently projected to pick 8th overall. Simultaneously, they’re also just 1.5 games out of first place in the division and still hold a reasonable chance to make the playoffs. That’s the NFC South for you. I’m not […]
full_text: NORMAN, OKLAHOMA - OCTOBER 31: Quarterback LaNorris Sellers #16 of the South Carolina Gamecocks breaks loose for a 30-yard gain against defensive back Peyton Bowen #22 of the Oklahoma Sooners in the second quarter at Gaylord Family Oklahoma Memorial Stadium on October 31, 2026 in Norman, Oklahoma. South Carolina won 42-25. (Photo by Brian Bahr/Getty Images) | Getty Images It’s that time of year again. The Atlanta Falcons are 3-7 going into their Week 11 bye, and currently projected to pick 8th overall. Simultaneously, they’re also just 1.5 games out of first place in the division and still hold a reasonable chance to make the playoffs. That’s the NFC South for you. I’m not going to spend my time wondering about the team’s fortunes over the remainder of 2026 here. Instead, we’ll be taking a look ahead at the 2027 NFL Draft. The class is not shaping up like many had hoped, with some of the top quarterback prospects struggling while other players emerge. There is a lot of talent here, just maybe not in the configuration many expected. Since this is an extra spicy bye week mock draft, we’re going to do something a little different. I will not be taking the chalk pick of offensive tackle at 8 in this simulation, instead choosing to go in a different direction. Based on the header image, I’m sure you can guess where that direction is. All I’m asking you to remember before flaming me is that 1) this is intentionally spicy, because who wants another boring tackle pick; and 2) this is a projection based on what I think could happen over the remainder of the NFL and college football season. I will only be picking in the first three rounds here because, quite frankly, I don’t have enough information on the Day 3 players at this point. But before we jump in to the mock, let’s take a look at the Falcons’ current haul of draft picks. These are based on projections before Week 11’s games, so they can and will change week to week. What are the Falcons current draft picks? Round 1, Pick 8 Round 2, Pick 39 Round 2, Pick 57 Round 3, Pick 70 Round 4, Pick 108 Round 6, Pick 218 Round 6, Pick 221 Round 7, Pick 229 This is the written version, but you can also find the mock draft in two alternate forms as well. On our YouTube channel: The mock is also available on all your favorite podcast platforms! You can listen to it directly here: Round 1, Pick 8: QB LaNorris Sellers, South Carolina This is a Week 11 mock draft, so I don’t have the luxury of seeing how Michael Penix Jr. fares over the remaining seven games. I have to make a call right now, and based on that, the Falcons will be looking for a new quarterback in this scenario. But who, and how to acquire them? Since, for the purposes of this exercise, we’re not considering free agent or trade options, our only avenue is the draft. With Atlanta selecting at 8th overall, options are also limited. The top guys will not be available, so who could be in play here? You might recall a mid-season mock draft from a few years ago where I sent a QB who was, at the time, being mocked in the second round to the Falcons inside the top-10. That QB was Jayden Daniels, and he ended up going second overall. I feel similarly about South Carolina’s LaNorris Sellers, who is currently being mocked in the early 2nd but absolutely has a chance to go top-10 when the draft arrives. Jayden Daniels was better than Sellers (and would likely be the unquestioned QB1 in this class), but that’s why Sellers might actually be available in the back half of the top-10. The answer is simple: the NFL is willing to take chances on quarterbacks with Sellers’ tools and electric playmaking ability, and I can’t think of a better offense to drop him into than Atlanta’s. At 6’3, 238, Sellers brings NFL size to the table. His athleticism is outstanding as one of the best rushing threats in the class, with breakaway speed and dynamic movement skills. Sellers also possesses terrific arm talent, although there’s quite a bit of refinement still needed in his game. I understand many will disagree. This QB class is going to provoke a lot of debate about who to take a chance on. It’s also a projection based on how Sellers has been playing of late—although the game against Georgia could significantly boost or hurt his stock. The Falcons need someone who can come in and immediate elevate their offense at quarterback, and I think the best way to accomplish that is by bringing in a legitimate dual-threat like LaNorris Sellers. Because of the floor he brings with his rushing and all the creative ways to incorporate him into an offense with Bijan Robinson, he’ll have an easier path to early success while he continues to build out his passing game skillset. Round 2, Pick 39: OT Elijah Page, USC With the Falcons passing on offensive tackle at 8, they’ll need to find one early in the second round. I think this is a spot where the team considers a small trade up to secure their chosen guy, but there could be some legitimate options here at 39. One of my favorites is USC’s Elijah Page, who brings the necessary physical profile (6’7, 315) that Bill Callahan looks for in his linemen. Page has been an outstanding pass protector, but took significant strides as a run blocker this season. That’s important, because I don’t think Atlanta will be considering tackles who they can’t trust to pave the way for Bijan Robinson. There’s still improvements he needs to make to become a plus starter in the NFL, but with his length, mass, and athleticism, Page has every opportunity to succeed with the Falcons. Page has primarily played left tackle in his career, so there will be a transition to the right side. It’s possible he eventually returns to the left side once Jake Matthews hangs up the cleats. Round 2, Pick 57: EDGE Princewill Umanmielen, LSU The Falcons should be getting Jalon Walker back healthy in 2027, and hopefully we’ll see enough from James Pearce Jr. to trust him as one of the team’s top pass rushers over the rest of the season. Atlanta extended Cameron Thomas to give the team a reliable third option who can do a bit of everything. Still, you can never have too many good edge rushers, and the strength of this draft class appears to be on the defensive line. The name Princewill Umanmielen might look familiar to you, as his brother Princely Umanmielen was drafted last season by the Panthers. Princewill actually looks like a more consistent and well-rounded prospect to me, as his run defense is significantly better than his brothers was coming out of college. Umanmielen had a slow start to his college career, but has taken massive steps over the past two seasons. He’s already got 12 sacks, 5 hits, and 22 hurries this season, and had 11 sacks, 5 hits, and 35 hurries the year prior. His run stop rate of 7.6% is also well above-average. Umanmielen is a strong finisher who can hold his own against the run at 6’4, 256, and would be an excellent complement to Atlanta’s young edge room. Round 3, Pick 70: S Ty Benefield, LSU Atlanta isn’t going to be able to replace Jessie Bates III, but they’ll have to find a new direction at safety regardless. My guess is that Atlanta is looking for a punisher in the box who is more capable in coverage than someone like DeMarcco Hellams. LSU’s Ty Benefield looks like a perfect complement for Xavier Watts, who can play closer to the line of scrimmage and use his superior size (6’3, 216) to take on more responsibilities against the run. Benefield is no slouch in coverage either. He’s notched three interceptions and two PBUs this season and has allowed a passer rating of just 31.3 thus far, which is outstanding. His missed tackle rate of 9.3% is well above average, and he moves better than you’d think for his size. That being said, his testing will be a major factor in his evaluation, and could push him significantly higher up the board if he comes in better than expected. What do you think about this potential draft class for the Falcons? Leave your draft takes…

title: Ravens drop 6th straight to Panthers, put season on life support
summary: The Baltimore Ravens dropped their sixth straight game in a rollicking, back-and-forth 35-33 loss to the Carolina Panthers on Sunday afternoon. After a wild 58 minutes that included seven lead changes and no less than a dozen jaw-dropping plays, Carolina took the lead on a Ryan Fitzgerald field goal with 1:47 to go. Baltimore’s potential […]
full_text: The Baltimore Ravens dropped their sixth straight game in a rollicking, back-and-forth 35-33 loss to the Carolina Panthers on Sunday afternoon. After a wild 58 minutes that included seven lead changes and no less than a dozen jaw-dropping plays, Carolina took the lead on a Ryan Fitzgerald field goal with 1:47 to go. Baltimore’s potential game-winning drive was snuffed out by a Jacoby Brissett interception, and the Ravens dropped to 4-7 . The currently sit 11th in the AFC – and in the 2027 draft order. That is starting to sound like a good thing for a team that should be considering major changes this offseason. The Ravens defense gave up the lead four different times on Sunday afternoon, including twice directly after scores from the offense. The offense turned the ball over twice and gained just eight yards across their first three drives of the second half. And outside of a Devontez Walker kickoff return touchdown, Baltimore’s special teams units struggled with sloppy ball-handling and poor coverage. And yet, the Ravens had two distinct chances to win this game late in the fourth quarter. The first was the Panthers’ penultimate drive, in which Baltimore’s defense could not dig their heels in and protect a one-point lead. Brissett’s gunslinging on the previous drive showed he was capable of driving into field goal range, but another collapse in pass protection forced him to throw a prayer out of bounds to avoid a sack. Except the pass did not make it to the sidelines, instead landing in the arms of Panthers linebacker Tyrel Dodson. In both instances, the Ravens could not be at their best when their best was needed. Despite thrilling wins over the Cowboys and Falcons, first-year head coach Jesse Minter’s oft-repeated mantra never fully took root in The Castle. And it is fair to question if he has lived up to his own standard. Brissett was rushing partially because Minter declined to take a timeout after a sack with 1:30 to go. 24 seconds later, Brissett threw a checkdown to Justice Hill to set up a 4th-and-1. Only then did Minter stop the clock, only for Brissett to restart it with a sneak that chewed up another 23 seconds before the pick. This is the second game in a row that Minter’s questionable timeout usage has costed the Ravens precious time in end-of-half situations – two contests that were decided by a total of five points. At the end of the day, the coaching staff is failing simple math problems – and struggling to keep their finger on the pulse of the game. To be fair, that pulse was all over the play. To borrow a phrase from a Saturday Night Live great, this game had everything: a replay-assisted safety; a wildcat flea flicker touchdown; a fumble out of the end zone, a muffed punt, and Walker’s return touchdown – all from the Ravens, all in the first 20 minutes. Per @espn research: The Ravens are the second team in the last 20 years to lose a game despite producing a safety and a kick return TD. They join Washington, who lost in Week 11 of 2015 (… and wait for it …) to the #Panthers at Bank of America Stadium. — Mike Kaye (@mike_e_kaye) November 23, 2026 The rest of the second quarter featured back-to-back Ravens touchdowns – both answered by the Panthers – and another muffed punt by LaJohntay Wester that was recovered at the 1 and led to a six-yard(!) quarterback sneak. The second half settled down, but there was still an end zone interception by T.J. Tampa; an incomplete pass that was challenged and overturned into a Derrick Henry fumble, and finally, perhaps mercifully, Brissett’s game-ending pick. The veteran does deserve credit for his first two games in Baltimore. He has racked up 616 passing yards – the team’s most in back-to-back contests since Weeks 5 and 6 of the 2024 season – and taken just four sacks despite a porous offensive line. His willingness to push the ball downfield has not only produced plenty of explosive plays, but also kept opposing safeties off the line of scrimmage to open up the run game. Derrick Henry and Justice Hill combined for 163 rushing yards on 19 carries, and the team’s overall 7.1 yards per carry was their best since Week 15 of last year. Several young players showed out, too. Walker provided a spark with his return touchdown, Tampa stopped the Panthers on the goal line virtually on his own, and second-year edge rusher Mike Green had his second straight two-sack game. Those developments are more important for the Ravens’ future, and they need to start looking in that direction. At 4-7, the season is on life support. You could argue it has already flatlined – and only what would be a shocking win over the Texans next week could jolt it back to life. Otherwise, a rushed post-bye (or one week later) return from Jackson would make little would be rendered moot, and the Ravens will stumble into another offseason with many questions, few answers, and limited ways to find more.
author: Nikhil Mehta

title: Ravens Report Card, Week 11: Mistakes and miscues mount in sixth straight loss
summary: The Baltimore Ravens dropped their fifth consecutive game on Monday night, losing to the previously winless Los Angeles Chargers by three points (23-20). Here are report card grades for the team’s position groups from another disheartening defeat in Week 10. Quarterback: C+ Jacoby Brissett made a number of good throws in this game and orchestrated […]
full_text: Nov 22, 2026; Charlotte, North Carolina, USA; Carolina Panthers linebacker Devin Lloyd (55) tackles Baltimore Ravens cornerback Nate Wiggins (2) during the fourth quarter at Bank of America Stadium. Mandatory Credit: Jim Dedmon-Imagn Images | IMAGN IMAGES via Reuters Connect The Baltimore Ravens dropped their fifth consecutive game on Monday night, losing to the previously winless Los Angeles Chargers by three points (23-20). Here are report card grades for the team’s position groups from another disheartening defeat in Week 10. Quarterback: C+ Jacoby Brissett made a number of good throws in this game and orchestrated five scoring drives. It was not his fault that the Ravens fumbled the ball multiple times and his pass-catchers dropped more than five passes. The veteran finished with a 24-of-37 passing line with 276 yards through the air. His touchdown pass came via a trick play to a wide-open Rashod Bateman for a 25-yard strike in the fourth quarter. Brissett was not perfect, however. He was inaccurate on some pass attempts and threw a game-sealing interception on the team’s final drive, which was an inexcusable mistake where he should have thrown the ball away. The Ravens may not have ultimately gotten down the field into position for a game-winning field goal, but there was time left to do so and Brissett’s interception cost them that opportunity. Running Back: C- It’s difficult to give a poor grade to the running backs when Derrick Henry and Justice Hill combined for 163 rushing yards, averaged over nine yards per carry and scored two combined touchdowns. However, while both were effective churning out yards on the ground, they also each lost a fumble. Hill’s fumble at the goal line negated a would-be long touchdown run in the first half that instead resulted in a touchback. Then, in the fourth quarter with the Ravens trailing by six points, Henry had the ball poked out after making a screen catch. It was a controversial call that maybe should have been ruled an incompletion, but nevertheless Henry’s ball security needs to be better. Fortunately, the Panthers did not score points off either of these turnovers — but they still costed the Ravens valuable points and possessions. Wide Receiver: C + Zay Flowers had his most productive performance in several weeks, reeling in a team-high eight receptions on 11 targets for 97 yards. He was open a lot and created yards in space on crossing routes, which has been Flowers’ bread and butter this season. He did have one drop just before halftime that would have been a long gain. Rashod Bateman started hot with 67 yards and a long touchdown catch early in the game, but only finished with two catches on six targets. Devontez Walker had a nice 34-yard grab on his only target. It was a quiet outing for Ja’Kobi Lane who was not credited with a target after receiving the most throws his way of anyone last week. Lane did draw an offensive pass interference in the first quarter but didn’t see another look after that. Tight End: C- Mark Andrews was not able to replicate his season-best performance from last week, as he caught just two passes for 14 yards in this game. Matthew Hibner had an almost identical stat line while Josh Cuevas caught only one reception for eight yards. The tight ends collectively seemed to have a much more positive impact in the run game but failed to do anything more than minimal complimentary work as pass-catchers. Offensive Line: B- This was definitely one of the offensive line’s better games this season — if not the best. They finally had a breakthrough showing in the run game, where they consistently won at the line of scrimmage and opened up big rushing lanes. The Ravens ran for 157 yards as a team and averaged 7.1 yards per carry, which was negatively skewed by one -13 yard attempt from Flowers that was blown up. In pass protection, the Panthers did have two sacks and six quarterback hits, so it was far from perfect. Brissett bought some extra time in the pocket, but also had a decent amount of time to throw on most of his dropbacks it seemed. Defensive Line: D+ For the second straight week, the Ravens didn’t do a great job stopping the run. The Panthers were able to rack up nearly 150 rushing yards and averaged 4.2 yards per carry. Chuba Hubbard scored twice and had a long 26-yard run. Travis Jones made some more impact plays with eight total tackles, one sack and one tackle for loss, while Calais Campbell had a quarterback hit and key third-down pass knockdown in the fourth quarter. The Ravens still do not generate enough consistent quarterback pressure through the interior, which is even more true without Nnamdi Madubuike in the lineup. Edge Rusher: C+ It was another standout outing from Mike Green, who continues to ascend in his sophomore season. Green had four solo tackles with two sacks, two tackles for loss and two quarterback hits. On the other side of the defensive front, Trey Hendrickso came close to recording his third sack of the season but came up short. Hendrickson did have a quarterback hit and tackle for loss, but he was also flagged for a clear roughing the passer penalty. The Ravens have unfortunately not been getting many splash plays from rookie Zion Young. Linebacker: C The Ravens’ starting linebacker duo put forth another middling overall game. Trenton Simpson had a team-high 10 tackles and Roquan Smith had nine tackles with one quarterback hit. While the counting stats are fine, their impact defending the run was evidently not there consistently. Smith was notably beaten a couple times in man coverage, including on a third-down conversion late in the fourth quarter against Tommy Tremble. Cornerback: C+ Nate Wiggins seemed to have a solid game without his name being called much. Starting in place of Marlon Humphrey was Chidobe Awuzie, who gave up a few catches in the first half alone including a touchdown in the red zone. T.J. Tampa saw expanded snaps as an outside corner and made two impressive plays on back-to-back reps in the second half. He broke up a short pass attempt in the red zone and then intercepted Bryce Young’s third-down throw that could have been a touchdown. Tampa also was beaten on a trick-play touchdown, but it was nice to see him come up with a turnover. Nickel corner Keyon Martin made a big open-field stop against Tet McMillan late in the game. Safety: C- Kyle Hamilton has uncharacteristically been on the receiving end of some long completions in coverage the past two weeks. He was beaten by Jalen Coker for a 35-yard grab in the first quarter and the Panthers quickly scored a touchdown afterwards. He was also stiff-armed by Hubbard on a tackle attempt — also uncharacteristic. He did have eight tackles and one tackle for loss. Malaki Starks also had a tackle for loss but appeared to be somewhat at fault for coverage issues as well on a few plays. Backup K’Von Wallace had a career-high seven tackles. Special Teams: D+ Devontez Walker made the biggest play of the game for the Ravens, returning a kickoff 86 yards to the house for a touchdown. That second-quarter splash gave the Ravens a temporary five-point lead and big momentum lift. Another positive was Riley Patterson making his lone field goal and four extra point tries. This grade is low because of LaJohntay Wester, who muffed two punts and lost one of them. The Panthers scored a go-ahead touchdown directly off of the fumbled punt that they recovered. He was fortunate to not have lost both, although the second was recovered by the Ravens at the one yard line and created terrible field position.

title: Ravens discussion: instant reactions to rollercoaster loss to Panthers
summary: The Baltimore Ravens lost their sixth straight game on Sunday afternoon, falling to the Carolina Panthers by a score of 35-33. A back-and-forth matchup came down to the final drives, and once again, Baltimore’s defense could not get off the field during a late drive with the game on the line. Carolina took a two-point […]
full_text: CHARLOTTE, NORTH CAROLINA - NOVEMBER 22: Mitchell Evans #84 of the Carolina Panthers is tackled by T.J. Tampa #27 of the Baltimore Ravens in the end zone for a touchdown during the first half of a football game at Bank of America Stadium on November 22, 2026 in Charlotte, North Carolina. (Photo by David Jensen/Getty Images) | Getty Images The Baltimore Ravens lost their sixth straight game on Sunday afternoon, falling to the Carolina Panthers by a score of 35-33. A back-and-forth matchup came down to the final drives, and once again, Baltimore’s defense could not get off the field during a late drive with the game on the line. Carolina took a two-point lead, setting Jacoby Brissett up for a potential game-winning score. Instead, he faced constant pressure in the pocket and had to throw up a prayer to avoid a sack that resulted in a game-ending interception. Here are Baltimore Beatdown’s instant reactions to the loss: Nikhil Mehta This game was drunk from the very start. The Ravens made their usual mistakes in all three phases – missed tackles, poor clock management, inept pass protection – but the Panthers tried to outdo them at every turn. There aren’t really any new takeaways. As in 2025, this team has been screaming at us, all year, that this is who they are. Jesse Minter’s Ravens simply cannot be at their best when the best is needed. In my opinion, their best is no longer needed. At 4-7, the season is effectively over. Winning out to snag a playoff spot – if that is even possible – is far-fetched even if Lamar Jackson comes back against the Steelers in Week 15. In fact, far-fetched might not be far enough. Baltimore is playing for a top-10 draft pick at this point. Maybe top-five. Kevin McNelis It almost feels worse to have the game be winnable at this point than to have the Ravens just get blown out. They had another double-digit lead, albeit early, which they squandered with miserable pass defense and multiple turnovers. Same stuff, different day. Now they have to worry about any lasting effects from a Derrick Henry concussion. At least Mike Green has started to show up big time. I like what I’m seeing from him, and if the Ravens can get Tavius Robinson to come back, they could have a pair of young EDGEs that would make it easier to build forward. Stephen Bopst It was simply another comedy of errors in Charlotte today. The Ravens continued their downward spiral by committing multiple errors that put a nail in their season. Justice Hill fumbled the ball out of the end zone, LaJohntay Wester muffed two punts, Derrick Henry fumbled, and to top it off Jacoby Brissett threw an awful game-ending pick. The Ravens were in position to win each of the last two games on the final drive but predictably gave the ball to the other team. Obviously, I want the Ravens to win, but continued losing is probably what it will take for some bigger changes to occur this off-season. Amongst all the other issues this year, I really am not seeing a lot of hope for the Jesse Minter led Ravens in the future. At the bare minimum, he was supposed to give this defense a boost which hasn’t come. Is it the players fault too? Yes, but I’ve seen a lot of other defensive coaches do a lot more with a lot less over the years. While I assume the front office will give Minter a grace year to build the defense with “his players”, the current results haven’t given me any indication that will change things. It will continue to baffle me that Minter was able to lead the Chargers to consecutive seasons of great defense with a worse collection of talent on paper.

title: Buffalo Bills Shout!outs: Records pile up in win over Dolphins
summary: The Buffalo Bills added another win to their record Sunday. Once again, it was a very awkward, weird game day where Josh Allen was sacked too many times, threw a pair of interceptions, but still managed to set a brand-new NFL record. Greg Rousseau turned in another multi-sack performance, and the Bills’ defense still hasn’t […]
full_text: The Buffalo Bills added another win to their record Sunday. Once again, it was a very awkward, weird game day where Josh Allen was sacked too many times, threw a pair of interceptions, but still managed to set a brand-new NFL record. Greg Rousseau turned in another multi-sack performance, and the Bills’ defense still hasn’t given up a touchdown. Yet, somehow, another backup quarterback managed to find openings and move his offense down the field enough to make things uncomfortable. But, much like the week before when the Bills handled business against the Jets, the outcome never really felt in question. Stalled drives were more of an annoyance than a problem. Scores were more of an expectation than a celebration. And, in the end, the Bills walked off the field with a 9-1 record and woke up Monday morning as the best team in the NFL. So, with another win in the books, it’s time to hand out a few more Shout! outs. _____________________________________________________________________________ Buffalo Bills — 9-1 record It’s been 35 years since the Bills started a season this well. And, with Sunday’s win over Miami, the 2026 team has officially matched a mark that hasn’t been reached in Buffalo since the days of Jim Kelly, Thurman Thomas, and company. The Bills are now 9-1 for the first time since 1991. pic.twitter.com/sXZyJDFib1 — Buffalo Bills PR (@BuffaloBillsPR) November 22, 2026 Buffalo Bills — Consecutive winning seasons It’s not just this season that’s worth celebrating. The Bills have now put together eight consecutive winning seasons, extending their own franchise record. That kind of consistency is hard to come by in the NFL, and right now, nobody else in the league has managed to sustain it for as long. The Bills 8 consecutive winning seasons also marks the NFL's longest active streak. https://t.co/6lLOmwK6Nz — Buffalo Bills PR (@BuffaloBillsPR) November 23, 2026 Joe Brady — Rookie head coach Joe Brady just keeps winning, and the list of coaches who can say they started their careers the way he has is getting pretty short. The Bills’ rookie head coach has joined some impressive company, and he’s only 10 games into the job. Joe Brady has joined Jim Harbaugh (2011 with San Francisco) and Jim Caldwell (2009 with Indianapolis) as the only rookie coaches since 2000 to begin with a 9-1 or better record. https://t.co/rqK4oTVeME — Buffalo Bills PR (@BuffaloBillsPR) November 23, 2026 Buffalo Bills offense — Consecutive scoring quarters The Bills’ offense hasn’t always been pretty, and there have definitely been a few frustrating stretches along the way. But even when things aren’t clicking, Buffalo has found a way to put points on the board. With points in both the first and second quarter today, the Bills have now scored at least one point in 23 straight quarters. That’s the longest streak in team history. pic.twitter.com/Hgzt7BMKoh — Buffalo Bills PR (@BuffaloBillsPR) November 22, 2026 Josh Allen — Miami touchdown streak Josh Allen has made a habit of putting up impressive numbers against the Miami Dolphins. While Sunday’s game wasn’t exactly one of his cleanest performances, he still managed to extend a streak that no other active quarterback has matched. Allen’s 18 straight games (incl. playoffs) with a passing TD against Miami is the longest active streak by any NFL QB against a single opponent. https://t.co/iMOf1vVABN — Buffalo Bills PR (@BuffaloBillsPR) November 22, 2026 James Cook — Rushing records James Cook is having himself quite a season. He’s finding the end zone every week, piling up rushing yards, and putting his name alongside some of the best running backs to ever wear a Bills uniform. He’s doing a pretty good job of rewriting the NFL record books with Josh Allen, too. Embeds: James Cook III is the first player in Bills history to have a rushing touchdown in nine straight games. pic.twitter.com/jDo80UHPyQ — Buffalo Bills PR (@BuffaloBillsPR) November 22, 2026 James Cook III has reached 10 rushing TDs on the season. Cook and Josh Allen are the first pair of teammates in NFL history to each rush for 10+ touchdowns in three consecutive seasons. pic.twitter.com/QD7nFPIoa1 — Buffalo Bills PR (@BuffaloBillsPR) November 22, 2026 Cook is the second Bill to ever reach 1,000 rushing yards in the first 10 games of a season, joining O.J. Simpson (1973 & 1975). https://t.co/Cz1MVC986N — Buffalo Bills PR (@BuffaloBillsPR) November 22, 2026 Greg Rousseau — Multi-sack games One sack just isn’t enough for Greg Rousseau anymore. The Bills’ edge rusher has been making a habit of bringing down opposing quarterbacks multiple times a game, and nobody in the NFL has done it more often this season. Greg Rousseau is now up to 10 sacks on the season. Today marks Rousseau’s fourth game of the year with 2+ sacks, the most multi-sack games by any player in the NFL this season. pic.twitter.com/gnKnwxEDCH — Buffalo Bills PR (@BuffaloBillsPR) November 22, 2026 Joe Andreessen — Special teams tackles You don’t have to be a starter to make a big impact, and Joe Andreessen has been proving that for two seasons now. The Bills’ linebacker has quietly become one of the NFL’s most productive special teams players, and Sunday’s performance added a couple more tackles to his growing total. Bills LB Joe Andreessen recorded two special teams tackles yesterday. Since the start of the 2025 season, Andreessen ranks second in the NFL with 35 special teams tackles. pic.twitter.com/3zR0YkzGI6 — Buffalo Bills PR (@BuffaloBillsPR) November 23, 2026 Tommy Doman — Passing accomplishments Who had Tommy Doman throwing one of the longest passes of the afternoon on their bingo card? The Bills’ punter got his chance to show off his arm Sunday. With his first career completion, Doman became the fifth punter in team history with a completion (Brian Moorman 3, Chris Mohr 3, Gregory Cater 1, Spike Jones 1). https://t.co/1xXQ03HGp4 — Buffalo Bills PR (@BuffaloBillsPR) November 22, 2026 Buffalo Bills — An unusual passing record Speaking of unusual passing statistics, Sunday’s game put the Bills in a rather exclusive club. It isn’t often that a quarterback throws for more than 300 yards and gets a little help through the air from his team’s kicking unit. In fact, it’s almost never happened. The Bills are the third team since 1950 to have a game in which their QB had 300+ passing yards and a kicker or punter with 30+ passing yards. pic.twitter.com/3gGgG9MtqJ — Buffalo Bills PR (@BuffaloBillsPR) November 22, 2026 _____________________________________________________________________________ The last few weeks may have felt a little average to Bills fans. But when you look at all these records, milestones, and accomplishments, it’s worth remembering that what we’ve come to consider an average Sunday in Buffalo is anything but average around the rest of the NFL.
author: Rachel Auberger

title: On Joe Brady’s decision for Buffalo Bills to receive the opening kickoff
summary: OK, we have to talk about the Buffalo Bills electing to take the football to begin games this season. While it does seem to perfectly align with the aggressive vibe of the team’s head coach, let’s work to get as close as possible a determination of whether or not it’s a good idea for the […]
full_text: OK, we have to talk about the Buffalo Bills electing to take the football to begin games this season. While it does seem to perfectly align with the aggressive vibe of the team’s head coach, let’s work to get as close as possible a determination of whether or not it’s a good idea for the Bills to be operating against the grain on this front. Now, of course, Buffalo can’t simply decide to take the football to begin each game. But Brady is electing to take it if his team wins the coin toss, and if the opponent wins it, it seems as though every other team will gladly defer to receiving the football at the start of the third quarter. Therefore, through 10 games, the Bills have been able to count on receiving the football to start the game. Earlier this season, I published two corresponding studies that examined how scoring right before the end of the half and “double-dipping” correlate to winning . I used a dataset that features all regular-season games from 2001 to 2025 and, at time of publication, the first three weeks of the 2026 season. This was the major finding from the first study: Teams that outscored their opponent in the final two minutes went on to win 64.5% of the time And the biggest revelations from the second study on double-dipping, that matter here: Teams that double dipped, which included a score of any kind, won at a 73.7% clip Those double dips occurred in 13.6% of the games The last sentence I wrote: “So, yes, teams should make a concerted effort to double dip. It correlates rather strongly with winning the football game.” And everyone would seemingly agree there, right? The double dip has become a phenomenon fans and media regularly mention as an objective teams should strive for in each game. And of course by taking the football to start the game, the Bills are eliminating their chances at said double dip. But note the second major takeaway from the double-dip study. The double dip is decently rare, something that happens in just a little under one out of every seven games. Part of the reason they don’t happen often because the double-dip opportunity only has about a coin-flip’s chance of materializing before halftime. From 2001 through Week 10 in 2026, the team that does not get the opening kickoff only had the football on the final drive of the first half 49.3% of the time. Even when kneeldowns were excluded, that number is essentially unchanged at 49.1%. So the presumption that a team starting the game with the football thereby leads to its opponent getting the ball last in the first half is quantifiably false. I also studied whether or not getting the ball first tends to lead to more overall possession in a game — which would be significantly valuable. It does not — which is probably expected — but there’s one notable aspect on this front. In that same enormous sample of over 6,600 games since the start of the 2001 season, the team getting the ball first averages 11.44 possessions per game while the other team averages 11.43. Let’s call that no difference. However, the first half tells a different story, and this is where things get interesting. The team receiving the kickoff averaged 5.93 offensive possessions in the first two quarters compared to just 5.42 offensive possesses for the team that did not get the ball to begin the game. That 0.51-possession difference is rather massive across such a large, 25-plus season sample. From that, rather unsurprisingly, the team that received the opening kickoff had an average halftime lead of +0.60 points and were leading in 47.7% of the games compared to the team not getting the ball first leading at the half 44.7% of the time. Of course, if kicking the ball first — to get the ball to begin the half — actually aids in a team’s chance to win the game, despite the rarity of a double dip occurring, the Bills have been doing it all wrong. Using that same dataset, I aimed to identify if there is any advantage to be had either way. When adjusting for the game’s point spread — to determine team quality — and home-field advantage, the team receiving the ball first won 49.8% of the games compared to a win 50.2% of the time for the club that kicks off to start the game , which does not create a convincing case whatsoever that kicking off or receiving the ball first impacts win probability. Brady’s put the ball down vibe aligns wonderfully with his to date steadfast decision to take the football to begin the game. And now we know that decision is analytically defensible.
author: Chris Trapasso

title: Takeaways from Bills win over Dolphins
summary: The Buffalo Bills beat the Dolphinss 26-9 in Week 11 at Highmark Stadium, in a game that was far from perfection from Joe Brady’s but felt more impressive than last week’s win over the Jets. The Bills are now 9-1. These are my takeaways from Buffalo’s victory. Josh Allen came out ready to let it […]
full_text: The Buffalo Bills beat the Dolphinss 26-9 in Week 11 at Highmark Stadium, in a game that was far from perfection from Joe Brady’s but felt more impressive than last week’s win over the Jets. The Bills are now 9-1. These are my takeaways from Buffalo’s victory. Josh Allen came out ready to let it rip And I loved it. Not necessarily because Allen always made the “right” decision determining at which level to throw the football. I want defenses to be forced to think about all possible variations of Buffalo’s offense. And Allen is the best player in football. The Bills slammed their foot on the gas pedal to begin this game, and while it didn’t amount to something like three-consecutive touchdown drives — which we’ve certainly witnessed during the Allen era — it led to three pass plays of 20-plus yards and two touchdowns in the first half as Buffalo built its lead. Allen seemed adamant about dicing the Dolphins secondary through the air, and not underneath. That is Allen being Allen. Allen didn’t have a carry against the Dolphins, which now amounts to, ironically, a similar place to where we were after the Patriots loss, when the Allen criticism centered around him throwing it downfield too frequently and not running nearly enough. And what happened after that? Allen averaged 11.1 yards per attempt and ran for 121 yards on 10 carries in a 37-34 win on the road against the Rams. The safety group has become a strength Amazing, right? Even if you don’t fully agree with me, it’s impossible it ignore the difference in the play of this group recently compared to the first month or so of the season. Cole Bishop is so perfectly positioned in his box/blitz role that asks him to cover the slot underneath. He’s become a weapon as an addition to the pass rush, and his size plus explosiveness and strength allow the Bills to defend the run respectably in dime, if needed. Good early returns on Amani Hooker, as he’s allowed four catches for 47 yards with two pass breakups, nine total tackles, and a quarterback hit on three pass-rush snaps in his two contests with the Bills. And, heck, new safety No. 3, Damar Hamlin, had the biggest splash play of the group against Miami, an impressive interception at the intermediate level. Jordan Hancock played outstandingly in the safety/slot hybrid role, and the Bills even got Jalon Kilgore and Sam Franklin Jr. onto the field in this contest. Buffalo’s collection of safeties suddenly features top-end talent and serious depth. The defensive stinginess post-bye This section could be very long, but I’ll keep it short with the Bills short week ahead of the enormous clash with the Chiefs. The Bills defense has faced a legendarily bad collection of quarterbacks after the bye. And it has played legendarily good football. I don’t care if I was the quarterback for the Ravens, Vikings, Jets, or Dolphins… 43 consecutive drives without allowing a touchdown in the modern NFL is incredible. The defensive front is led by two serious stalwarts in Greg Rousseau and Deone Walker. The rotational pieces are playing soundly. The linebacker group is flying around. The cornerbacks hold their own. And I just raved about the play from the safety position. Of course, the five-game stretch that’ll likely go a long way in deciding the AFC’s No. 1 seed in the playoffs, begins now. And this defense will face a serious uptick in quarterback quality. But there’s no doubting Buffalo’s defense has drastically improved its play from where it was before the bye. Both can be true at the same time. Bills got serious WR1 and WR2 production! Now, said WR1 and WR2 were probably flipped from what Bills fan expect, but against the Dolphins, the Bills got five catches for 101 yards from Khalil Shakir and eight catches for 91 yards and a touchdown from D.J. Moore. Clearly, Joe Brady read the article I wrote last week about Shakir deserving more targets and put my suggestion into practice in Week 11. Here’s the updated figures on Shakir’s production when he gets more looks: [continuing push for Khalil Shakir to be more featured in Bills O] Shakir went 5-101 on 9 tgts vs. Miami He now has 11 career games w/ 8+ tgts & in four of them, he's eclipsed 100 yds In those contests he's avg'd – 6.7 catches – 76.7 yds That = 114 rec + 1,304 yd season pace — Chris Trapasso (@ChrisTrapasso) November 23, 2026 And Moore was as advertised, certainly worth the cost of a second-round pick, against the Dolphins. He was targeted 10 times and six of his snags went for first downs. He won against one-on-one man coverage on the outside. His presence is massive to this offense. And it showed in Week 11. Deep-depth players shined In an ideal world, the Bills starters would’ve sat for the entire fourth quarter, but this is the NFL, where even margins that appear big on paper typically aren’t quite as sizable in actuality on the field. We can’t forget, the Dolphins were only trailing by a touchdown, 17-10, entering the four quarter against the Chiefs in late September. And Miami got the score to 31-24 against the Bengals late in the fourth quarter a few weeks later. Anyway, the Bills were afforded the ability to play backups late in this game, and the deep depth got after it. Shaq Thompson looked shot out of a cannon on his snaps — and he actually played early in the second half. Kilgore had four tackles without a miss. Javon Solomon had two more pressures on just six pass-rush snaps. On that note, despite a tiny 35-snap sample, the third-year rotational edge rusher has a 17.1% pressure rate entering Week 12. Tre’Davious White had a pass breakup that drew a large roar from the crowd. And Maxwell Hairston had a knocked away a pass too in the second half. The reinforcements reinforced Buffalo’s defensive brilliance of late in this game. *One final note on this game — I LOVE that Brady showed a variety of different looks, including a trick play on special teams, the threat of another, and a gadget play on the end-around flea-flicker.
author: Chris Trapasso

title: Buffalo Bills RB James Cook III makes NFL history in Week 11
summary: Buffalo Bills running back James Cook III has spent much of the 2026 season putting together one of the most consistent stretches of rushing production in NFL history. With another strong performance against the Miami Dolphins on Sunday, Cook now has a place on the all-time leaderboard all to himself.  With Sunday’s performance, which included […]
full_text: ORCHARD PARK, NEW YORK - NOVEMBER 22: James Cook #4 of the Buffalo Bills runs the ball during the third quarter of a game against the Miami Dolphins at Highmark Stadium on November 22, 2026 in Orchard Park, New York. (Photo by Lauren Leigh Bacho/Getty Images) | Getty Images Buffalo Bills running back James Cook III has spent much of the 2026 season putting together one of the most consistent stretches of rushing production in NFL history. With another strong performance against the Miami Dolphins on Sunday, Cook now has a place on the all-time leaderboard all to himself. With Sunday’s performance, which included 89 rushing yards and a touchdown, Cook became just the second player in NFL history to rush for at least 75 yards and score a rushing touchdown in nine consecutive games, moving past three former NFL running backs who had each reached eight straight. Notably, he’s the only player in league history to put up those numbers in one season. James Cook III has now rushed for 75+ yards and a TD in 9 consecutive games, surpassing LaDainian Tomlinson (8 games in 2006) and John Riggins (8 games in 1983) for the longest single season streak in NFL history. pic.twitter.com/U4P8DTKExs — Buffalo Bills PR (@BuffaloBillsPR) November 22, 2026 Cook entered the game tied with Pro Football Hall of Famers John Riggins and LaDainian Tomlinson, along with George Rogers, for the second-longest streak in NFL history. Riggins accomplished the feat in 1983, Rogers did it across the 1985 and 1986 seasons, and Tomlinson matched them in 2006. The 27-year-old Cook joined that group during Buffalo’s Week 10 victory over the New York Jets. He rushed for 157 yards on 18 carries, including a career-long 74-yard touchdown run in the second half of the Bills’ 31-12 win. Now, only Terry Allen stands ahead of Cook. Allen reached 10 consecutive games with at least 75 rushing yards and a touchdown while playing for Washington across the 1995 and 1996 seasons. With nine straight games behind him, Cook is now within striking distance of a record that’s stood for 30 years, but the road won’t get any easier. Kansas City and New England are next on Buffalo’s schedule, and the dates next to those names are just as challenging as the opponents. The Bills have just three days to rest, recover, and prepare to host the Chiefs on Thanksgiving night. If Cook is going to catch Terry Allen, he’ll have to keep his streak alive through one of the toughest stretches of Buffalo’s season.
author: Rachel Auberger

title: Buffalo Bills OLB Greg Rousseau sets career high in sacks during 2026 season
summary: Buffalo Bills outside linebacker Greg Rousseau has reinvented himself this year. A new position, a new number, new coaches and an entirely new defensive scheme. And the results? Is it too early to start throwing around the word legendary?  Maybe, but Rousseau is certainly making a case for it. With two sacks against the Miami […]
full_text: ORCHARD PARK, NEW YORK - NOVEMBER 22: Kyle McCord #14 of the Miami Dolphins is sacked by Greg Rousseau #15 of the Buffalo Bills for an 8-yard loss during the first quarter at Highmark Stadium on November 22, 2026 in Orchard Park, New York. (Photo by Bryan M. Bennett/Getty Images) | Getty Images Buffalo Bills outside linebacker Greg Rousseau has reinvented himself this year. A new position, a new number, new coaches and an entirely new defensive scheme. And the results? Is it too early to start throwing around the word legendary ? Maybe, but Rousseau is certainly making a case for it. With two sacks against the Miami Dolphins on Sunday, Rousseau has officially entered uncharted territory in his NFL career. His 10 sacks this season are a new personal best. Greg Rousseau is up to 9 sacks on the year, establishing a new career-high and marking the most sacks by a Bill in the first 10 games of a season since Lorenzo Alexander (10 sacks) in 2016. pic.twitter.com/4ZHZAZirZj — Buffalo Bills PR (@BuffaloBillsPR) November 22, 2026 Rousseau sacked Miami quarterback Kyle McCord for an eight-yard loss that forced the Dolphins to punt after a five-play first drive. Then in the second quarter, it was an almost identical play. Rousseau dropped McCord for another eight-yard loss. Greg Rousseau is now up to 10 sacks on the season. Today marks Rousseau’s fourth game of the year with 2+ sacks, the most multi-sack games by any player in the NFL this season. pic.twitter.com/gnKnwxEDCH — Buffalo Bills PR (@BuffaloBillsPR) November 22, 2026 Rousseau entered the NFL in 2021 as a defensive end, spending his first five seasons in Sean McDermott’s defensive system. Along the way, he worked under Leslie Frazier, McDermott himself, and Bobby Babich as defensive leaders, while learning from defensive line coaches Eric Washington and Marcus West. Then came 2026, and just about everything changed. Jim Leonhard took over as defensive coordinator, bringing a new scheme that moved Rousseau from defensive end to outside linebacker. Bobby April III became his new position coach, giving Rousseau his third position coach and fourth defensive leader in six NFL seasons. Somehow, through all that change, Rousseau is putting together the most productive season of his career. He recorded four sacks as a rookie in 2021, eight in 2022, five in 2023, eight again in 2024 and seven last season. Those eight-sack performances had been his personal best until Sunday. Of course, Rousseau didn’t exactly ease into his new role — he came roaring in right from the start. He opened the season with three consecutive two-sack games, becoming the first player in Bills history to accomplish that feat. Only two other players in NFL history had ever done it. For a player who spent the offseason learning a different position in a new defense, the transition has looked remarkably smooth. With seven games remaining, Rousseau has already accomplished something he hadn’t managed in any of his previous five seasons. The question now isn’t whether the changes worked. It’s just how far Rousseau can take them.

title: Buffalo Bills improve to NFL-best 9-1 with 26-9 over Miami Dolphins
summary: In the immediate aftermath of the Buffalo Bills’ Week 11 win over the Miami Dolphins, many will scratch their heads wondering what they watched unfold Sunday afternoon. To be clear her: What a strange win by the Bills. Buffalo’s offense barely resembled the group most have watched in 2026. It’s important to step back a […]
full_text: ORCHARD PARK, NEW YORK - NOVEMBER 22: James Cook III #4 of the Buffalo Bills runs up the middle for a one-yard touchdown against the Miami Dolphins during the second quarter at Highmark Stadium on November 22, 2026 in Orchard Park, New York. (Photo by Bryan M. Bennett/Getty Images) | Getty Images In the immediate aftermath of the Buffalo Bills’ Week 11 win over the Miami Dolphins, many will scratch their heads wondering what they watched unfold Sunday afternoon. To be clear her: What a strange win by the Bills. Buffalo’s offense barely resembled the group most have watched in 2026. It’s important to step back a moment, however, and realize that Buffalo has built a good, often great team. The Bills haven’t trailed in a game since October 18 against the Las Vegas Raiders ( hat tip: Carson Hayek ). Buffalo has also won three consecutive games by 17 or more points. What about the defense? Well, that group hasn’t allowed a touchdown in three straight games. It may be true that the Bills didn’t execute their most impressive game plan of the season, and that they strayed too far away from their true identity until crunch time. It’s clear that quarterback Josh Allen didn’t have his typically dominant effort against the Dolphins, even though he did throw for 304 yards, but he didn’t need to play lights out. Interestingly, Allen attempted zero rushes. In fact, during a first-half 4th & 1 situation, Allen handed the ball off to running back James Cook III, who scampered through the right side of the line to move the chains. The intent seemed clear that the move was to avoid exposing Allen to unnecessary contact, at least. That move can only work so well when you ask the quarterback to drop back 45 times. As a result, Miami’s defense hit Allen six times, sacking him on three occasions. Most believed that Buffalo would use their dominant rushing attack to try and wear down the Dolphins’ trio of backup defensive tackles in the first half. It was tough sledding early, perhaps surprisingly to Brady and the offense, and Cook had just 13 carries for 36 yards and a touchdown at halftime. Allen was forced into two consecutive interceptions late in the second quarter, with a third erased due to penalty. Then consider the decisions on special teams. First there was the surprising fake punt that proved successful thanks to a pretty 30-yard throw and completion by rookie punter Tommy Doman Jr. Doubling down on surprise (as much as is possible in today’s rulebook), the Bills then decided to declare an onside kick attempt after a score. Analyst Adam Archuleta wondered if they saw something on film to warrant the try, and if they’d take the delay-of-game penalty instead of running it. We know now, they didn’t attempt the onside try. As has been the case in so many games this season, the second half was a different story on offense. The return to form just took a bit longer. Late in the fourth quarter, Archuleta mentioned the curious shift in game plan on offense. Understandably, they had entered four-minute offense territory, but the point was well-understood as a discourse on their pass-heavy approach early in action. The Bills looked like the better team all game long, but it also seemed like they missed out on a lot of points they’d otherwise score. They don’t call the NFL a week-to-week league for nothing, and divisional games are always tough to predict regardless of record and any familiarity (or lack thereof) with the opponent. I keep being called back to the strangeness of this game. Is it possible they were using Week 11 as an opportunity to put a fair amount of new things/alternate tendencies on tape for the gauntlet facing them the next month? Certainly, there’s potential for it to be the case. It’s true that Buffalo has a very short week to prepare for the 8-2 Kansas City Chiefs, which could have played into the offensive game plan when you consider Allen’s shift to playing dropback, quick-release football from the pocket — that also erased him from the rushing column. I’m not the only one to consider this move, as evidenced by a tweet from ESPN Bills beat reporter Nick Suss that wondered if they were “giving the Chiefs a crapton of looks they have to prepare for on a short week, even if the Bills don’t plan on using any of them again on Thursday.” Is it possible that situation played into the decisions made in Week 11? Again, One Bills Drive will never admit to it, and rightfully so, but it’s possible that they used today’s game as an opportunity to stress KC’s pre-game load ahead of Thursday night. True or otherwise, it’s difficult to spend too much time ripping apart a team that blows out its opponent, while covering the enormous 16.5-point spread. The Bills continue looking really good even on off days, and Buffalo once again prove to be too much to handle for the Dolphins. You could say that about most of their opponents right now. Will that be the case Thursday? We’ll find out if the Bills can add to the right kind of “just deserts” for your Thanksgiving Day celebration!
author: Matt Byham

title: Bills vs. Dolphins Week 11 postgame analysis: Buffalo’s win never in doubt
summary: The Buffalo Bills (9-1) beat the Miami Dolphins (1-9) at Highmark Stadium, their sixth straight win and the third game in a row without allowing a touchdown. Buffalo finished with 405 total yards to Miami’s 185. Here are my notes from the game, taken as it happened. 1st Half 2nd Half Final Thoughts Buffalo did […]
full_text: ORCHARD PARK, NEW YORK - NOVEMBER 22: James Cook III #4 of the Buffalo Bills celebrates after scoring a touchdown in the second quarter against the Miami Dolphins at Highmark Stadium on November 22, 2026 in Orchard Park, New York. (Photo by Joe Hrycych/Getty Images) | Getty Images The Buffalo Bills (9-1) beat the Miami Dolphins (1-9) at Highmark Stadium, their sixth straight win and the third game in a row without allowing a touchdown. Buffalo finished with 405 total yards to Miami’s 185. Here are my notes from the game, taken as it happened. 1st Half Bills get the ball to start the game again (10th straight game opening with the possession). Start with their usual run first/PA offense. They certainly believe they came to impose their will today. Several play-action rollouts from Josh Allen in this first drive. The run game has been contained so far (Buffalo finished with 95 rushing yards on 27 carries, 3.5 yards per carry). That run from James Cook from the FB position is a good addition to the playbook. Tough play to stop. Blocks in the interior remind me of the way they block for the tush push (Cook: 22 carries, 89 yards, 1 TD). Josh Allen is sacked on 3rd down. Free rusher from inside, really? Tyler Bass’ FG is good, 3-0 Bills (Allen was sacked 3 times in the game). Bills defense starts hot again , containing the Dolphins’ run game and leaving the field on 3rd down. Davison Igbinosun is playing great ball at the moment (Miami punted on every first-quarter drive). Another offensive drive and the heavy PA game continues. However, players aren’t getting open downfield, and Josh is forcing it. A fake punt pass by Tommy Doman, great completion for a 1st down. Keleki Latu with the reception. From their own 20, I don’t like it. Unnecessary and very risky (30-yard completion; the Bills never punted all game). Josh forces a deep pass outside and flirts with an INT. I like it, though. A high pass to Keon Coleman? It’s supposed to be a bigger chance of a big play than an INT. Another FG with the run game not working and the pass catchers not being able to create separation. Bills 6-0 (Bass: 54-yard FG). The defense continues to play really well. Another impressive drive. Got lucky on 3rd down, though. Chris Bell has to catch that perfect pass by Kyle McCord, deep. Damar Hamlin and Cole Bishop clearly beat on the play, but the rookie bubbled it (McCord: 12-of-33, 102 yards, 36.4% completion rate). Josh Allen starts to take the checkdowns available to him, and it makes all the difference in the world. The offense is moving downfield easily (Ty Johnson: 7 catches on 8 targets, 55 yards). DJ Moore is so important. No hesitation by Josh throwing to him (Moore: 8 catches, 91 yards, 1 TD). Josh misses Dawson Knox on a check-and-release route, already in the red zone. It would’ve been a walk-in TD to the veteran TE. He had nobody ahead of him. Very next play, TD Bills. Josh makes up for the previous misfire, finds Moore on a crossing route in the back of the endzone (4-yard TD, capping a 12-play, 79-yard drive). XP is good. 13-0 Bills. Dolphins finally can move down the field a bit, starting with great field position from their kick return. Run game could move the sticks a bit and put them in FG range. 13-3 Bills (Daniel Carlson, 52-yard FG; Miami had 6 kick returns for 159 yards). Good to see Tre’Davious White back for some snaps. Wanna see the same with Shaq Thompson. Those vets can be valuable depth pieces late in the season or even in the playoffs. Also great to see rookies like Kaleb Elarms-Orr and Davison Igbinosun playing better and better as the year progresses. DJ Moore is so reliable. Great catch on 3rd and 12. 1st down. Keon Coleman with a catch-and-run on a quick slant, getting very physical with the YAC. Love to see it. After forcing it and almost getting intercepted, Josh quickly recognizes Ty Johnson open in the flat and delivers it, the RB does the rest. 1st and goal Buffalo. James Cook punches it in. 20-3 Bills (1-yard TD, capping an 11-play, 57-yard drive; Cook went over 1,000 rushing yards for the season). Another 3-and-out by the defense. The opponents they’re facing are questionable for sure, but we can’t deny how good they’ve looked recently. Deone Walker is a nightmare for IOLs, and Ed Oliver is too quick on one-on-ones. Greg Rousseau has really become a top edge rusher, and the miscommunication issues are gone. Impressive (Bills defense: 2 sacks, 8 QB hits, 5 tackles for loss, and 3 three-and-outs forced; Rousseau had 2 sacks, 10 on the season, a career high). Great play by the Dolphins’ young duo. Chop Robinson beats Spencer Brown inside and gets to Josh’s face, hitting his arm as he throws. The ball goes up, and Jacob Rodriguez intercepts it. Worse than the INT is DJ Moore getting hurt on the play, with what looked like a nasty ankle sprain. Despite great field position, the Dolphins offense can’t generate anything. DeWayne Carter, Greg Rousseau, and Deone Walker with incredible plays in a row. FG is good. 20-6 Bills (Carlson, second 52-yard FG; he went 3-for-3 on the day). DJ Moore is back and makes a huge catch after Allen shakes Chop Robinson off his shoes. Bills close to FG range. 3rd and 10, Josh throws an awful INT in the middle of the field. The safety was sitting there in the cover 3. The Dolphins give the Bills the ball back, great play by Damar Hamlin. INT, Bills get the ball back in the middle of the field (Hamlin’s first interception of the season). What is Josh doing here? Forces it deep, and it’s intercepted again. A foul on the play gives the Bills an extra chance. Screen from Josh to Moore gives them a few yards, but that’s it. End of the 1st half. 20-6 Bills (Allen finished with 2 interceptions officially). 2nd Half Miami starts well. Good run by Ollie Gordon II, and a good completion by McCord to Caleb Douglas put them in the red zone (the Dolphins gained more yards on that first drive of the 2nd half than in the entire first half). Igbinosun was turned around by Douglas on that slant . Luckily, the Dolphins WR dropped it. Would’ve been a TD. Another stand by the Bills D. Dolphins FG is good. 20-9 Bills (Carlson, 27 yards). Bills D in a historic run without allowing TDs right now. More than 35 consecutive drives doing so (third straight game without allowing a touchdown; the Dolphins finished with 185 total yards and 3.4 yards per play). The run game starts to work better, but the passing game continues to struggle. Josh doesn’t look good, and nobody other than Moore can get open (Allen: 27-of-45, 304 yards, 1 TD, 2 INT). Tyler Bass’ FG is no good. 20-9 Bills and, with the way they’ve played, they’re giving these Dolphins a chance to believe (Bass finished 4-of-5 on field goals). Buffalo’s D continues to dominate. Great play by Cole Bishop on 3rd down here. Punt. Khalil Shakir with some good plays for the Bills on this drive (Shakir: 5 catches, 101 yards). Penalties are killing the offense right now. Josh escapes a sack and completes a pass to Shakir to, at least, put Bass in better FG range. His FG is good. 23-9 Bills. End of the 3rd (Bills: 7 penalties for 48 yards). Delay of game on the kickoff. This is new for me. Did they declare going for an onside kick here? Weird. Ollie Gordon II continues to find some success running the football (Miami: 20 carries, 99 yards, 5.0 yards per carry). Shaq Thompson in for Terrel Bernard in this drive. Dee Alford, after getting beat by the same route early on another 4th down in this same drive, makes the play to close this drive on a 4th down. Buffalo ball (the Bills defense got 2 fourth-down stops). Good offensive drive to (practically) close the game. Buffalo has almost 15 more minutes of ball possession than the Dolphins. It hasn’t been pretty or exciting, but it has been efficient (time of possession: 36:45 to 23:15; 25 first downs to 10). 4th and goal, 2 min warning. Bass FG is good. 26-9 Bills (28 yards). Bills’ D forces 4th down but can’t get out of the field there. Great…
