title: Buffalo Bills stock report in hard-fought win Miami Dolphins
summary: The Buffalo Bills outlasted the Miami Dolphins this week, winning 26-9 in what was an ugly, hard-fought game. Divisional contests are never easy, so I was instantly wary of the 16.5-point spread given Buffalo’s 8-1 record and Miami’s 1-8 record entering play. While the Bills never seemed to be in jeopardy of losing this afternoon, […]
full_text: ORCHARD PARK, NEW YORK - NOVEMBER 22: James Cook III #4 of the Buffalo Bills jogs onto the field before the game against the Miami Dolphins at Highmark Stadium on November 22, 2026 in Orchard Park, New York. (Photo by Joe Hrycych/Getty Images) | Getty Images The Buffalo Bills outlasted the Miami Dolphins this week, winning 26-9 in what was an ugly, hard-fought game. Divisional contests are never easy, so I was instantly wary of the 16.5-point spread given Buffalo’s 8-1 record and Miami’s 1-8 record entering play. While the Bills never seemed to be in jeopardy of losing this afternoon, they definitely did not play as well as they could have. Miami’s scrappy defense fought hard, giving Buffalo’s high-powered offense trouble throughout the afternoon. At the end of the day, a win is a win whether it’s pretty or ugly, and an ugly win is far preferable to a pretty loss. There were plenty of positives to glean from today’s contest, but there were definitely some negatives, as well. Here are our horns up and horns down for Buffalo’s victory over Miami. _____________________________________________________________________________ Horns Up: Greg Rousseau In what has already been a career year, Rousseau just added to his growing stat line today. In the first half, he was an absolute menace, totaling two sacks and pressuring quarterback Kyle McCord consistently. The two sacks brought Rousseau into double-digits for the first time in his career, as he entered the day with eight. The switch to Jim Leonhard’s 3-4 front has maximized Rousseau’s ability, and he continues to shine in what is likely to be his first Pro Bowl season, and potentially his first All Pro season. Rousseau finished the game with three tackles in addition to those two sacks. Horns Up: DJ Moore Buffalo’s top wideout was the brightest spot in the passing game, especially in the first half. Moore saw seven targets in the first half, catching all of them for 79 yards and a score. Moore also had an injury scare late in the second half, as he seemed to hyperextend his knee while trying to play defense on a batted pass that was ultimately intercepted by linebacker Jacob Rodriguez. Moore was quarterback Josh Allen’s go-to guy on third downs, making plays to extend drives when Buffalo needed him most. He ultimately finished the game with 8 catches for 91 yards and a score on 10 targets. Horns Down: Josh Allen Sometimes, I really don’t know what Allen is looking at during games. Sure, Allen’s first interception came on a batted ball where right tackle Spencer Brown was beaten by Chop Robinson. The second one, though, was a pure force where he tried to hit Khalil Shakir over the middle. He didn’t see safety Zayne Anderson, who made the interception. Allen had a third interception negated by a penalty on a similarly boneheaded throw, as he hurled the ball down field into a sea of teal. For much of the first half, it looked like Allen was trying to hit on big plays repeatedly rather than progressing through his reads. There were far too many unnecessary forces and unforced errors from Allen today. He’s going to need to be much, much better on Thursday if Buffalo wants a shot at beating the Kansas City Chiefs. Allen surpassed 300 yards on the day, completing 27-of-45 passes for 304 yards, 1 touchdown, and 2 interceptions on the day. Horns Up: Tyler Bass Bass nailed his first two kicks, staying perfect in field goals on the season. He made a 43-yard field goal to cap Buffalo’s first drive, and he hit a 54-yard kick to end Buffalo’s second drive. He made his lone extra point attempt in the first half, as well. He missed his first kick of the season to kick off the third quarter, as he hooked another 54-yard attempt wide to the left. I didn’t expect him to be perfect all season, so I won’t dog him about finally missing one. After Bass missed the entire 2025 season due to a core muscle injury, it’s been great to watch Bass be nearly automatic this season. He made two more field goals in the second half, so he was 4-of-5 on the day, adding two PATs to his ledger. Horns Up: Tommy Doman Jr. Let’s go beyond the great kickoffs here. In the first quarter, Doman threw a beautiful pass to tight end Keleki Latu on a fake punt, extending Buffalo’s second drive and allowing them to kick a field goal. I joked to my dad that it was the best pass of the game, and while it definitely was at that point, it really may have been one of the better throws that happened in the game. It was a 30-yard completion for Doman, who just added another positive to what has been a strong rookie season. Horns Up: Maxwell Hairston Hairston came in from Cheektowaga to break up a third-down pass on Miami’s first drive of the second half, keeping Miami out of the end zone and forcing a field goal attempt. Hairston started on the far side of the field, trailed his man all across the grass, and broke up the throw on the near side. It was a really nice play overall, and while it might have gone as a footnote for other players, it was great to see the second-year man have a positive impact on today’s game. His counterpart, rookie Davison Igbinosun, was solid again, as well. Buffalo’s cornerback depth was tested today, and with the caveat that it came against backups quarterback Kyle McCord, the cornerback depth passed that test. Hairston finished with one tackle and that pass breakup. Horns Down: O’Cyrus Torrence On Buffalo’s first drive, Torrence slid outside and let Jordyn Brooks burst through the middle untouched for a sack on Josh Allen. In the third quarter, Torrence jumped for a false start penalty one play after left tackle Dion Dawkins committed a holding penalty, pushing Buffalo even farther away from the end zone and a potential first down. On the whole, Buffalo’s offensive line struggled against a feisty Dolphins front. Torrence, in particular, seemed to struggle. Horns Up: Khalil Shakir It’s a constant refrain in my house that Shakir needs the football more. My wife, in particular, calls him the team’s most underutilized offensive piece. Today, Shakir went over 100 yards receiving for the sixth time in his career including playoff games. It could have been an even better day, but he dropped a pass early in the first quarter where he was covered tightly, but the ball hit him right in the chest. Making sure that Shakir stays involved should be an essential action for the offense moving forward, as he is one of the league’s best after the catch, and he can do plenty of damage down field, as well. Shakir finished with 5 catches for 101 yards; he also had two rushing attempts for two yards on lateral swing-passes. Horns Down: Overall Entertainment What an ugly football game this was. The Bills were sloppy, and while Miami was gritty, they don’t have the offensive firepower to have threatened too seriously throughout. Horns Up: Greg Dortch Not only was he excellent on kickoff returns again, returning one try for 36 yards and another for 37, but he executed the fake punt catch to perfection once again. Instead of giving the Dolphins a chance at downing a punt inside Buffalo’s 10-yard line, Dortch settled in, made it look like he was going to make a catch, and then he watched the ball fly harmlessly over his head. It bounced at the two and went right into the end zone, giving the Bills the ball at the 20 instead of in a terrible spot. Buffalo’s special teams has been good in general, but Dortch in particular has been excellent. Horns Up: Damar Hamlin Buffalo’s veteran safety made a big play late in the first half, intercepting a Kyle McCord pass to keep the Dolphins from scoring before halftime. On the play, Hamlin laid a big hit on Chris Bell, who got JACKED UP and was examined for a chest injury. Hamlin was correctly ruled down by contact, but it was a great play to hang onto the ball after a big collision with Chris Bell, from? Louisville! Bell, fortunately, was okay after the big hit. Hamlin finished with just that interception on the stat…
author: Sean Murphy

title: The Optimist: Eight days to clean up after a weird win
summary: I’m curious how the Carolina Panthers are going to show up against the Tampa Bay Buccaneers, on the road and in primetime, next Monday night. How they respond to their worst loss of the season while reeling from their current two-game winning streak will tell us a lot about who the Panthers are going to […]
full_text: CHARLOTTE, NORTH CAROLINA - NOVEMBER 22: Bryce Young #9 of the Carolina Panthers looks on before the football game against the Baltimore Ravens at Bank of America Stadium on November 22, 2026 in Charlotte, North Carolina. (Photo by David Jensen/Getty Images) | Getty Images I’m curious how the Carolina Panthers are going to show up against the Tampa Bay Buccaneers, on the road and in primetime, next Monday night. How they respond to their worst loss of the season while reeling from their current two-game winning streak will tell us a lot about who the Panthers are going to be for the rest of the season. They have seven games remaining. Four of them are against non-divisional opponents. All four of those opponents—the 7-2 Minnesota Vikings, the 7-2 Cincinnati Bengals, the 6-4 Pittsburgh Steelers, and the 6-4 Seattle Seahawks—are either first or second in tight divisional races. Nothing is getting easier for the Panthers down the stretch. We would be spending a lot of time today discussing the nuances in the term “unnecessary roughness” if the Carolina Panthers defense had not managed to hold the Baltimore Ravens scoreless in the final minutes of their tight, wacky, and ultimately enjoyable game yesterday. Instead, the Panthers managed to win anyway. That is a feat that eluded them in close, awkwardly called games against the Denver Broncos and Green Bay Packers. If they want to be considered contenders in—or even make—the playoffs then they need that kind of behavior to become routine instead of remarkable. In short, their current Jekyll and Hyde routine needs to change. What I liked. . . Will Lee III Let’s take a moment to marvel at a rookie cornerback, who had missed the last two and a half games and corresponding weeks of practice with a hamstring injury, stepping right back into a starting role and making multiple game changing plays. We might have expected that of somebody like Jaycee Horn who made an argument for himself in college as a top ten pick in the NFL Draft. Lee, on the other hand, was the 129th overall pick in the 2026 NFL draft. A fourth rounder saved a a touchdown by forcing a fumble for a touchback, deflected a bad decision by Jacoby Brissett into the ready hands of Tyrel Dodson for the game-sealing interception, and pulled down an ultimate stat line of four tackles, one pass deflected, and two forced fumbles. There are some aggression-related penalties to clean up in his coverage, to be sure, but the kid is still a rookie. That he’s even in position to draw—what have honestly been questionable-at-best—pass interference flags suggests the Panthers may be have an embarrassment of riches in their secondary. The rest of the defense Todd Wash’s defense surrendered 25 of the 33 points that the Ravens scored yesterday. The game wouldn’t have been nearly as close without a special teams miscue and the offense falling apart around their own goal line. The first half was rough, and the team clearly misses having Bobby Okereke in the middle next to Devin Lloyd, but adjustments were made. The Ravens had five possessions in the second half, resulting in two punts, a fumble, a touchdown, and an interception. That’s fine work overall. Mike Jackson had a great game in his first week back from injured reserve. Princely Umanmielen stepped up in the fourth quarter. Tre’Von Moehrig stepped up after a few down weeks. Overall, this was a step forward for a unit that has been trying to find its feet ever since the Tampa Bay Buccaneers knocked them down in Week 7. The tight ends, again The Panthers have been struggling to find their wide receivers for a few weeks now and that has hardly stopped them on offense. Offensive coordinator Brad Idzik and quarterback Bryce Young turned to the team’s surprisingly deep group of tight ends and have quickly begun making lemonade. Mitchell Evans, Darren Waller, and Tommy Tremble combined for nine receptions for 104 yards on nine targets. That was the bulk of Young’s passing in the first half. Success there opened things up for Tetairoa McMillan and Jalen Coker to see more targets in the second. Receivers ultimately combined for 12 receptions, 143 yards, and a touchdown on 20 targets. Many of those missed targets came on stalled drives in the first half, while the completions were largely in the second half after both teams managed adjustments. The Panthers are learning to play to their talent and stress opposing defenses in multiple ways and it is keeping them on the field. I’d prefer a balanced attack that can find the receivers and the tight ends throughout the game, but adaptation is how teams win. I’m thrilled to see the Panthers doing it in season and in game. Chuba Hubbard Kudos again to the engine of this offense. 27 carries for 120 yards, two touchdowns, and and a two-point conversion run are nothing to sneeze at. Hubbard combines violence with patience in a way that is simply beautiful to watch sometimes. Go back and watch his two-point conversion play. It doesn’t happen without Hubbard taking a beat to let the play in front of him develop. Penalty Progress The presnap penalty palooza of weeks passed slowed down against the Ravens. They had three penalties total in the first half and one of those was a false start on Torricelli Simpkins who was in for an injured Robert Hunt for about one whole play. That stuff happens. The Panthers ended with six penalties for 54 yards, including a handful of highly questionable pass interference and unnecessary roughness flags. Nature is healing. What I didn’t. . . Short yardage play calling, again The Panthers continue to get ahead of themselves when they don’t have very far to go. Yesterday they were 3/8 when they had three or fewer yards to gain. The five failures were split fairly evenly between rushes and pass attempts, with the glaring sin being Young’s goal-line interception. They escaped yesterday, but this once again threatened to make the difference if the Ravens had been a slightly better team. The Tampa Bay Buccaneers next week, the Minnesota Vikings the week after, the Cincinnati Bengals in Week 14, the Pittsburgh Steelers in Week 15, and the Seattle Seahawks in Week 16 all threaten to be better teams. The rushing defense Derrick Henry, who has clearly lost at least one step, averaged 7.2 yards per carry. Justice Hill, a career back up and return man, averaged 11.5 yards per carry. Up next are Bucky Irving and the Bucs who averaged only 5.4 yards per carry en route to 258 yards rushing against many of these same Panthers in Week 7. This is more than just missing Okereke and Mike Jackson being back won’t make every difference in the world. The Panthers cannot count on Lee forcing another fumble-for-a-touchback-miracle to save a touchdown and the game. What is Bryce. . . Bryce Young threw for a career-high 173 yards under pressure against the Ravens, completing 10 of 15 passes with 2 TDs and an INT. Young led his 14th career game-winning drive, tied for the most by a QB age 25 or younger since at least 1950. @BALvsCAR | #KeepPounding pic.twitter.com/X9HkXey0P8 — Next Gen Stats (@NextGenStats) November 22, 2026 Young’s career is turning into the embodiment of the phrase “two things can be true.” When the offensive line gave Young time yesterday, things didn’t always go well for the Panthers. Look no further than series where Young surrendered a safety to see bad decisions compounded by time to over-analyze the field. Extra time can be multiplied by superior athleticism, but apparently it can also be diminished without it. Yes, John Metchie had a bad drop on that series, but that third down was all Bryce. However, you also cannot deny that the man can remain cool and collected under pressure. He honestly seems to play best when forced to make a relatively quick decision. Of course, that relies on his receivers to get open quickly. The seeds of a good player are there. Young remains a top 8 statistical passer in the league through Week 11. That’s enough to give him…

full_text: CHARLOTTE, NC - OCTOBER 25: Carolina Panthers quarter back Bryce Young (9) fumbles the ball in a pass attempt from a hit by Tampa Bay Buccaneers Payne Durham (87) during an NFL football game between the Tampa Bay Buccaneers and the Carolina Panthers on October 25, 2026 at Bank of America Stadium in Charlotte, N.C. (Photo by John Byrum/Icon Sportswire via Getty Images) | Icon Sportswire via Getty Images The Carolina Panthers have accomplished a first under head coach Dave Canales: they have won two games in a row that they were favored in. Two-game winning streaks are rare in recent Panthers history, but nowhere near as rare as the all-impressive three-game winning streak. That kind of thing hasn’t been seen in these parts since Weeks 1-3 of the 2021 NFL season. They have the opportunity to return to winning ways this week on the road against the Tampa Bay Buccaneers, but only if they can overcome the relatively short odds that favor the Bucs this week. Check out FanDuel for all your sportsbook needs . Week 11 Spread : Panthers: +2.5 (-105) Buccaneers: -2.5 (-115) O/U 44.5 (-110/-110) Moneyline Panthers: +120 Buccaneers: -142 Inconsistent performances and weird luck make you a road underdog against a divisional opponent with nearly half your win total, I guess. Both the Bucs and the Panthers have had seasons marked by significant injuries and both teams look to be getting healthier as they approach December. The Panthers have returned Mike Jackson and Will Lee III to their secondary and will, hopefully, return Brady Christensen and Jonathon Brooks to their offense next week. full_text: CHARLOTTE, NORTH CAROLINA - OCTOBER 25: Baker Mayfield #6 of the Tampa Bay Buccaneers greets Bryce Young #9 of the Carolina Panthers after a football game at Bank of America Stadium on October 25, 2026 in Charlotte, North Carolina. title: Panthers vs Ravens: Recap and reaction
summary: It wasn’t always pretty, but the Carolina Panthers were able to make just enough plays to come away with a 35-33 win over the Ravens. First Quarter It was a disaster start for the Panthers. The defense did their job and forced a three and out on the first drive, punt the punt took a […]
full_text: CHARLOTTE, NORTH CAROLINA - NOVEMBER 22: Chuba Hubbard #30 of the Carolina Panthers scores a touchdown against the Baltimore Ravens during the second quarter of the game at Bank of America Stadium on November 22, 2026 in Charlotte, North Carolina. (Photo by Grant Halverson/Getty Images) | Getty Images It wasn’t always pretty, but the Carolina Panthers were able to make just enough plays to come away with a 35-33 win over the Ravens. First Quarter It was a disaster start for the Panthers. The defense did their job and forced a three and out on the first drive, punt the punt took a Ravens bounce and stopped inside the five yard line. Things went south after that. John Metchie dropped a first down pass. Two plays later, Young froze in the pocket a bit and was tripped up for a safety. On the second play of the ensuing Ravens possession, they lined Justice Hill up in the wildcat. He ran a sort of reverse to Jacoby Brissett. Zakee Wheatley got caught with his eyes in the backfield, and he let Rashod Bateman run free for an easy deep touchdown. Trevor Etienne ran the kickoff back out to the 50 yard line, but the offense once again did nothing. Chuba Hubbard had a couple of okay runs, but Young continued to look uncomfortable. It was another punt, this time after one first down. It went into the endzone, which started the Ravens next drive on the 20 yard line. They worked their way down the field with an extended drive that featured a lot of quick passes, screens, and runs. The defense kept everything in front but couldn’t get off the field on third downs until the Ravens got all the way to the 10 yard line. They were able to take advantage of the condensed field and force a field goal to make it 12-0. Chuba Hubbard started the ensuing drive with a powerful run for eight yards. That was followed by a deep shot to Jalen Coker for 35 yards. On the next play, the Panthers ran almost the same trick play that the Ravens scored with, and they also scored on it with a deep pass to Mitchell Evans to end the first quarter. Second Quarter The Ravens picked up a big chunk with a pass to Zay Flowers over the middle to get moving again. A couple of plays later, Justice Hill broke free for what looked like a touchdown run. Will Lee caught him around the 10 yard line, but Hill held him off with a stiff arm. At the last second before Hill crossed the goal line, Lee punched the ball out and it ricocheted through the back of the end zone for a touchback. The offense capitalized on the momentum by going three and out and punting the ball away. The Ravens wouldn’t let them off that easy though. LaJohntay Webster muffed the punt, and Brycen Tremayne was able to wrestle the ball away for the fumble recovery. This time the offense was able to take advantage. They handed the ball to Hubbard twice, and on the second one he was able to break free off the left side. He dove across the goal line without fumbling to put the Panthers up 14-10. Of course, the Ravens ran the kickoff back for a touchdown. There was a flag on the play, but the officials decided to pick it up without explaining what it was or why it was picked up. Trevor Etienne gave Chuba Hubbard a breather and broke a carry off right tackle for 19 yards. That came after a roughing the passer penalty, so the Panthers quickly found themselves in Ravens territory. Young found his tight ends for a couple of third down conversions and to move Carolina inside the ten. A couple plays later, he found Tetairoa McMillan in the middle of the field for a touchdown to put the Panthers back ahead. There was a penalty on the Ravens on the extra point, and the Panthers elected to accept the penalty to go for two from the one yard line. Young handed to Hubbard, who found space off the left side to make it 22-19 Panthers. The defense followed that with a wholly uncompetitive drive. They missed a series of tackles to let the Ravens pick up first downs on plays that looked like they weren’t going anywhere. Justice Hill was able to break free again, and this time he made it all the way to the endzone for a touchdown. The offense went nowhere and quickly punted it away. Webster muffed the punt again, but two different Panthers whiffed potential recoveries. The Ravens ended up on top of it on their own one yard line. The defense let them pick up a few large chunks of yards to get out to midfield. It could have been worse, but Rashod Bateman dropped an open pass that could have taken Baltimore into field goal range. Instead, the Ravens had to settle for a Hail Mary that went out the back of the endzone. Third Quarter The Panthers got the ball coming out of the half, and Anthony Tyus ran the kickoff out around the 40, which he had been doing most of the day. Hubbard continued to run the ball well, and he had a 26 yard carry that took the ball down to the three yard line. He punched it in two plays later. Jaelan Phillips blew up another Ravens trick play to put them behind the sticks. That led to the punt, and the Panthers offense was able to keep their momentum going. Bryce Young found Tetairoa McMillan for a long gain into Ravens territory. A couple of plays later, he completed a long pass over the middle to Darren Wallker to put the Panthers in goal to go. They couldn’t put points on the board though. Young threw an interception while trying to force a pass to McMillan in the back of the end zone. The defense made sure it didn’t hurt too bad. They forced a quick punt right back after a Princely Umanmielen sack on third down. After a first down, John Metchie took a bubble screen and ran it 19 yards into the red zone. The Panthers tried three straight runs, but Rasheed Walker didn’t seem to realize that. He pass blocked on the third down carry and basically backed into Hubbard’s lap, resulting in a three yard loss on the play. The Panthers settled for a Ryan Fitzgerald field goal. The third quarter ended with Devin Lloyd getting called for unnecessary roughness for diving on a diving player for the second straight week. Fourth Quarter On the second play out of the break, Brissett checked the ball down to Derrick Henry. Will Lee met him right at the catch and poked the ball away. It was originally ruled incomplete, but Dave Canales challenged and got the call overturned. The offense did their part and got Bryce Young sacked on the first two plays of the Panthers’ possession before promptly punting the ball back to a new returner. Sam Martin’s punt rolled down to the one yard line, but Malcolm DeWalt stepped on the goal line while picking the ball up while no one was around him, giving the Ravens a free touchback. Derrick Henry promptly ripped off a 19 yard run, then Derrick Brown got called for a very soft roughing the passer. Brown made a couple of stops to try to make up for it and force a fourth down, but the Ravens were able to pick it up with a crosser to Zay Flowers. Another completion in the middle of the field to Flowers converted a third down. On the next play, Derrick Henry ran through a couple of Panthers tacklers for a touchdown to put the Ravens ahead 33-32. The offense hopped back onto the back of Chuba Hubbard. He had a few more good runs, and Bryce Young converted a couple of third downs with completions to Tetairoa McMillan and Tommy Tremble. The two minute warning hit with the Panthers driving on the edge of the red zone. McMillan left the field with a lower body injury after the play. A couple plays later, Jalen Coker got mashed by a helmet to helmet hit. It wasn’t flagged, and the Panthers were charged for a timeout due to the injury. McMillan returned to the game, but Young’s pass to him on third down was tipped away. They had to settle for a Ryan Fitzgerald field goal to go up 35-33 with 1:47 to go. The Ravens had all three timeouts and that much time because of that no-call on the helmet to helmet hit. After a nine yard gain on first down, Princely Umanmielen sacked Jacoby Brissett to set up third and long. The Ravens got…

full_text: Photo by Logan Bowles/Getty Images | Getty Images Missing Bobby Okereke against the Derrick Henry-led Baltimore Ravens is sure to hurt, but it may get balanced out by returning Will Lee III and Mike Jackson. That will be the big story-line to watch for me in interim defensive coordinator Todd Wash’s third week at the helm of a healing defense. On the other side of the ball, we only have our eternal questions. Which version of Bryce Young shows up today? Why don’t we tell him every game is in Atlanta? Will Rasheed Walker place any other Panthers on IR this week? Not much new for these ho-hum Panthers. With the 3-6 New Orleans Saints facing the 7-1 Chicago Bears on the road, the 3-6 Tampa Bay Buccaneers visiting the 7-2 Detroit Lions, and the 3-7 Atlanta Falcons on their bye, the Panthers (2-1 against the NFC South) have the projected easiest week in the division. They could very well hold on to lead in the NFC South race with a loss today. That may seem somewhere between embarrassing and hilarious when compared to the NFC North. The Panthers would rank fifth behind the 6-4 Green Bay Packers in that widely lauded division, but consider this: Nobody else in football has to play every NFC South team twice, so maybe the whole South is just that tough. title: 10 Bears Takes: An 8-2 start, but the true test is next on a short week
summary: Following Sunday afternoon’s 21-13 victory, the Chicago Bears find themselves at 8-2 heading into a critical mid-season divisional matchup on Thanksgiving morning. For a second straight week, it was not pretty. Turnovers have continued to be an issue, and overall, they simply didn’t look like a team that 11.5 points should have favored. There’s no […]
full_text: CHICAGO, ILLINOIS - NOVEMBER 22: Jeffery Simmons #99 of the Chicago Bears celebrates a sack in the second quarter of the game against the New Orleans Saints at Soldier Field on November 22, 2026 in Chicago, Illinois. (Photo by John Fisher/Getty Images) | Getty Images Following Sunday afternoon’s 21-13 victory, the Chicago Bears find themselves at 8-2 heading into a critical mid-season divisional matchup on Thanksgiving morning. For a second straight week, it was not pretty. Turnovers have continued to be an issue, and overall, they simply didn’t look like a team that 11.5 points should have favored. There’s no questioning this team’s legitimacy as a contender, but with the heat about to turn up on their remaining seven games, better play must follow. With a short week ahead, we’ll blast through our 10 Bears Takes before we turn the page to the Detroit Lions on Thanksgiving. 1. Following their 21-13 victory over the New Orleans Saints, the Bears are riding high at 8-2 with two critical tests ahead. How will things look on a short week after back-to-back uninspiring performances with first place on the line? Coming into the game, the Bears closed as 11.5-point favorites. That line alone probably gave fans a sense of confidence, but to be fair, this has been a team that hasn’t trailed in five weeks. That said, this was the second straight week it was clear the Bears were the better team, yet they still failed to pull away from an inferior opponent. Some might see this mindset as nitpicky, and while that might be fair, this team has much higher expectations than simply a winning season and a playoff berth. When they traded for Jeffery Simmons (who we will talk about more in a few), they were signaling to the entire league (and fan base) that they believe they can win a Super Bowl now and in the near future. Now, don’t get me wrong– no team will play consistently good football over a 17-game season. Looking around the league, there are plenty of very good teams that don’t perform the way most expect a few times a year. That said, at least for the Bears, they’ve had two straight games where they aren’t playing well on offense, and more importantly, they are turning the ball over too much. The good news is that their defense is playing at a level where they can afford these growing pains while still winning games. That said, the offensive performances have dipped over the last few weeks, and that’s something they’ll need to figure out heading into the final seven games of the season. For as hot as the Bears have been (five wins in a row), the Lions are even hotter. Not only have they won six straight, but they’ve outscored their opponents by a +76 margin. We’ll dive more into the specific matchup later, but simply put, Chicago must play better football if they expect to come away with a win on Thursday afternoon. Both teams appeared relatively healthy coming out of Sunday’s games, so the war of attrition might not be as big a factor as it will be for other teams playing on a short week. Either way, the Bears must take a step forward and play cleaner football games over the next two weeks if they plan to win one (or both). The good news: Typically, the best teams in the league play at their highest level when the spotlight is the brightest. 2. The Bears have yet to trail in a game since Caleb Williams returned from his hamstring injury five games ago. The last time the Bears had this type of streak? 1985. No matter how you cut it, that’s impressive. Williams, like the entire offense, wasn’t at his best for a second straight game. Despite that, they did just enough to support a defense that keeps moving in the right direction. Admittedly, the offense hasn’t looked quite the same over the last two weeks, and part of that has been the passing game. Williams’ accuracy hasn’t been quite as good, and the offensive line isn’t holding up like they should in pass protection. Not having a consistent run game has been a notable issue, but even with all that in mind, they haven’t trailed in a game in close to 50 days. We all know what the offense is capable of, and maybe playing higher-level competition will bring out the best in them. At the beginning of the season, they were tasked with scoring 30-plus each game, or they might lose because the defense was playing so poorly. Week 5’s blowout loss at Lambeau Field was a prime example of both units playing at their absolute worst. Since then, the defense has been playing at a Top 10 level, and even when the offense has failed to score 30 points, they have built big leads and held on to them. Overall, the Bears haven’t been playing their best football, but in some ways, they’ve been playing the best complementary brand of football we’ve seen all year. Winning in different ways will serve them well down the stretch, and unlike last year, they haven’t had to conjure every ounce of good luck to finish off games. There’s still plenty to improve upon over these last seven contests, but sitting at 8-2 thanks to a five-game winning streak is about as good a start that any team could hope to mount. Their streak of not trailing in games will be heavily tested on Thursday against a Lions team that has rarely trailed during their six-game winning streak. 3. Jeffery Simmons came up with a hat trick on Sunday. The last time a Bears defensive tackle had three or more sacks? It’s been over a decade. Before Sunday, the last time a Bears defensive tackle registered three or more sacks was when Jeremiah Ratliff did it on October 19th in 2014. To be exact, it’s been 12 years, one month, and three days. Similar to many of the markers the Bears have been matching this season, it’s been a while. When general manager Ryan Poles traded two first-rounders (plus) for Simmons, the hope was that he would have enough of an impact to change the trajectory of their defense for years to come. Even in the most optimistic outlook, I’m not sure anyone in the organization could have foreseen the magnitude of impact the 29-year-old would have over his first three games with his new team. Since coming over from Tennessee, Simmons has five sacks, six tackles for loss, and 14 total tackles. Not only is he producing in the box score, but his presence has allowed his linemates around him to rack up numbers. The number of double-teams Simmons has seen has opened things up, especially for the likes of Montez Sweat and Austin Booker on the edge. In the three games with Simmons in Chicago, the defense has 13 sacks and a much higher pressure rate, while allowing only four points on most of those disruptions. Not only that, but the defense is giving up an average of 18 points per game and just under 304 yards per game. Opposing teams’ rushing efficiency has dipped, and quarterbacks are seeing much more pressure. Simply put, it’s proving the theory that all the Bears needed was a game-wrecker who would move everyone’s role down a notch and allow them to benefit from it. Since Simmons’ arrival in Week 8, the Bears have improved in EPA/dropback (-.24), pressure rate without blitzing (+2.6), sack rate (+1.8), and rushing success rate allowed (-6.7). The secondary still leaves some to be desired, but the Bears are still well on pace to have the best third-down percentage in NFL history. Assuming they can get Kyler Gordon back at some point over the next few weeks, and maybe even Coby Bryant at some point in December, it’s not hard to see a path to a true Top 7-10 defense. For now, we’ll just enjoy the impact Simmons has made and how much that will help them in the next few years. 4. Even with Kyle Monangai back in action against the Saints, the running game’s struggles persisted– why it might be time to look inward, namely at center Garrett Bradbury. It was good to see Monangai back in the lineup, and although he didn’t take a ton of snaps in his first game back in a month and a half, it was somewhat to be expected, especially with a short week ahead. That said, the…

title: Bears vs. Saints: Inside the Snap Counts, Stats, and What Was That Game Plan?
summary: Did this feel like a Chicago Bears preseason game plan to anyone else? I’m not saying Ben Johnson looked past the New Orleans Saints, but the offensive game plan was run-heavy and fairly generic, and Dennis Allen’s defensive game plan was fairly vanilla. Perhaps, with the short week ahead to face the Detroit Lions on […]
full_text: CHICAGO, ILLINOIS - NOVEMBER 22: Head coach Ben Johnson of the Chicago Bears runs onto the field after his team's win against the New Orleans Saints at Soldier Field on November 22, 2026 in Chicago, Illinois. (Photo by Geoff Stellfox/Getty Images) | Getty Images Did this feel like a Chicago Bears preseason game plan to anyone else? I’m not saying Ben Johnson looked past the New Orleans Saints, but the offensive game plan was run-heavy and fairly generic, and Dennis Allen’s defensive game plan was fairly vanilla. Perhaps, with the short week ahead to face the Detroit Lions on Thanksgiving, they spent some of last week’s prep on their NFC North rival because they were confident they could beat the Saints. Chicago’s running game had a few explosives, but it was mostly a plodding, grind-it-out day, and Johnson stuck with it because I think he wanted to keep the clock moving. After they went up 16 to 0, it seemed like Johnson never felt the Saints had a chance to come back, and with the way his defense was playing, he was content to coast to the 21 to 13 win. Speaking of the defense, Allen was content to rush four most of the day and force the Saints to methodically work their way down the field. According to Next Gen Stats, the “Bears defense generated 24 pressures and 6 sacks against the Saints, their most pressures in a game since Week 9, 2018. Five of Chicago’s sacks came with a four-man rush, tied for the second-most by any defense this season.” Even though the score was closer than we all expected, the Bears controlled this game from start to finish. The Saints made it a one-score game before the half, but the Bears forced a three-and-out on New Orleans’ first possession of the third quarter, then went on an 11-play, 63-yard drive that ended in a field goal to push it to 19 to 10. Again, I don’t think they looked past the Saints, but back up two scores, this coaching staff felt confident they could ride it out because they were the better team, which is why they (possibly) went into it with that game plan in the first place. Tight end Colston Loveland alluded to a lack of enthusiasm. “I think we started slow and we didn’t really have the enthusiasm, I feel like, on a couple drives and then had turnovers and penalties, which hurts,” he said in his postgame presser via ESPN’s Courtney Cronin . “But I think there’s some good to take away for sure, too. I think it’s just in the run game, finishing, straining. I had a couple I fell off of that could have been two, three, four more yards. So I think that’s the difference.” There wasn’t any panic from the sideline during the game, and even in Ben Johnson’s postgame presser, he didn’t give off a disappointed vibe. The Good, Better, Best locker room speech, which was low-key after the narrow win over the Buccaneers, felt just as upbeat and as fun as usual. Again, I don’t think they looked past the Saints; I think they gave the Saints the attention they felt they deserved, with an eye toward Thursday’s battle for the North. Back to the numbers… The Bears had more total yards (311 to 307), more first downs (18 to 17), and had a better time of possession (30:28 to 29:32). Chicago’s 311 yards is the fewest they’ve had in a win since September 28, 2026 when they only had 271 in a 25 to 24 win in Las Vegas over the Raiders. The Saints ran more plays (71 to 58) and had a better third-down conversion rate (47.1% to 41.7%). Both teams had two turnovers, and the Saints were flagged 7 times for 30 yards, while the Bears were flagged 3 times for 15. Let’s look at the Bears’ playing-time breakdown and a few individual stats from the game. OFFENSE Caleb Williams had a ball tipped into the air and intercepted, and he was sacked twice, but I thought he played a solid, low-risk game. He wasn’t asked to do much, but he made a few plays when he needed to, and scrambled when he had to. Kyle Monangai’s return didn’t jump-start the running game as we hoped, but he seemed to be on a pitch count. D’Andre Swift had the ball ripped out of his hands as he fell to the ground on a nice play by the defender, but that’s still his third fumble this season, tying a career high. Rookie Zavion Thomas had a 29-yard kickoff return, along with 86 yards on offense, and he’s beginning to look like a player worthy of more touches. He also looked really excited to talk with Tom Brady! After an impressive day vs the Saints, rookie @ftfzayy_ earned @TomBrady 's #LFG Player of the Game! @NFLonFOX @ChicagoBears pic.twitter.com/Y27pxawtHp — FOX Sports (@FOXSports) November 22, 2026 DEFENSE Jeffery Simmons had a great debut for the Bears, and his second game was more of the same, but yesterday against the Saints was incredible. According to Next Gen Stats , Simmons had 6 pressures in the game, and those came against four different Saints offensive linemen. All 6 pressures came in one-on-one matchups, tying for the most by a defensive tackle this season. He also lined up on the edge on two of his sacks. Montez Sweat recorded the first safety of his career, and this was Chicago’s first safety since Khalil Mack in 2020. Clark Phillips III got the start at nickel and picked up the first sack of his four-year career. Before this game, Jordan ven den Berg had only 2 total tackles on the season. Tory Taylor had 3 punts with a 46.7 average (40.0 net), with 2 dropped inside the twenty-yard line. Noah Sewell had 2 special teams tackles. title: Winning ugly is still winning, and the Bears will take it
summary: No matter what way you try to swing it, the Chicago Bears have now won five games in a row. They sit with an 8-2 record after their 21-13 win over the Saints on Sunday, and even though it wasn’t always pretty, it was effective, and they don’t factor for style points in the standings. […]
full_text: No matter what way you try to swing it, the Chicago Bears have now won five games in a row. They sit with an 8-2 record after their 21-13 win over the Saints on Sunday, and even though it wasn’t always pretty, it was effective, and they don’t factor for style points in the standings. The Bears got off to a hot start offensively coming out of their bye week, but they stumbled across the finish line the rest of the way there. However, their defense was able to smother the Saints’ passing attack all afternoon, which helped the Bears pick their fifth win in the six home games they’ve played all season. Here are some of my takeaways from Chicago’s victory. Jeffery Simmons is out of this world In each of his first two games with the Bears, Jeffery Simmons was able to prove his dominance in the stat sheet and on film. He had a sack in both of those games, and he made several key plays against the run before the bye week. Somehow, he had an even better game in Week 11, tallying three sacks in the Bears’ win over the Saints on Sunday. The NFL is made up of some of the best athletes in the world, and yet, Simmons finds a way to make offensive linemen look like mere children. His elite get-off speed, his play strength at the point of attack, and ability to work through double-team blocks all combine to make him a valuable asset for Chicago’s defense. His presence has elevated the likes of Montez Sweat, Austin Booker, and Devin Bush to make plays, and it’s no surprise that the team’s defense has been much better after acquiring him. Jeffery Simmons has elevated the Bears' defense since he joined the team in Week 8: – Significantly better against the pass and the run – Blitzing a lot less but getting the same amount of pressure – Sacking the QB about once every 10 dropbacks pic.twitter.com/AFRVdcgm8o — SūmerSports (@SumerSports) November 22, 2026 With a perfect 100.0 PFN DT Impact grade , Simmons is tied for the best analytical season by a defensive tackle since 1999, placing him amongst the likes of only Aaron Donald and Quinnen Williams. The Bears have been getting phenomenal return on their investment with him. The offense is experiencing Groundhog Day The Bears’ offense started out strong on Sunday. They made a field goal on their opening drive, and though their second drive ended in a turnover on downs, they moved the ball down the field and made it into field goal range before their failed fourth-down conversion. Their following two offensive drives resulted in touchdowns. However, once a Caleb Williams pass got deflected and intercepted in the second quarter, everything seemed to shut down for Chicago. For the record, I’m not blaming Williams for his interception. He made the right read to throw to Luther Burden on that play, and if he threw the ball any higher to avoid the defensive lineman’s deflection, Burden wouldn’t have been able to make the catch. Things just happen in football sometimes. But from then on, the Bears looked lifeless on offense. Ben Johnson relied heavily on a run game that didn’t work. The Saints’ run defense, which has been a weakness of theirs in 2026, swallowed up gaps, especially along the interior. Those problems in the trenches translated to pass protection, as Williams was sacked twice and blitzed heavily. Chicago didn’t have much of an answer from there, but luckily, the defense held up to ensure its lead could stay intact. The hot start and subsequent cooling off after an interception is exactly what happened two weeks ago in the Bears’ narrow win over the Buccaneers. That becoming a trend certainly wouldn’t become ideal. Chicago’s first-world problems I can complain about the Bears’ lack of offensive execution for much of the second half, and there are valid criticisms to be made about the offense’s performance. Expecting more from a team with Super Bowl aspirations isn’t being pessimistic; it’s just adjusting the standard to which you hold your teams. If you’re a little worried in the face of this win, I don’t blame you. But again, it’s a blessing that the Bears find themselves in this position to begin with. The fact that there’s uncertainty in the midst of a five-game winning streak in an 8-2 season shows just how far this franchise has come. Gone are the days of Matt Eberflus blowing leads with horrendous clock management and passive defense. Gone are the days of Matt Nagy running a stationary offense or John Fox trotting out the worst offenses known to mankind. It’s entirely reasonable to have a bad taste in your mouth after a narrow win over a three-win team like the Saints. But the fact that we’re over-analyzing these victories shows that the Bears are in a much better position than many other teams around the NFL. Even when things aren’t pretty, they’re still resulting in wins. We know that Chicago has the personnel, both in the coaching staff and on the roster, to achieve much more. That’s not something to be disappointed in; that’s something to take solace in as the fanbase celebrates yet another victory.

full_text: CHICAGO, ILLINOIS - JANUARY 04: Grady Jarrett #50 of the Chicago Bears and Montez Sweat #98 of the Chicago Bears sack Jared Goff #16 of the Detroit Lions in the first quarter at Soldier Field on January 04, 2026 in Chicago, Illinois. (Photo by Patrick McDermott/Getty Images) | Getty Images The traditional Thanksgiving games in Detroit and Dallas don’t always feature high stakes, but this Thursday’s Noon kickoff in Motown between the Chicago Bears and the Detroit Lions will see the winner move into first place in the NFC North. Both teams won today to move to 8-2 to set up the critical NFC matchup, and with the Minnesota Vikings loss tonight, the winner on Thanksgiving will end the week as the two-seed in the NFC. Our partners at FanDuel Sportsbook list the Bears as a road favorite (-2.5), with the Chicago moneyline at -132, and the point total over/under at 55.5. The Bears haven’t beaten the Lions since 2023, and they haven’t won in Detroit since 2021, which was also the last time they won a Thanksgiving game. In their two games a season ago, the Lions won big at Ford Field 52 to 21 in Week 2, then won on a last-second field goal in the season finale 19 to 16 at Soldier Field. So Bears head coach Ben Johnson is still looking for his first win against his former team, and you know that will be a big part of the narrative leading up to the game. The Bears didn’t cover today’s 11.5-point spread against the New Orleans Saints, but they jumped out to a 16-0 lead, then held on and coasted to a 21 to 13 win. The Bears have won five in a row, and they never trailed once in any of those games. The Lions are on a hot streak of their own, winning their sixth straight today, 31 to 21 against the Tampa Bay Buccaneers. Running back Jahmyr Gibbs is having an outstanding year for the Lions and is among the leading candidates for the NFL Offensive Player of the Year Award, but he’s just one of several weapons Chicago’s defense will need to contend with. title: Bears vs. Saints: Saints throw up a Prayer, the Bears and the Pope deny the Plea
summary: Bears v. Saints Pregame Soldier Field hosts a 7-2 Chicago Bears team coming off the bye and riding a four-game winning streak against a 3-6 New Orleans Saints squad still searching for consistency. Chicago has been efficient enough to win close ones and dominant enough to pull away in others, with Caleb Williams guiding an […]
full_text: Nov 22, 2026; Chicago, Illinois, USA; Chicago Bears quarterback Caleb Williams (18) rolls out against the New Orleans Saints during the second half at Soldier Field. Mandatory Credit: Talia Sprague-Imagn Images | IMAGN IMAGES via Reuters Connect Bears v. Saints Pregame Soldier Field hosts a 7-2 Chicago Bears team coming off the bye and riding a four-game winning streak against a 3-6 New Orleans Saints squad still searching for consistency. Chicago has been efficient enough to win close ones and dominant enough to pull away in others, with Caleb Williams guiding an offense that has scored at least 27 points in each of those recent victories. New Orleans arrives with a defense that has struggled to slow opponents and an offense that has flashed but rarely sustained drives long enough to put pressure on better teams. In a loaded NFC North where the Bears are tied with the Lions and Vikings at the top, this is the kind of home game a contender is expected to handle. Whether Chicago treats it that way or turns it into another unnecessary tight one remains to be seen. First Quarter: Business as Usual, Then a Stall Chicago opened with a methodical 10-play, 46-yard drive that ended in a Cairo Santos 41-yard field goal. D’Andre Swift handled the early work on the ground, but the drive stalled outside the red zone. New Orleans managed little on its first possession. Later in the quarter, the Bears put together a longer march that ultimately ended in a turnover on downs. Observation: The opening drive was the version of the Bears offense that has kept them in the conversation all year—short gains, no negative plays, and a kick to put points on the board. Gooch Hot Takes: A field goal on the first drive is fine. Turning a long second drive into a turnover on downs is the kind of inefficiency that keeps games interesting when they shouldn’t be. The Bears are dominating the time of possession, but not the scoreboard. The Saints’ run defense has been well above its season performance – whether or not that is because they are up for it in a “regular season Super Bowl” or the Bears o-line is falling down on the job is up to you. I’ll say this – I’m pretty much done with the Garrett Bradbury era, and the sooner the Bears go to Logan Jones, the better. Second Quarter: Two Touchdowns, a Missed PAT, and a Late Response Williams hit Swift for a 3-yard touchdown to make it 10-0. After a New Orleans turnover, Chicago needed only three plays (including a 30-yard Zavion Thomas run) to get into the end zone again. Williams found Colston Loveland for a 15-yard score. Santos missed the extra point, leaving it 16-0. New Orleans finally answered. Travis Etienne broke a 46-yard run (the longest rush the Bears have allowed this season) to set up a short touchdown pass from Tyler Shough to Alvin Kamara. The Saints added a late field goal as the half expired. Final first-half score: 16-10. Williams finished the half efficiently (roughly 10-of-13 or 10-of-14 for around 113 yards and two touchdowns) with one interception mixed in. Shough had a quieter day overall but produced the late scoring drive. Chicago controlled time of possession for most of the half. Observation: The Bears offense moved the ball in chunks when it avoided negative plays and capitalized on the turnover. The defense was mostly solid until Etienne’s big run opened the door. The missed extra point and the late Saints points turned a potentially comfortable lead into a one-score game at the break. Gooch Hot Take: Going up 16-0 on the road against a struggling team and then giving up 10 points in the final few minutes is the kind of thing that makes the second half more stressful than it needs to be. The Bears had some bad luck with the batted pass interception and the doink and over field goal, but they’ve missed key opportunities to turn the game into a blow-out. Williams looks sharp when the protection holds, and his throws are on time. The bigger question is whether the defense can get back on track going into the second half. Allen has sat back in zone too often – he needs to get back to his blitzing ways. Halftime Thoughts 16-10 feels like the version of this Bears team that keeps finding ways to make games closer than they need to be. Williams was efficient and effective for most of the half, the ground game got going in spots, and the defense created the turnover that led to the second score. But the missed PAT, the late defensive lapses, and the Saints’ ability to generate a couple of explosive plays mean this is still a one-score game instead of the double-digit lead it should. Chicago controlled time of possession and clearly has the better roster, but New Orleans has shown it can hang around if you give it a short field or a big run. The second half is simple for the Bears: finish drives, stop the explosive plays, and stop turning a 16-0 cushion into a chase. If they play the way they did for the first 25 minutes, this should still be theirs. If they keep spotting points the way they did late in the half, the Saints will hang around longer than anyone wants. 3rd Quarter Rundown The Bears came out of the half looking like they remembered they were the better team. They stopped the Saints on the opening drive. They answered the Saints’ late first-half push with an 11-play, 63-yard drive that ended in a Cairo Santos 35-yard field goal, pushing the lead back to 19-10. It wasn’t flashy, but it was the kind of methodical possession that keeps a shaky opponent from building any real momentum. New Orleans got the ball to start the half and couldn’t do much with it—short gains, stalled drives, and no real threat to cut into the lead. Williams stayed efficient, the run game chipped away, and the defense mostly closed the windows that had opened late in the second quarter. For a team that had just watched a 16-0 cushion shrink to six points, this was the response you want: controlled, professional, and enough to restore some breathing room without turning it into a shootout. Gooch Hot Take: Zavion Thomas came alive in this game – he terrified the New Orleans kickoff team to the tune of two kicks out of bounds. And he delivered in the passing game and the running game. 4th Quarter: The Bears Put it Away The safety was the punctuation mark. Montez Sweat got home on Tyler Shough in the end zone for a seven-yard loss and two free points, making it 21-10 with plenty of clock still left. That sequence felt like the Bears finally putting a foot on the throat instead of letting the Saints linger. New Orleans had a couple of chances to make it interesting, but the offense never found another explosive play or sustained drive the way it had in the second quarter. The Bears’ front controlled the line of scrimmage late, Williams avoided the big mistake, and the clock management was clean enough. No late drama, no collapse, just a defense that matched the offense’s first-half production and refused to let the game stay uncomfortably close. While Allen probably still could have timed up his blitz packages better – the Bears were the better team, the Better overall team, and they showed it when it mattered. Gooch Hot Take: Bears again overcame some bad ball luck and man. Jeff the absolute BOSS Simmons. Has a trade ever looked better? Final Game Thoughts Bears 21, Saints 10. On paper, this was supposed to be a comfortable home win against a 3-6 team, and it ended up being exactly that—once Chicago stopped spotting free points. Frankly, I think the Saints are a much better team than their record would indicate – they have playmakers on both sides of the ball. Young and Granderson were in the Bears backfield regularly, and Olave killed the Bears time and time again. The first half was the version of this team that makes you nervous: efficient enough to build a lead, then loose enough to let a lesser opponent crawl back into it with an explosive run, a short-yardage score, and a long field goal. I was hoping to see the Bears solve…

title: 5 questions with SB Nation’s Hogs Haven to preview Bengals vs. Commanders
summary: The Bengals are one of the hottest teams in the NFL right now and are currently positioned to win the AFC North. But after a whirlwind past few weeks, wherein the team traveled to Spain, followed by two primetime games, they can’t afford many slip-ups if they want to earn home playoff games. To help […]
full_text: The Bengals are one of the hottest teams in the NFL right now and are currently positioned to win the AFC North. But after a whirlwind past few weeks, wherein the team traveled to Spain, followed by two primetime games, they can’t afford many slip-ups if they want to earn home playoff games. To help preview the big Monday Night Football game between the Bengals and the Commanders, we tapped the knowledge of Andrew York of SB Nation’s Hogs Haven. We asked five big questions about their season and this game. Here’s our chat. 1.) AC: What have you seen from Jayden Daniels in year three–in both the good and the bad? I know there have been injuries, but has he continued to instill belief that he is “the guy”? AY: I think he’s very much “the guy.” There have been problems on offense, but I’d lay them mainly at the feet of OC David Blough, who is a 1st-time playcaller and has only been a coach at all for 2 years prior to this one. A rash of injuries hasn’t helped, including season-ending injuries to LT Laremy Tunsil and WR Terry McLaurin, two of the best players on offense. Jayden has played at a relatively high level and has really adapted his playstyle this year to play more from the pocket in an effort to keep him healthy. He’s also adapted reasonably well to an offense that attempts more plays under center, though he is clearly more comfortable in shotgun. Overall, he’s had a 97.1 passer rating this year despite the aforementioned problems with the rest of the offense. 2.) AC: Washington is 3-5-1 this year. What have been the biggest issues, and how safe is Dan Quinn’s job after 2025? AY: One of the biggest issues has been injuries to key players, with $74M of this year’s salary cap on injured reserve . Another has been having two first-time coordinators in OC David Blough and DC Daronte Jones, though Jones at least has considerably more coaching experience than Blough (primarily under Vikings DC Brian Flores). Another problem has been penalties, with the Commanders having the most yards erased by penalty in the NFL. Overall, the Commanders have looked like a poorly-coached team to start the season, though they have shown signs of improvement as the season went on. Dan Quinn’s job should not be safe. At this point, I think he needs to win this terrible division in order to be retained, as the team’s problems look to be due more to coaching than anything else. However, reports indicate owner Josh Harris wants to be patient and almost certainly won’t fire Quinn in-season. So he has at least until the end of the season to prove his worth, and the Commanders schedule will be much softer at the end than it has been so far. 3.) AC: The Commanders’ pass defense is ranked towards the bottom of the league in pass yards allowed per game. What can they do to stifle the red-hot Cincinnati trio of Joe Burrow, Tee Higgins, and Ja’Marr Chase on Monday Night? AY: It’s clearly not a great matchup for the Commanders, but I think their overall pass defense has looked much better since their Week 7 bye. This is probably driven mostly by two things: the return of CB Trey Amos from a lengthy injury and the addition of Steve Wilks to the coaching staff. Trey Amos was Washington’s 2nd-round pick in the 2025 draft and has looked like a high-level starter since joining the team last year, but was recovering from nagging injuries to start the season. The return of Amos leaves Washington with a good trio of CBs in Amos, Amik Robertson, and Rasul Douglas, but it’s a steep drop-off after that group. Although Washington hired a new DC this past offseason, they didn’t change over any of their defensive position coaches. This is perplexing for two reasons: 1) Washington has fielded one of the NFL’s worst defenses the past two years and surely the position coaches deserve some of the blame, and 2) new DC Daronte Jones was brought in to install a Brian Flores-like defense that is effectively unique in the NFL, so he should have brought in some position coaches who know how to teach it. Steve Wilks is a respected former defensive coordinator with a particular focus on coaching DBs, which was the position group with the most problems to start the season. The DBs have looked considerably more disciplined and competent since Wilks was brought in to help. 4.) AC: While the Commanders are theoretically alive in the playoff picture, they have an uphill climb to make the postseason. Assuming they have relatively high picks in the first couple of rounds (they currently hold their own picks in all seven rounds of the 2027 draft), what are some of your highest priorities to get them back to 2024 form? AY: GM Adam Peters seems to have a philosophy (that I agree with) of filling holes in free agency and drafting for talent over need. That being said, I think the biggest needs in terms of star power are at WR and EDGE. Those are premium positions, and right now we have a lot of depth at those positions, but no real stars, so I think that’s where I’d focus for our 1st-round pick. In terms of later rounds, we could certainly use a new LG, C, and more depth at DT, S, and CB. 5.) AC: As it stands, Cincinnati is 5.5-point favorites on the road on Monday night, per FanDuel. How do you see this one playing out, and how can Washington get the upset? AY: I’m actually surprised it isn’t a higher point spread. If I had to make a score prediction, it would probably be something like 35 – 31 in favor of the Bengals. I think it will be high-scoring, and I’d bet the over on points. As mentioned earlier, it’s a bad matchup for Washington. The strength of Washington’s defense is more in run defense, whereas the Bengals are elite at passing the ball. Washington has been better at defending the pass since their bye, but the teams they have faced since then are the Eagles, Rams, and Giants, none of which have been prolific passing teams. At the same time, I think Jayden Daniels has a bit of a friendly rivalry with Joe Burrow as another LSU Heisman winner, and it sounds like Jayden played in Joe Burrow’s shadow a bit while at LSU, so I wouldn’t be surprised if Jayden feels like he has something to prove in this game. I think for Washington to get the upset, Jayden has to have a stellar game, and the pass defense has to continue to show that improvement against a better passing offense than they have faced all year. Washington also needs to stay healthy and figure out the penalties that have haunted them all season. I would also love to see Washington commit to the run game with the return from IR of RB Jacory Croskey-Merritt, since the Bengals seem to be a bit weaker against the run than the pass. Our thanks to Andrew York and Hogs Haven for the chat. For the other side of our conversation, you can check it out over on their site.
author: Anthony Cosenza

title: Chase Brown adapting in a pass-first offense
summary: A few weeks ago, I wrote that the Bengals shouldn’t trade for a running back at the deadline, even with Chase Brown’s yards per carry sitting in the mid-3s. Fast forward to Week 11, and the Bengals have won five straight, scored 30-plus in five straight, and Brown has quietly turned into exactly the kind […]
full_text: A few weeks ago, I wrote that the Bengals shouldn’t trade for a running back at the deadline, even with Chase Brown’s yards per carry sitting in the mid-3s. Fast forward to Week 11, and the Bengals have won five straight, scored 30-plus in five straight, and Brown has quietly turned into exactly the kind of back this offense needs. It just doesn’t look like the 2025 version. The Bengals are throwing the ball more than anybody in the NFL. They have the league’s highest passing rate, and Brown is averaging just 12.6 carries a game. If you’re judging him by rushing totals, you’re grading the wrong test. Here’s the stat that matters: Brown has more receptions than any running back in the NFL. Add the fact that he’s become one of the more reliable pass protectors in the league, and you’ve got a back who touches almost every part of what makes this offense go. Brown knows it, too. He told the AP that the emphasis right now isn’t on running the football, that he understands his role, and that he’s “not going to lose in pass protection.” “Maybe we’re not leaning on the run right now,” Brown said. “At some point we will.” Zac Taylor: “The best protecting backs in the NFL” Zac Taylor didn’t hold back when asked about his running backs this week, especially with a Washington defense coming up that likes to send linebackers. “We’re challenging our backs, these linebackers this week are really good blitzers, they’re really physical,” Taylor said, “but we have the best protecting backs in the NFL,” referencing both Brown and Samaje Perine. That’s a big statement, and it tracks with what we’ve seen. Joe Burrow is in the middle of a historic run, with four or more total touchdowns in five straight games, tying Peyton Manning’s NFL record. That doesn’t happen if blitzing linebackers are getting free shots at him. A lot of that credit goes to the guy standing next to him in the backfield. Taylor also praised the buy-in from the whole running back room. “Guys have bought in and understand their role and play their role to as high a level as we need them to,” he said. For a fourth-year back coming off a 1,000-yard rushing season, that’s not nothing. It’s easy to say you’ll do whatever it takes to win. It’s harder to do it when the box score isn’t rewarding you for it. Now for the good news on the ground. Brown is averaging 4.6 yards per carry over his four games since the bye, a real jump from where he was early in the year. That’s the same slow-start, strong-finish pattern we saw from him in 2025, when he finished with 1,019 rushing yards and a team-record 69 catches. The Bengals have also leaned on the run to close out wins over Baltimore and Atlanta. And according to the AP, Cincinnati’s runs are being stuffed at the sixth-lowest rate in the league. The line isn’t getting blown up; the volume just isn’t there because Burrow, Ja’Marr Chase, and Tee Higgins are carving people up. Taylor said the staff is listening to the players about what’s working in the run game. “We’re willing to take feedback from guys who are in-game operating and seeing looks in the run game,” he said. “We’ll look at the pictures, and we’ll quickly get to those answers.” A good week to run it If there was ever a week for Brown’s “at some point we will” to come true, it might be Monday night in Washington. The Commanders have the fifth-least efficient run defense in the NFL, and they’re without defensive tackles Daron Payne and Javon Kinlaw, who are both on injured reserve. I’m not saying the Bengals will suddenly turn into a ground-and-pound team. They shouldn’t. But a 20-carry night for Brown against a banged-up front wouldn’t shock me, and it would be a nice reminder that this offense can beat you more than one way heading into December. Either way, Brown has already proven his value this season, just not in the way most of us expected.

full_text: The Cincinnati Bengals are gearing up for their second straight primetime game. Tonight they will be playing against the Washington Commanders on the road. The Bengals actually got quite a bit of help from Sunday’s slate of games. The Pittsburgh Steelers lost to the Philadelphia Eagles, which dropped them to 6-4, tied with the Cleveland Browns for second place. The Jacksonville Jaguars also lost. They ironically fell to the New York Giants, which is the team the Commanders are trying to catch for the NFC East. That means the Bengals can work their way into at least the No. 3 seed (without diving too deep into tiebreakers with so many games left. Washington will need to slow down Joe Burrow and this red-hot passing attack. The Commanders have struggled to slow down most offenses, and injuries have piled up for them on both sides of the ball. Cincinnati’s defense will have to contain Jayden Daniels from extending plays to keep the home-run plays to a minimum. That is something they have been up to these past couple of weeks as they’ve seemingly turned a corner. How do you think this will play out on Monday Night Football? Who Dey! full_text: When Demetrius Knight Jr. ran back a 27-yard fumble recovery for a touchdown in Week 1, it was more than just the Bengals’ first score of the season. It set the tone that this Bengals’ defense was going to change games this season and be a lot better than the last two seasons. On this week’s episode of “Run Through the Jungle,” Alex Frank and Jason Garrison discuss how the Bengals’ defense may actually be good. It’s Knight’s scoop-and-score and other plays so far this season that have set the tone for that side of the ball, and it’s not far-fetched to say that Dexter Lawrence’s sack late in the fourth quarter against Tennessee saved the season. Jason wrote a column this week on whether he would buy or sell 15 hot Bengals takes that have been scattered throughout the Internet this week. Alex reveals his answers to those takes, including whether he’s buying this being the best Bengals team in franchise history. The Bengals are in Washington on Monday Night Football this week to face the Commanders. Alex and Jason preview the game and give their biggest keys to the game.

title: Browns: Run game has a chance to get rolling after the bye
summary: The Cleveland Browns have struggled on offense in several areas this season, and the rushing game is no exception. full_text: (Photo by Lauren Leigh Bacho/Getty Images) | Getty Images The Cleveland Browns have struggled on offense in several areas this season, and the rushing game is no exception. As the Browns use the bye week to rest up for the final seven games of the season and a potential playoff run, the numbers from the run game are not pretty. Running back Quinshon Judkins leads the team with a meager 423 rushing yards, followed by quarterback Deshaun Watson with 266. Judkins is averaging just 3.4 yards per rush, not exactly what you want to see from your top running back, and has six games with fewer than 50 rushing yards. It’s not all Judkins fault, of course, as the offensive line has taken time to coalesce with five new starters, and opposing defenses are not exactly afraid of the pass game, which makes it that much harder to run the ball. The good news is that the final seven games provide ample opportunity for the Browns to get the run game in gear as they will face some of the league’s worst run defenses. Let’s run through the teams the Browns will be facing to see where they currently rank* when it comes to stopping the run: Week 12 vs. Las Vegas: 1,511 rushing yards (ranked No. 31) and 13 rushing touchdowns allowed (tied for No. 21) Week 13 & 18 vs. Cincinnati: 1,115 rushing yards (ranked No. 20) and 8 rushing touchdowns allowed (No. 16) Week 14 vs. Atlanta: 1,191 rushing yards (ranked No. 26) and 10 rushing touchdowns allowed (tied for No. 18) Week 15 vs. New York Giants: 1,094 rushing yards (ranked No. 18) and 7 rushing touchdowns allowed (tied for No. 11) Week 16 vs. Baltimore: 1,059 rushing yards (ranked No. 15) and 14 rushing touchdowns allowed (tied for No. 30) Week 17 vs. Indianapolis: 1,478 rushing yards (ranked No. 30) and 10 rushing touchdowns allowed (tied for No. 18) As the weather starts to turn colder, the Browns are going to need their running game to function at a higher level if they hope to stay in the playoff race in the AFC. The schedule is set up well for them to accomplish that goal, which would also help open up the passing game and provide the “explosive plays” that have been missing for most of the season. Accomplish that, and the playoff dreams just might turn into playoff reality. *Stats are heading into Week 11’s slate of games. Bring the Dawg Pound with you on the SB Nation app! summary: Several standout players have emerged on the Cleveland Browns roster this season, but a few in particular have stood out above the rest. As we asked you in DBN’s Feed, All-Pro and Pro Bowl seasons could be coming for a few players on the Browns roster: Carson Schwesinger continues to be a star on defense […]
full_text: Several standout players have emerged on the Cleveland Browns roster this season , but a few in particular have stood out above the rest. As we asked you in DBN’s Feed, All-Pro and Pro Bowl seasons could be coming for a few players on the Browns roster: Carson Schwesinger continues to be a star on defense after a very strong rookie season. He has recorded ten tackles so far this season and has really become an important player on the Browns’ defense. He has a great ability to make plays and even contribute as a pass rusher at times, making him an extremely versatile player. In his ninth season in the NFL, Denzel Ward has been exceptional in the secondary. In his 10 games, he has recorded three interceptions, 38 combined tackles, and 12 passes defended. Ward is the type of player opposing teams have to game-plan for, so even when he isn’t directly involved in a play, he still has an impact on the game. On offense, Harold Fannin Jr. has really impressed and has a case for most valuable player through the first ten games. He has been one of the more versatile players on the Cleveland offense, recording 44 receptions, 544 receiving yards, and four touchdowns. title: NFL playoff simulation has Browns moving up; only 2 AFC North teams make it
summary: As Cleveland Browns fans enjoy the bye week with whatever they have planned, a less-than-interesting Week 11 slate of games kicked off on Thursday and continues on Sunday and Monday, while six teams sit on the sidelines. A few games could be interesting for the Browns playoff chase, but the team will head into Week […]
full_text: As Cleveland Browns fans enjoy the bye week with whatever they have planned , a less-than-interesting Week 11 slate of games kicked off on Thursday and continues on Sunday and Monday, while six teams sit on the sidelines. A few games could be interesting for the Browns playoff chase , but the team will head into Week 12 as the sixth or seventh seed in the AFC playoff picture . Cleveland’s schedule gets interesting following the bye week, with the Browns having a chance to improve in a number of areas . Given the tiers of teams in the AFC , Cleveland’s chances to make the playoffs are now -154 on FanDuel Sportsbook , just behind the Pittsburgh Steelers (-275). Just six teams in the AFC have negative betting odds to make the playoffs, because the Buffalo Bills have been taken off the board with a spot almost locked up. An NFL playoff simulation by Pro Football Network has the Houston Texans, winners on Thursday Night Football, overtaking the Steelers for the last playoff spot, and the Browns moving up to the sixth seed: We simulated the rest of the season using PFN’s NFL Playoff Predictor. 🔮 Here’s the projected playoff bracket 👀 pic.twitter.com/QBo8zogNJ6 — Pro Football Network (@PFN365) November 19, 2026 Given their history and play this season, it is no surprise that the simulation has the Kansas City Chiefs knocking off Cleveland in the opening round of the playoffs. Projecting the two top seeds to make the Super Bowl is as “chalk” as it gets, but would not be surprising. Do you think the Browns make the playoffs? If so, what seed will they get? summary: Cleveland Browns fans were spoiled in only one way upon “The Return,” and that was with kicker Phil Dawson. full_text: Cleveland Browns fans were spoiled in only one way upon “The Return,” and that was with kicker Phil Dawson . In 14 years with the Browns, Dawson made 98% of his extra points and 84% of his field goals. After a while, Cleveland fans started assuming that Dawson would just make every kick. Following Dawson, there has been a bit of a turnstile of kickers, with a few providing moments of hope that they could fill the Browns’ Legends’ shoes . Second-year kicker Andre Szmyt is next up on the list, and he’s regularly getting “Brownies” awards for his work . One of our DBN regulars, Suke21, has also given the kicker a great nickname: Whether it is the home kicker or the visitor, Cleveland has been the hardest place for the specialists over the last five seasons: Every fanbase blames the kicker Some of you should be blaming the building: pic.twitter.com/QzglUSPqtP — Stick to the Model (@StickToTheModel) November 19, 2026 If the above data were only the home kickers, skill could easily be the reason for the big gap between teams. While Browns kickers have the majority of the attempts in their home games, talent alone cannot be the sole reason for the wide differences, given that all visitors are also in the data. There are a number of variables that play a role in kicks, including weather, field conditions, sight lines, and the fans. The pressure of kicks also changes depending on the importance of each game and attempt. For now, Browns fans should appreciate “Cnsnnt’s” ability to hit kicks at home and celebrate when visitors struggle.
