title: Washington Commanders 2026 Week 10 Stats Roundup – Defense
summary: This just-post mid-season, two-part stats roundup takes a look at what advanced stats and productivity metrics can tell us about how the Commanders’ players compare to the rest of the league through Week 10 of the 2026 regular season. The first part examined individual player performances on offense.  Now we’ll turn our attention to the […]
full_text: LANDOVER, MD - OCTOBER 11: Washington cornerback Amik Robertson (2) defends a pass intended for Giants wide receiver Darnell Mooney (17) during overtime of the New York Giants versus Washington Commanders National Football League game at Northwest Stadium on October 11, 2026 in Landover, MD. (Photo by Randy Litzinger/Icon Sportswire via Getty Images) | Icon Sportswire via Getty Images This just-post mid-season, two-part stats roundup takes a look at what advanced stats and productivity metrics can tell us about how the Commanders’ players compare to the rest of the league through Week 10 of the 2026 regular season. The first part examined individual player performances on offense. Now we’ll turn our attention to the defense. Apologies to special teams fanatics, I simply ran out of time. The following graph from RBSDM.com plots run defense efficiency against pass defense efficiency for every NFL team through Week 10: Like on offense, the Commanders have been just a little below league average in efficiency in both phases on defense this season. Through Week 10, the run defense lags just slightly more than the pass defense. But neither aspect says championship contender. There have been a few more bright spots on defense than offense, although some have been muted by injury. But it won’t come as any surprise that the standout performances have been outnumbered by mediocrity and worse. Let’s take a look at what the advanced stats say about the Commanders’ individual player performances. I’ll introduce the key metrics as I work through the player groups. Edge Defenders Edge defenders (ED) make crucial contributions in the pass rush and run defense. Advanced stats provide greater insight into player performance in both phases than traditional production totals. Pass Rush Pressure Rate provides a more complete account of pass rush impact than sack totals. Sacks are fairly rare events. Their totals are prone to effects of sparseness, which can limit their utility as performance metrics. Pressures measure the impact of the pass rush beyond sacks, and provide more robust data sets to work with. Pressure rate in the pass rush is simply the percentage of pass rush attempts on which a defender generated a pressure. As discussed in the OL section, scoring pressures has an element of subjectivity and requires making judgement calls. Consequently, even expert observers will have differences of opinion on some plays. To make matters worse, PFF and PFR clearly have different thresholds for counting hurries, which make up the majority of pressures. Consequently, it is not possible to cross check between sources. I have chosen to go with PFF pressure counts because their lower threshold results in larger data sets. Run Stop Rate is a major improvement over tackle counts for measuring impact in run defense. It places tackles in context of down and distance to reveal their effect on drive success. It is not technically an advanced stat, since it simply repackages official stats in more meaningful form. A stop is a tackle which results in a failure for the offense. It is defined as a tackle which holds the offense to under 40% of the yards to gain on first down, 50% on second down, or prevents a conversion or score on third or fourth down. Stops on later downs are potentially drive-ending plays, with similar impact to turnovers. Run stop rate is the percentage of running plays on which a defender generated a stop. It is worth noting that it is an incomplete measure of an ED’s impact run defense, since it does not reflect plays on which an ED forces the run inside. To the best of my knowledge, there is no quantitative metric for edge setting. Odafe Oweh leads the Commanders in sack total (5), but lags his fellow EDs in generating pressure on a consistent basis. Different fans will look at that in different ways. He is also among the worst EDs in the NFL at generating run stops, though he still has some way to fall to reach the level of former Commanders Jacob Martin (2.6%, 73/74) and Chase Young (1.9%, 74/74). Oweh’s numbers have fallen off the cliff in his first season with Washington. In 2025, he generated a 13.8% pass rush pressure rate, which ranked 29 th out of 120 EDs, and an 11.4% run stop rate, which ranked 3 rd out of 120 EDs. Throughout his career, he has always been a productive run defender until this season. K’Lavon Chaisson is second on the team with 3.5 sacks, but has been the most impactful ED in terms of generating pressure. He ranks a little above league average in that regard. His run stop rate is also down from previous seasons, but not as dramatically as Odafe’s. Dorance Armstrong’s pressure rate this season has fallen from 15.4% prior to his season-ending injury in 2025. He has continued to be the best run stopper among the Commanders EDs, registering a 7.4% run stop rate, but only played 82 run defense snaps, which fell just short of criteria for inclusion in the ranking set. His run stop rate is just below the 75 th percentile for EDs. Joshua Josephs has played sparingly. To date, he has generated a 5.0% pressure rate in 60 pass rush attempts, and 4.4% run stop rate in 46 run defense snaps. The Commanders might be bringing him along slowly for a reason. Interior Defensive Line Commanders’ interior defensive linemen were ranked by pass rush pressure rate among 96 iDL with 220 or more defensive snaps, and by run stop rate among 98 iDL with 98 or more run defense snaps. Whatever one thinks about the value of his contract, Daron Payne was the Commanders’ best interior defender in both phases before his season-ending injury. Through 6 games, he logged 7 tackles, 7 assists, 2 TFL, 1 FF, 1 sack, 5 QB hits, and 17 total pressures. His pressure rate sits at the 71 st percentile for iDL, and just lagged teammate Charles Omenihu at the third decimal place. Payne is the team’s top run stuffer, and still leads the Commanders with 10 run stops, despite missing three games. Javon Kinlaw is not far behind Payne in run stop rate. He was less productive in the pass rush, before ending his season on IR. Tim Settle’s pressure rate seems fairly low compared to all iDL, but it’s not bad for a nose tackle, whose job frequently involves making opportunities for teammates. He is more of a lane clogger than a pursuit defender in the run game. Charles Omenihu gets less playing time than the starters, as a rotational DE. But he has consistently applied pressure in the pass rush, with 1 sack, 7 QB hits, and 16 total pressures to date. He generated stops on 4.0% of 76 run defense snaps, placing him at the bottom 10% for iDL. Shy Tuttle was signed as the rotational nose tackle, but has taken on new responsibilities across the front following the loss of Payne and Kinlaw. His run stop rate is not bad for a nose tackle. He does not generate much pressure on the QB, directly. Deatrich Wise has not played enough to qualify for the rankings. He has achieved a 5.6% pressure rate in the pass rush, and 4.8% run stop rate. Johnny Newton has played just 41 defensive snaps in 2 games since returning from IR. Cornerback At the risk of sounding like a broken record, the way CB performance is usually measured just doesn’t make sense. Interceptions are high impact plays, and pass breakups can be. But at best, they account for less than 1% of the coverage snaps of the league’s most productive ballhawks. Where else in football do we put so much weight on a what a player does less than 1% of the time? Well, fumbles, but other than that, not often. Receivers are usually evaluated based on receiving yardage. So it makes sense to base the primary metric of coverage performance on yardage containment. title: Washington Commanders 2026 Week 10 Stats Roundup – Offense
summary: This just-post mid-season, two-part roundup serves two purposes. First, it provides a statistical snapshot to give readers a look at how the Commanders’ players stack up against the rest of the league. Secondly, it provides reference ranges to help fans make sense of the advanced metrics and productivity stats I use in my weekly Stats […]
full_text: LANDOVER, MARYLAND - NOVEMBER 01: Sam Cosmi #76 and Lucas Patrick #63 of the Washington Commanders line up against the Philadelphia Eagles during the first half of the NFL game at Northwest Stadium on November 1, 2026 in Landover, Maryland. (Photo by Scott Taetsch/Getty Images) | Getty Images This just-post mid-season, two-part roundup serves two purposes. First, it provides a statistical snapshot to give readers a look at how the Commanders’ players stack up against the rest of the league. Secondly, it provides reference ranges to help fans make sense of the advanced metrics and productivity stats I use in my weekly Stats and Snaps articles. Productivity metrics, like yards per rushing attempt and interception rate correct raw production totals for differences numbers of opportunities to enable analytically sound comparisons between players. They give us a better idea of what a player is likely to produce with his next touch of the ball, rather than telling us how many touches he’s had. Advanced stats, derived from film breakdown, provide deeper insights into individual performance, despite some significant limitations. These include metrics like yardage allowed in coverage and pressures allowed in pass blocking. While advanced stats and productivity metrics can take us beyond the limitations of traditional production stats, they are less familiar. Consequently, most readers won’t have the same sense of what are good and bad numbers as they would for stats like total receiving yards and interceptions. In this two-part round-up, I will present the key metrics for each position group on offense and defense in percentiles, to illustrate how the Commanders’ players compare to other players at their positions around the league. Most of the metric are used in my weekly stats and snaps. But a few of the more labor intensive ones are reserved for my offseason articles (e.g. Catch Rate Over Expectation). The figures in this article can then serve as reference material for the Stats and Snaps articles for the rest of the season. I’ll kick things off with the offense. The following graph from RBSDM.com plots rushing efficiency against passing efficiency for every NFL team through Week 10: The Commanders’ have been just a little below league average in efficiency in both phases on offense this season. That is not to say that there haven’t been some bright spots on offense. But it won’t come as any surprise that they have been outnumbered by mediocre performances and worse. Let’s take a look at what the advanced stats say about the Commanders’ individual player performances. I’ll introduce the key metrics as I work through the player groups. Quarterback ESPN’s total QBR is the closest thing there is to a statistically valid all-in-one performance metric for a player at single position. It is derived from Expected Points Added (EPA) per play, which measures a player’s impact on the team’s scoring potential each drive. However, it improves on EPA/play by taking game situation into account through weighting of clutch plays and garbage time. Values are scaled from 0 to 100. QBR considers a QB’s total contribution on offense – passing and running – and should not be confused with the official NFL stat Passer Rating, which only takes into account passing stats. Turnover-Worthy Play Rate (TWP%) is a measure of ball security I calculated just for this roundup. It is simply the percentage of offensive plays on which a QB threw an interception or fumbled. I used fumbles rather than lost fumbles because it generally comes down to chance whether a fumble is lost or not. Hence, I named it turnover-worthy play rate, rather than turnover rate. It was included for reasons that will become apparent. QBR percentiles are derived from ESPN’s leaders’ board , which only lists the top 31 QBs by playing time. TWP percentiles were calculated for the 32 QBs with 240 or more offensive snaps. Franchise QB Jayden Daniels , is currently the 14 th ranked QB by total QBR, just a little above league average. That is not bad for a QB working with up and down pass protection and a rag-tag band of backups and injury replacements for a supporting cast. One area where he really stands out is protecting the football. Prior to throwing two picks against the Giants, last week, he was the leader in TWP%. Even after the two picks, he is near the top of the league in ball security. Marcus Mariota got three starts and completed two games, including the Commanders’ first win against the Seahawks. He didn’t get enough playing time to qualify for ESPN’s leader board. If he had, his 74.8 QBR would slot in at 5 th place, between Josh Allen and Drake Maye on the league leaders board, and first place on the Commanders. He has not fumbled or thrown a pick this season. Athan Kaliakmanis took over when Mariota was injured against the Colts, and played about as well as you’d expect from a 7 th round rookie, thrust into action without many first team practice reps. His QBR from that game put him below the lowest ranked QB (Justin Herbert 30.1). He threw 1 interception in 54 snaps against the Colts. Twelve of the 32 ranked QBs but the ball in harms way at a higher rate than that. Running Back Rushing Average (Yds/Att) adjusts total rushing yards by numbers of opportunities to permit meaningful comparisons between players. It is a standard stat, and self-explanatory. Success Rate (Success %) places rushing yards in the context of down and distance to provide an alternative view on the impact of a runner’s production. A rushing play is considered successful if the runner scores or gains at least 40% of the yards to gain on 1 st down, 60% on 2 nd down, or 100% on 3 rd down. Success rate is the percentage of successful rushing attempts. While rushing average treats all plays the same, success rate better recognizes the value of clutch plays in short yardage and goal line situations. Yards Before Contact per Rushing Attempt (YBC/Att) reflects a combination of two factors: RB elusiveness and run blocking. As such, it is more an indicator of the health of the rushing offense, overall, than an individual player stat. That said, when one RB on team stands out from the others, it can be taken as an indicator of RB performance. It might surprise some fans to learn that the running backs’ stats have improved as the season has progressed. Rachaad White has got the most playing time, with Bill Croskey-Merritt sidelined with a groin injury. As we move into the second half of the season, his rushing average has risen to just above league average at 4.2 Y/A. His 46.2 % success rate, on the other hand, is well below average. Bill Croskey-Merritt last played in Week 5, when he looked very good in the tie with the Giants. His stats are dragged down by the first four games of the season, when the run blocking was terrible. Both White and Bill have exactly the same YBC/Att which, surprisingly, is right on league average. Austin Ekeler has had 33 attempts for 109 yds. His 3.3 Y/A rushing average and 39.4% success rate are both near the bottom of the league. He averaged 1.9 YBC/Att, a little lower than the other running backs. Before his season ending injury, Jeremy McNichols averaged just 3.4 Y/A on 10 carries. He is often used in short yardage situations, where his 70.0% success rate might be a better indicator of his value to the team, albeit in a limited sample. He averaged 2.2 YBC/Att, just like Bill and Rachaad. Wide Receiver Yards per Route Run (Y/RR) is a major improvement over Receiving Yards for comparing receivers because it corrects for the major confounding influence – playing time – to let us see which receivers made the most of their opportunities, rather than simply telling us which ones got the most opportunities. Similar to Y/RR, Catch Rate Over Expectation (CROE) eliminates the confounding effect of depth of target to allow us to see which receivers are best at catching the football, without being tricked into thinking…

title: Washington Commanders vs Cincinnati Bengals Week 11: Five Questions with Cincy Jungle
summary: It’s week 11 of the NFL season and the 3-5-1 Washington Commanders will be facing a 7-2 Cincinnati Bengals team at home at Northwest Stadium in Landover, MD on Monday (today) at 8:15 p.m. ET. The Bengals started the season slow, losing in week 3 to the Steelers and in week 4 to the Jaguars, […]
full_text: It’s week 11 of the NFL season and the 3-5-1 Washington Commanders will be facing a 7-2 Cincinnati Bengals team at home at Northwest Stadium in Landover, MD on Monday (today) at 8:15 p.m. ET. The Bengals started the season slow, losing in week 3 to the Steelers and in week 4 to the Jaguars, but have since won 5 straight games including a big division matchup last week against the Steelers that left the Bengals as the leader of the AFC North. On offense, the Bengals are coached by head coach and playcaller Zac Taylor and offensive coordinator Dan Pitcher. The Bengals have the 6th-ranked offense in the NFL, but it is extremely pass heavy, with the highest pass rate over expectation in the NFL. Thus far, it hasn’t been a problem, as the Bengals have the NFL’s top-ranked pass offense and 30th-ranked rush offense . This has resulted in the trio of Joe Burrow, Ja’Marr Chase, and Tee Higgins being the most productive QB/pass catcher trio in the NFL since 2006 . The success of the Bengals’ offense (and particularly passing game) has also been enabled by the 2nd-best offensive line in the NFL in terms of pressure rate allowed. On defense, the Bengals are in their second year of DC Al Golden, who was the Bengals’ linebackers coach in 2020-2021 before going on to coach defense at Notre Dame and then returning to the Bengals as DC in 2025. Golden runs a pretty simple and coverage-based defense that typically rushes four and leaves a light box (meaning six or fewer defenders in the box). The Bengals actually take this style of defense to an extreme, with the lowest blitz rate in the NFL , the highest rate of light boxes in the NFL, and yet the 3rd-highest rate of man or mixed-man coverage. As a result, the Bengals allow the 2nd-most yards per carry in the NFL, all while allowing the 13th-fewest yards per pass attempt in the NFL. So why might the Bengals almost dare opponents to run on them? I imagine it has something to do with the fact that teams tend to abandon the run when they are down multiple scores. The Bengals defense really seems to be built around the idea that their offense will be able to establish a lead early and the defense just needs to maintain that lead. As a result, Bengals’ opponents pass on them at a 59.6% rate (11th-most in the NFL), despite their glaring weakness being run defense. This could be a good week for Washington to try to establish the run and for Jayden to gain yards on scrambles. This should also be a big week to throw to TEs, as the Bengals are allowing the 3rd-most passing yards to TEs in the NFL (right behind Washington, who are allowing the 2nd-most passing yards to TEs). I asked Anthony Cosenza of Cincy Jungle five questions to better understand the state of the Bengals and what to look for in this game. 1) The Bengals offense seemed a bit lackluster to start the season, but has really taken off since then. What accounts for their surge in offensive production? Unfortunately, in the Zac Taylor era, Joe Burrow and Co., have had many years of slow offensive starts. All offseason and into the early portions of the regular season, the Bengals tried to run a lot of under center and “12 personnel” looks, to mixed results, at best, even though they started off 2-0. Since, the team has transitioned back to their “bread and butter” of shotgun looks and spread their weapons out to create mismatches. To boot, their offensive line has been playing pretty well overall this season. While it hasn’t translated to a ton of run game success, they are arguably the best passing offense in the league right now. 2) The Bengals have the 1st-ranked passing offense in the NFL, but the 30th-ranked rushing offense . Why can’t they get the run game going and do you think they should try anything different to get it going? I think it’s a myriad of factors. First, I think they’ve compiled an offensive line that is better built in a spread offense with a high volume of pass attempts. After the Bengals’ demolition of the Steelers on Sunday night, tackles Orlando Brown Jr., and Amarius Mims were on the postgame interview, and rhetorically asked about any other tackle tandem in the league that is asked to play the style the Bengals employ. Secondly, the run game just takes a backseat to how the offense is run. When Joe Burrow, Ja’Marr Chase, and Tee Higgins are playing at a high level, Taylor is going to lean on that trio. Their lack of any notable extensions, free agency additions, and/or trades at the position also points to the run game being a secondary option in this offense. 3) The Bengals defense has transformed from one of the worst in the NFL the last few years to about league average this year. How did they manage that transformation and what’s your overall assessment of the defense now? The short answer is in the additions of Dexter Lawrence II and Jonathan Allen at defensive tackle. Those two have been downright amazing on the field, as well as in the locker room for a group that was both young, and downright lost just a year ago. But, those two have opened up a number of opportunities for others, too. Boye Mafe has been a great Trey Hendrickson replacement at edge, while the line has allowed their two second-year linebackers (Barrett Carter and Demetrius Knight II) to play a bit more freely. And, while the Bengals have marginally improved in overall run and pass defense statistics, the big key has been their penchant for creating game-swinging plays in the form of both sacks and turnovers. 4) Who is one Bengals player on offense and one on defense that Commanders fans probably don’t know much about, but should? On offense, and for any other team, I’d point out Samaje Perine, who is a personal favorite because of his work ethic, and ability to do all things–especially “the dirty work”. But, given his history with Washington, I’ll go with Drew Sample, who is a hybrid blend of a blocking tight end, H-Back, fullback, and occasional pass-catcher. On defense, I think I’ll go with either DE Myles Murphy, or DT Kris Jenkins, Jr. Both guys were high picks (Murphy a 2023 first-rounder, and Jenkins at 2024 second-rounder), but they’ve long been rotational guys buried on the depth chart. While they have also been part of a rotation this year, the duo has combined for 4.5 sacks, and have stepped up at times when others get a little quiet. 5) How should Washington gameplan for this matchup on both sides of the ball? I think Washington will need to be prepared to score 30-plus points, first and foremost. Unfortunately for the Commanders, they have key players on I.R. for other facets I’d readily point out. Without Terry McLaurin, Stefon Diggs will need to have a big game against an up-and-down Bengals secondary that is seemingly missing Dax Hill this week, while Washington’s interior defensive line will want to exploit Dalton Risner’s impending absence, even though Javon Kinlaw and Daron Payne are also on I.R. Daniels should also lean on any/all tight ends who can contribute, as that has been an Achilles Heel for the Bengals’ defense most of the year. A companion article to this with my answers to Anthony’s questions is linked here . Thanks again to Anthony Cosenza for taking time out of his day to answer our questions about the Bengals.

title: How 2026 Washington Commanders could have looked a lot different
summary: On a non-football Sunday for Washington fans, I thought it would be “interesting” to play the “What-If” game. As is always the case, the What-If game can be played a variety of ways. I chose the path below. My goal was to look at how Washington could have looked heading into the 2026 season if […]
full_text: On a non-football Sunday for Washington fans, I thought it would be “interesting” to play the “What-If” game. As is always the case, the What-If game can be played a variety of ways. I chose the path below. My goal was to look at how Washington could have looked heading into the 2026 season if a few different choices were made. Keep in mind, this is just for discussion purposes ONLY! 2021-2024 NFL Draft Redos Just think, for a second, about what could have been… 2021 NFL Draft Christian Darrisaw over Jamin Davis Jamin Davis was selected with the 19th overall pick in the first round. Christian Darrisaw was selected four picks later by the Minnesota Vikings. Davis is currently on the Steelers practice squad, while Darrisaw has been the Vikings starting left tackle since he was drafted in 2021. * If Darrisaw was the pick in 2021, Adam Peters wouldn’t have had to send third- and seventh-rounders in 2025 and second- and a fourth-rounder in 2026 to the Texans for Laremy Tunsil. 2022 NFL Draft Chris Olave over Jahan Dotson Washington held the 11th overall pick in the first round. Ron Rivera ended up trading that pick to the New Orleans Saints, who selected Ohio State wide receiver Chris Olave . Five picks later, Rivera select Penn State wide receiver Jahan Dotson. Dotson was traded to the rival Eagles and never did anything. He is currently the third wide receiver for the Atlanta Falcons and has 137 career receptions for 1,872 yards and 14 touchdowns, while Olave is a second team All-Pro who has 347 career receptions for 4,462 yards and 21 touchdowns. 2023 NFL Draft Christian Gonzalez over Emmanuel Forbes Washington held the 16th overall pick in the first round. Ron Rivera chose Mississippi State cornerback Emmanuel Forbes. With the next pick, the New England Patriots chose Oregon corner Christian Gonzalez. Forbes was cut by Washington and claimed by the Rams. He’s currently a backup corner. Gonzalez is one of the best corners in the NFL, making second team All-Pro in 2024 and the Pro Bowl in 2025. 2024 NFL Draft Cooper DeJean over Mike Sainristil Adam Peters traded away pick No. 40 to the Philadelphia Eagles in exchange for Nos. 50 and 53. Philly took Iowa defensive back Cooper DeJean with the 40th overall pick and Washington chose Mike Sainristil 10 picks later and followed that up with Ben Sinnott at pick 53. Mike Sainristil has currently been benched by Washington and Ben Sinnott has just 21 receptions for 190 yards and three touchdowns in his two-and-a-half-year career. The 6-foot, 200-pound DeJean was named to the PFWA All-Rookie team in 2024 and was a First-team All-Pro and Pro Bowler in 2025. NOT Trading Chase Young Ron Rivera used the No. 2 overall pick in the 2020 NFL Draft on the “dynamic” Ohio State EDGE. Young burst onto the scene as a rookie, collecting 44 tackles, 10 for a loss, 7.5 sacks, four forced fumbles and three fumble recoveries on his way to being named defensive rookie of the year. In week 10 of the 2021 season, Young tore his ACL. He missed the remainder of the year and didn’t return to action until Week 16 of the 2022 season against the 49ers. He would play in just three games and did not record a sack. Young looked to be rounding back into form in 2023. He had five sacks through seven games, but was traded to the 49ers for a 2024 third-round comp pick which ultimately became Luke McCaffrey. Young would sign a one-year deal with the Saints in March of 2024. He played in all 17 games recording 5.5 sacks. He signed a three-year, $51M contract in 2025. That year, over 12 games, he recorded 11 tackles for a loss, 10 sacks, two forced fumbles and three fumble recoveries. Trough nine games this season, Young is tied for third in the NFL with eight sacks. NOT Trading for Marshon Lattimore During the 2024 season, Washington needed cornerback help. Before the trade deadline in 2024, Peters gave up a third-, fourth- and sixth-round pick in the 2025 draft for Lattimore and a fifth-rounder . This trade turned out to be a complete disaster for Washington as Lattimore was not healthy, and when he was, he was a liability on the field. Between the second half of 2024-2025, Lattimore played in just nine regular season games (and three playoff games in 2024), recording 31 total tackles and one interception. There was some really solid talent in the middle rounds of that 2025 draft and I imagine Washington could have found some contributors. What could have been… For the purposes of discussion (and my own sanity), I thought it would be “interesting” to take a look at what the 2026 Commanders COULD have looked like. I know, I know… but Mark, we may never have been bad enough in 2024 to land the second overall pick to select Jayden Daniels if we had Darrisaw, Olave, Gonzalez and Young. My rebuttal to that would be – but we still had Ron Rivera, and somehow he’d have still messed things up. OFFENSE: QB: Jayden Daniels RB: Jonah Coleman : 2026 4th round pick WR: Chris Olave WR: Terry McLaurin/Treylon Burks WR: Antonio Williams TE: Chig Okonkwo LT: Christian Darrisaw LG: Dylan Fairchild : 2025 3rd round pick C: Logan Jones : 2026 2nd round pick RG: Sam Cosmi RT: Josh Conerly DEFENSE EDGE: Chase Young DT: Daron Payne DT: Javon Kinlaw DT: Tim Settle EDGE: Odafe Oweh (yeah, I still have us signing him) ILB: Sonny Styles ILB: Frankie Luvu/Leo Chenal CB: Christian Gonzales CB: Trey Amos CB: Cooper DeJean S: Xavier Watts : 2025 3rd round pick S: Nick Cross

title: Has Rasul Douglas been the Washington Commanders’ best free agent addition?
summary: Following an extended time period on injured reserve for 2025 second-round pick Trey Amos, the Washington Commanders added Rasul Douglas late in free agency, signing the veteran just before the start of training camp in July. At the time, there were multiple questions surrounding the addition of a soon-to-be 31-year-old cornerback for a team that […]
full_text: EAST RUTHERFORD, NJ - NOVEMBER 12: Washington Commanders Cornerback Rasul Douglas (29) intercepts a pass intended for New York Giants Wide Receiver Malik Nabers (1) during the second half of the National Football League game between the Washington Commanders and New York Giants on November 12, 2026, at MetLife Stadium in East Rutherford, NJ. (Photo by Gregory Fisher/Icon Sportswire via Getty Images) | Icon Sportswire via Getty Images Following an extended time period on injured reserve for 2025 second-round pick Trey Amos, the Washington Commanders added Rasul Douglas late in free agency, signing the veteran just before the start of training camp in July. At the time, there were multiple questions surrounding the addition of a soon-to-be 31-year-old cornerback for a team that desperately needed playmakers in the secondary. Douglas worked behind fellow cornerbacks Mike Sainristil and Amik Robertson to start the season, and while he only played 38% of the team’s total defensive snaps in Week 1, Rasul immediately made a mark with his physical play style. Rasul Douglas blew that play up! pic.twitter.com/Fp7VQpQBO8 — COMMANDERS FOOTBALL (@HogsHaven) September 13, 2026 Eventually, Douglas would take over a full-time role for the Commanders’ defense in Week 4, logging 85% of the total defensive snaps and recording 5 tackles, 1 assist, 2 stops, 1 interception, and 1 pass defended versus the Colts. Post-game, Rasul proved his fit for Washington’s competitive culture, stating the secondary’s improved performance was not good enough, as the team didn’t win the matchup. The following week , Douglas backed his words with his own play, finishing second on the team with 9 tackles and 1 assist while being graded with 4 receptions for 39 receiving yards allowed on 9 targets by Pro Football Reference. Trey Amos returned to the lineup in Week 6, and while his return, along with the addition of safety Nick Cross, has been attributed to the improvement of the Commanders’ secondary, Douglas’ performance as a third cornerback cannot be overlooked. Since Week 6 in San Francisco, Washington’s defense has given up just 18.5 points per game and the secondary has not allowed more than one passing touchdown in each of those contests. While that stretch did include games against the struggling Eagles and last week’s road trip to New York, it also included games against the 49ers and Rams. Through Week 10, per @SFdata9ers, Douglas has a league-low 39.6 allowed passer rating while also leading the team in interceptions with 3, including a game-sealing grab at Metlife Stadium. Passer Rating Allowed when Targeted Data: @FantasyPtsData | min. 30 targets pic.twitter.com/BBaJJXm9v9 — SFdata9ers🏈📊 (@sfdata9ers) November 20, 2026 RASUL DOUGLAS CALLS GAME. pic.twitter.com/5q7ahQYaoa — NFL (@NFL) November 13, 2026 Identified in the off-season as a potential fit for Daronte Jones’ defensive scheme, in addition to being a ball-hawk, Douglas has been a sure tackler, recording 29 total tackles (22 solo) on the season and 7 passes defended; just 2 behind full-time starter Amik Robertson. With Robertson’s availability in question for Monday night’s matchup against the Cincinnati Bengals’ elite passing offense, Douglas may be called on to prove his value yet again, but fans may take comfort in the fact the Commanders’ cornerback ranks 9th on Pro Football Network’s cornerback grading list headed into Week 11. 🔒 The 10 best NFL CBs by PFN coverage grading this year 🏈 1. Trent McDuffie, LAR (96.9) 2. Denzel Ward, CLE (92.8) 3. Nohl Williams, KC (92.7) 4. Joey Porter Jr., DAL (91.1) 5. Nehemiah Pritchett, SEA (90.7) 6. James Pierre, MIN (90.0) 7. Kristian Fulton, KC (89.9) 8. Isaiah… pic.twitter.com/ebREOtIwvt — Pro Football Network (@PFN365) November 20, 2026 What is the best part of Rasul Douglas’ performance thus far? He was signed to a 1-year, $1.8 million agreement with only $580k of guaranteed money and up to $2 million available in incentives. Those numbers rank him 95th on Spotrac’s average cornerback contract rankings, yet halfway through the season, Douglas is playing at a top ten level. That makes the free agent addition arguably the best of Adam Peters’ off season acquisitions so far and a player the Washington Commanders should consider keeping around next season.

full_text:
The 2027 NFL draft is still months away, but with the 2026 season underway, we're starting to track pick order in Round 1. Which teams are in position to add elite prospects in the top 10 next April? What about the top five ... or even at No. 1?

 What follows is not the current draft order based on records. It is a projection of what ESPN's Football Power Index thinks the order ultimately will be by the end of the season. Each week during the season, the FPI projects the draft order by simulating the remainder of the season 10,000 times. Game probabilities are based primarily on the model's team ratings and game locations. The draft order is determined by the records the model projects for each team after 17 games, as well as each team's average draft position across the simulations.

 So where do things stand? Here are the full sortable projections, complete with each team's chances to pick in the top five, in the top 10 and at No. 1.

title: NFL Week 11: Big takeaways, questions and fantasy spin from Sunday's games
summary: Our NFL Nation reporters react to all the action, answering the biggest questions coming out of each Sunday game. Here's what we learned from Week 11.
full_text:
The Sunday slate for Week 11 of the 2026 NFL season  began with several blowouts.

 With Josh Johnson at quarterback, the Cardinals couldn't get anything going offensively in a loss to the Chiefs. Miami also struggled on that side of the ball against Buffalo in quarterback Kyle McCord 's second start. And the Titans' defense allowed touchdowns on the Cowboys' first six drives, leading to a 21-point defeat.

 Elsewhere in the early window, the Panthers came out on top of a shootout against the Ravens. The Eagles pulled off an upset over the Steelers with backup quarterback Joe Milton . The Bears won their fifth straight game, while the Lions won in their first game without edge rusher Aidan Hutchinson ( knee injury ) this season.

 In the late window, both New York teams pulled off wins. And Raiders rookie quarterback Fernando Mendoza almost came back against the Broncos, but a pick-six ended a potential go-ahead drive late in the fourth quarter. The 49ers capped things off Sunday night with a resounding win over the Vikings in Mexico City.

 Our NFL Nation reporters react to all the action, answering lingering questions coming out of each game. Fantasy football analysts Matt Bowen and Tristan Cockcroft also have fantasy takeaways from each matchup.

 Let's get to it with the biggest lessons from Sunday.

 
 Jump to: 
 MIN-SF |  JAX-NYG  | LV-DEN 
 NYJ-LAC |  BAL-CAR 
 NO-CHI  |  PIT-PHI |  TB-DET 
 TEN-DAL | MIA-BUF |  ARI-KC 

 Catch up on Thursday's game: 
 IND-HOU 

 
 

 

 San Francisco 35, Minnesota 10 
 Catch up on the action: Box score | Recap  | Instant analysis 

 

 49ers 
 Is the 49ers' pass rush ready to take off? The 49ers' defensive line has caught plenty of recent flak for a lack of pressure and production. During their week of practice in Colorado Springs, edge rusher Nick Bosa vowed that he would be better and so, too, would the defensive front. Bosa was right, as the Niners harassed Vikings quarterback Kirk Cousins for much of the night. Bosa collected his first sack of the season, and the 49ers' pressure forced several errant Cousins throws, including safety Ji'Ayir Brown 's pick-six. The Niners finished with one sack but affected Cousins consistently for most of the night. The Niners pressured Cousins on 15 of 39 dropbacks and he averaged 4.0 yards per attempt with an interception and a sack when San Francisco didn't blitz.

 What to make of the QB performance: Brock Purdy undoubtedly heard all the doubts about how he'd fare against Brian Flores' exotic defense after a couple of rough outings previously. But coach Kyle Shanahan said this week that Purdy's previous experience playing against that scheme should help him and that Purdy wouldn't be surprised by anything Flores could throw at him. That proved true Sunday night, as Purdy finished 21-of-26 for 255 yards with three touchdowns and no interceptions. That included 17-of-19 against the blitz with two touchdowns and 12 first downs on the 20 dropbacks in which Minnesota brought five or more pass rushers. -- Nick Wagoner 

 Next game: vs. Seahawks (Sunday, 4:25 p.m. ET)

 
 

 Vikings 
 What should we take from Kirk Cousins ' second start? At one point in the first half, Cousins appeared to be telling right tackle Brian O'Neill that he was being hit on every dropback. Heavy pressure eventually limited the Vikings' attempts to push the ball downfield and made it all but impossible to mount a comeback. Cousins has added a higher level of accuracy and decision-making to the Vikings' offense in his two-game stint, but the 49ers' pass rush, which sacked him once, made him frenetic.

 Most surprising performance: The Vikings absorbed a blow pregame when cornerback Isaiah Rodgers was declared inactive because of a quad injury he suffered in practice. And while Rodgers' absence alone was not the sole cause, the defense appeared uncomfortable and on its heels from the start. Purdy did what no other opposing quarterback had been able to do this season: find the parts of the field vacated by the Vikings' blitz packages. Purdy faced the Vikings' blitz on 20 of his first 26 dropbacks, and he completed 89% of his passes in those situations for two touchdowns and 12 first downs. -- Kevin Seifert 

 Next game: vs. Falcons (Sunday, 1 p.m. ET)

 
 

 Fantasy football takeaway: Justin Jefferson scored 13.7 points in the Sunday night loss to the 49ers, catching seven of nine targets for 87 receiving yards. Jefferson did lose a fumble, but he has now brought in 16 of 22 targets for 160 yards in the two games played with Cousins at quarterback. With a favorable upcoming schedule (ATL, CAR, @NE), Jefferson is set up to produce consistent WR1 numbers. -- Bowen 

 

 

 N.Y. Giants 23, Jacksonville 18 
 Catch up on the action: Box score | Recap 

 

 Giants 
 Are the Giants for real? This was putting the rest of the NFL on notice, even good teams. Playing coach John Harbaugh's Giants is not going to be easy. New York thoroughly beat the Jaguars at home for its first win this season against a team with a winning record at the time. It was a statement game for these Giants, especially for a defense that held Jacksonville to one touchdown in six red zone trips and forced two Trevor Lawrence interceptions. After a week when they clearly didn't like the idea that they were overmatched against good teams, this was proof that they belong -- and they are heavy favorites to win the NFC East.

 Most surprising performance: LB Abdul Carter . The pressure finally paid off with sacks. The second-year edge rusher came into Sunday with two sacks this season despite being second in the NFL in pass rush win rate. He doubled that sack total by halftime and finished with five QB hits. Carter and the Giants had Lawrence under pressure all afternoon.  -- Jordan Raanan 

 Next game: at Colts (Sunday, 1 p.m. ET)

 
 

 Jaguars 
 Was this offensive performance an aberration or a troubling sign for the rest of the season? The Jaguars scored only one touchdown after putting up 115 points in the past three weeks. In six trips to the red zone, they had the one TD, four field goals and one turnover on downs. They already entered Sunday without center Robert Hainsey (knee). Then in the second half, left tackle Walker Little went down with a knee injury. The Jaguars have bounced back from bad performances before -- they put up 35 points the week after scoring just 13 in Denver -- and the Jaguars get a good matchup against Tennessee, which allowed 51 points to Dallas on Sunday.

 What to make of the QB performance: Lawrence topped 300 yards, but this was one of his worst performances of the past two-plus seasons. He was under heavy pressure (hit five times and sacked three times in the first half) and his receivers were unable to get much separation, but his two interceptions came on under- and over-thrown passes. It's the first time he has thrown multiple interceptions in a game since an overtime victory over Arizona in Week 12 last season. -- Michael DiRocco 

 Next game: vs. Titans (Sunday, 1 p.m. ET)

 
 

 Fantasy football takeaway: Jaguars RB Bhayshul Tuten (who has been dealing with ankle and foot injuries) scored 8.3 fantasy points and played only 43% of the snaps. It's fair to question whether the ailments are hindering his performance, as he has totaled 53 fewer rushing yards than expected the past three weeks, per NFL Next Gen Stats. Tuten's Week 12 matchup is outstanding (Tennessee), but it's best to temper expectations to high-end fantasy RB2 levels. -- Cockcroft 

 

 

 Denver 38, Las Vegas 24 
 Catch up on the action: Box score | Recap 

 

 Broncos 
 How much can rookie RB Jonah Coleman help fix what ails this Broncos offense? Yes, the Broncos won -- again. They made it far more difficult than it needed to be -- again. But an offense in desperate need of something to lean on found a spark with the blunt force of Coleman. Just when the Raiders looked as if they were poised for an upset after tying the score at…

title: Week 11 NFL highlights: Best plays, moments, touchdowns, more

full_text:

title: How active NFL players continue to redefine all-time sack list
summary: Myles Garrett's torrid pace up the all-time sack list paces active players making their moves among the greats.
full_text:
Last season, defensive end Myles Garrett won his second Defensive Player of the Year award after setting the NFL's single-season record with 23 sacks for the Cleveland Browns . 
 
 This season, he'll continue his climb up the NFL's all-time sack list as a member of the Los Angeles Rams  after a blockbuster trade  in June -- making the Rams favorites to win the Super Bowl, according to DraftKings Sportsbook, heading into the season. 
 
 Garrett entered the season with 125.5 career sacks, which was tied for 20th in NFL history and third among the other six active players --  Von Miller  (No. 9), Cameron Jordan  (No. 17), Calais Campbell  (No. 25), T.J. Watt  (No. 26), Danielle Hunter  (tied for No. 27) and Khalil Mack  (T-29th) -- in the top 30.  
 
 
 
 
 Joining the top 30 soon could be  Aaron Donald ,  who unretired  to join Garrett on the Rams' defensive line. Donald entered the season at 111 sacks and was two behind 30th.  
 
 
As we look at how the sack list is redefined this season, we'll highlight milestones across the NFL landscape. We will update this file as the active players move up, and we'll add nuggets and milestones throughout the season. 
 

 

 Week 11 update 

 With Garrett and Donald on bye and Hunter still not playing as he continues to deal with injury, this week marked the first where none of the top active players recorded a sack. 

 

 Week 10 update 

 While Garrett didn't record a sack Sunday, Donald got his first sack of the season -- finishing with 1.5 to move ahead of Chandler Jones and Justin Houston for 31st at 112.5. 

 Hunter missed his first game of the season, and the rest of the list failed to record a sack.  

 

 Week 9 update 

 In his first game since Week 1, Garrett made his presence felt. He had three sacks to move ahead of Dwight Freeney, Derrick Thomas and Rickey Jackson for 18th on the list. He was the only one of the active leaders to record a sack this week. 

 

 Week 8 update 

 With two players on bye and Garrett out, only two of the five active players that played this week recorded sacks, but they were impactful. 

 Miller recorded his first sack as a Cowboy Sunday, moving him ahead of Terrell Suggs and into a tie with Jason Taylor for seventh.

 Watt added two sacks of his own, moving him ahead of Simeon Rice and Clyde Simmons for 23rd. He now has 7.5 sacks on the season. 

 

 Week 7 update 

 Hunter and Watt were the only ones to record sacks this week, with Hunter jumping back over Campbell in the rankings. 

 

 Week 6 update 

 With Garrett still out, it was another quiet week on the sack front. Of the active leaders, it was the oldest that recorded the lone sack of the week in Campbell. He moved back in front of Hunter. 

 

 Week 5 update 

 Hunter was the only player among the active leaders to record a sack this week, moving him ahead of Campbell to No. 26 all-time. Hunter now has three sacks through five games. 

 

 Week 4 update 

 Watt kicked off things in Week 4 on "Thursday Night Football" in an impactful way. He had one sack, one forced fumble and a fumble recovery to move his total to 4.5 sacks on the season. Other than that, there wasn't much activity with Garrett still on IR. 

 

 Week 3 update 

 There wasn't much movement on the list this week with only Mack (1) and Hunter (.5) recording sacks. Watt, Campbell, Hunter and Mack (in that order) now make up 25 to 28 on the all-time list. Along with Campbell, the three top active leaders -- Miller, Jordan and Garrett -- have yet to record a sack this season.  

 

 Week 2 update 

 The second week of the season saw little movement near the top of the career list, but Watt's hot start continues, with the defensive end recording 1.5 sacks to now put him at 3.5 through two weeks (No. 2 in the NFL this season) and break a tie with Campbell to move to 25th. 

 Hunter (27th) and Mack (29th) also recorded one sack apiece over the weekend to break ties and move up one spot on the list. 

 Donald (33rd) made his  season debut on "Monday Night Football" against the Giants after taking two years off. He finished with three tackles, one for a loss, but did not record a sack. 

 

 

 Week 1 update 

 Of all the active sack leaders, Watt was the only one to record a sack, finishing the game with two to move to a tie with Campbell for 25th. 

 And while Donald was held out of the Rams' Week 1 game, Garrett will be out for at least the next four after failing to record a tackle in Australia and landing on injured reserve after having to have arthroscopic surgery on his knee.

 After the Rams' opening loss, Garrett said this was " the worst version of myself that I've put out there."

title: NFL Week 11 arrivals: George Kittle rocks luchador mask ahead of SNF in Mexico
summary: NFL stars continue to turn game-day arrivals into their own weekly fashion showcase.
full_text:
The forecast affects the game plan for how NFL players put together their Week 11 looks.

 

 And Sunday's arrivals will call for a little more wardrobe strategy.

 With morning temperatures near freezing expected in Denver before an afternoon climb into the 40s, players arriving for the  Raiders - Broncos  game have an opening for coats and chunky knits. Showers in Chicago could make weatherproof outerwear a smart finishing touch, while temperatures approaching 70 in Southern California give the New York Jets and Los Angeles Chargers room to keep things lighter.

 On the East Coast, Sunday's forecast leaves room for fall outfits without going full winter. Morning temperatures in the 50s in Buffalo should give Miami Dolphins and Buffalo Bills players an opening for sweaters and light jackets, while Jacksonville Jaguars and New York Giants arrivals in East Rutherford, New Jersey, call for similar layers under cloudy skies, with rain possible later in the day.

 From practical layers to outfits built for the spotlight, here are the standout arrivals from Week 11.

 
 Sunday's best 
 Playing in Mexico City on "Sunday Night Football," players from the San Francisco 49ers and Minnesota Vikings arrived in looks fit for the location. 49ers tight end George Kittle rocked a mask and shirt that paid homage to luchador Penta, while Fred Warner had a Mexico national team kit on. Vikings running back Aaron Jones Sr . kept his sombrero trend alive in a full mariachi look.

 

 Denver Broncos linebacker Alex Singleton paid homage to former Broncos linebacker Tom Jackson by wearing Jackson's jersey before facing the Las Vegas Raiders . Jackson, a fixture at ESPN as a Hall of Fame broadcaster, died on Friday . He was 75.

 

 Dallas Cowboys wide receiver CeeDee Lamb hit the blue carpet in a plush charcoal jacket, wide-leg plaid trousers and chunky black boots. A scarf tied to his burgundy leather bag added a pop of color to the pregame look.

 Bryce Young goes with a modernized throwback flavor to the late 1990s and early 2000s aesthetic. Think Allen Iverson redefining NBA wardrobe attire with the baggy Reebok track pants and hats with titled swag. The modern unique addition here is the pants appear satin-like look that almost looks like Liquid Metal.

 Young doesn't make many statements with his words, but he does it with his actions. And this fit feels like he's tapping back into California childhood energy he grew up on. The LA hat slightly titled to the side shows that element too. It translated to his play as the Panthers put up 30-plus points on Baltimore Ravens .

  -- Cameron Wolfe 

 

 
 Thursday night fashion 
Texture did the talking in C.J. Stroud 's arrival. The Texans quarterback sported a gray knit polo paired with relaxed light-wash jeans, while a black woven bag, brown shoes and a blue-faced watch added the finishing touches.

title: NFL players with most at stake over rest of 2026: Pickens, McCarthy, Cousins
summary: Big money on the line for George Pickens and Brian Branch? QB1 role at stake for J.J. McCarthy? Here are 11 players with something to prove over the next seven weeks.
full_text:
Thanksgiving week is the start of the sprint to the end of the NFL's regular season . And while there are players who know their teams don't have much to play for between now and then, there are plenty more who have quite a bit riding on what happens over the rest of the 2026 campaign.

 Those stakes can be different things. For some, it's money, especially for young players on rookie deals who haven't yet signed a potentially lucrative second contract. For others, it's opportunity. There are rotational players who want to establish themselves as starters and veterans hanging on who want to stick in the starting lineup for another season.

 
 Subscribe: 'The Bill Barnwell Show' 

 
 I'll take a look at 11 of those players who have the most to gain or lose over the remainder of the season, inspired by what they did in Week 11 and what's to come over the rest of the year.

 

 
 Jump to: 
 Cousins |  Metcalf | Pickens 
 McCarthy  |  Lassiter | Rice 
 Branch  |  Shough  | Andrews 
 Watson | Van Ness 

 
 

 

 Kirk Cousins , QB, Minnesota Vikings 
 Well, the honeymoon is over. Last week, Vikings fans who had witnessed two months of Kyler Murray and Carson Wentz struggling to move the ball welcomed Cousins back with open arms, and despite a few hiccups, the good outweighed the bad. Cousins threw for 207 yards and two touchdowns in a comfortable victory over the rival Packers .

 On Sunday in what amounted to a de facto home game for the 49ers in Mexico City, the magic dissipated. A great outing from Cousins likely wouldn't have made the difference on a day when the vaunted Vikings defense allowed the 49ers to score touchdowns on three of their first four drives in a 35-10 loss , but coach Kevin O'Connell might have hoped to find out.

 

 Instead, playing a pass defense that Dak Prescott and the Cowboys picked apart last week , the Vikings struggled. Cousins went 26-of-38 for 235 yards with a brutal pick-six on an underneath pass that Ji'Ayir Brown jumped and returned to the house without even needing to break stride. After a touchdown on their second drive of the game and a field goal on their third, the Vikings didn't score again the rest of the way, with Justin Jefferson losing a fumble and two fourth-quarter drives failing on downs. 

 Cousins bears the brunt of the blame for the interception, and I suspect he'll wish he played better. But the most notable clip of this game from a Vikings perspective will probably be Cousins shouting at his offensive linemen on the sideline; he was knocked down seven times in the loss. And the issues that plagued Minnesota during the collective stints of Murray and Wentz at quarterback are likely to create problems for it against good teams moving forward.

 Again, they couldn't run the ball.  Aaron Jones Sr . had a physically impressive finish to his touchdown run, but the Vikings turned 21 carries into 69 yards and five first downs. Jordan Mason had a 16-yard carry, but it came against San Francisco's backups in the fourth quarter with Wentz on the field. The run game was mostly hopeless with Cousins out there.

 An absent run game and a trailing game script takes Cousins away from play-action, which is where he has been at his best as a pro, 2026 included. The Raiders couldn't run the ball, either, but Klint Kubiak is excellent at creating throws for his quarterback with play-fakes, run game be damned. Before his  trade to the Vikings , Cousins was third in the NFL in QBR when using play-action and 14th in the league when he was dropping back as a pure passer. Seven of Cousins' eight interceptions with the Raiders came in those pure dropback situations.

 On Sunday, Cousins was effective using play-action, going 7-of-12 for 91 yards, averaging 7.6 yards per throw. Without it? He went 19-of-26 for 144 yards, averaging 5.5 yards per attempt. That included the pick-six, too. With nothing threatening Brown downfield or any sort of run fake to throw off his read, the 49ers safety was able to come from the backside of the play and poach Cousins' attempted slant to Brown, all but deciding the contest late in the first half.

 Cousins has made more than $333 million in his career and has a minimum of another $10 million on the way in 2027. While many players on this list might have significant money riding on their performance over the rest of this season, that's probably not as important for Cousins. What might matter, though, is opportunity. If Cousins thrives in his second stint with the Vikings, O'Connell & Co. will likely bring him back as their starter in 2027, especially given the regrets the organization has about letting everyone from Cousins to Sam Darnold to Daniel Jones (and now potentially J.J. McCarthy ) walk out the door in years past. And even if the Vikings decide to go in a different direction, a successful second half from Cousins likely would earn the 38-year-old a starting opportunity somewhere else next season.

 

 There's still plenty of time for Cousins to get things right, and there won't be many teams capable of getting a multi-touchdown lead on Brian Flores' defense over the rest of the season. After mostly unbridled enthusiasm from all sides about Cousins returning to the Vikings, though, the blowout loss was the coming-back-to-Earth moment for everyone involved.

 

 

 
 

 DK Metcalf , WR, Pittsburgh Steelers 
 

 George Pickens , WR, Dallas Cowboys 
 Let's start with two wideouts who were essentially part of a multi-deal trade of sorts. The Steelers didn't want to re-sign Pickens, who was one year from unrestricted free agency, and traded him to the Cowboys  in 2025 for a third-round pick. That third-rounder became Drew Allar , who is playing behind Aaron Rodgers at quarterback. The Steelers filled their need for a top wideout by sending a second-rounder to the Seahawks for Metcalf. The Seahawks used that pick to move up and select a cornerstone safety in Nick Emmanwori .

 This sure looks like a three-team trade where two teams won and the Steelers lost. And it's not ideal to see your top wideout finish the day with as many receiving yards as personal foul penalties, but that was the Steelers' situation Sunday. In a frustrating loss to the Eagles , Metcalf caught just one pass on four targets for 2 yards before being ejected late in the third quarter  for attempting to poke cornerback Cooper DeJean in the eye. Rodgers dropped back 53 times and was sacked five times, but he spent most of the day targeting rookies Germie Bernard and Max Hurleman .

 This was probably rock-bottom for Metcalf's very disappointing tenure in Pittsburgh. In addition to trading that second-round pick to the Seahawks for Metcalf, the Steelers gave their new wideout a four-year, $132 million extension. (Emmanwori will make less than $12 million combined over his four-year deal in Seattle.) Metcalf racked up a career-low 850 yards in his first season with the Steelers before a late-season suspension after getting into an altercation with a fan ; he had just two catches in last season's playoff loss to the Texans .

 Though Rodgers was optimistic  about the blossoming connection with his training camp roommate this summer, Metcalf has looked even more detached from the offense this season. He's on pace to finish with just 738 receiving yards and three touchdowns, both of which would be career lows. His 1.3 yards per route run is also a career low, down from his 1.9 YPRR in Seattle and 1.8 YPRR a year ago.

 At his best, Metcalf has shown the ability to win downfield and overwhelm smaller defensive backs in contested-catch situations. Rodgers didn't make that throw very often in 2025, as Metcalf was targeted just 14 times on deep shots all season. Seven of those throws came in two games, suggesting that the Steelers had it as a priority heading into the game a couple of times and then forgot about getting Metcalf the football for multiple weeks.

 With Mike McCarthy in the fold in 2026, Rodgers has targeted Metcalf…

title: Bills' Grand Theft Auto VI-themed jab at Dolphins tops NFL Week 11 trolls
summary: NFL teams remained petty in Week 11, led by a post from the Buffalo Bills.
full_text:
Grand Theft Auto VI has taken over the entertainment world since its release Thursday. The video game's reach also carried over to the NFL, becoming the theme of a petty post Sunday.

 

 The Buffalo Bills defeated the Miami Dolphins 26-9 led by its defense. Buffalo gave up only 185 yards and picked off Dolphins quarterback Kyle McCord once. Josh Allen had two interceptions himself, but he also threw for 304 yards and a score.

 Other teams such as the New York Jets and Chicago Bears tapped into the GTA VI space, but the Bills' attempt felt more direct as they faced the Dolphins. The victory prompted Buffalo to post a custom game cover inspired by that of GTA VI, which is set in "Vice City," a fictional version of Miami. Instead of it reading "GTA VI" across the cover, the Bills added: "Bills Win" with players scattered throughout it.

 

 Here are the top trolls from NFL's Week 11.

 

 Carolina Panthers 35, Baltimore Ravens 33 
 It required a late stop, but the Carolina Panthers pulled out a wild victory against the Baltimore Ravens .

 Carolina went ahead on a 37-yard field goal with 1:44 left. Baltimore received possession with a chance to go ahead before Jacoby Brissett was picked off with 36 seconds left, clinching the Panthers' win.

 A clever caption kicked off Carolina's trolling as it wrote: "Came down to the wire," with "the wire" being a reference to the iconic HBO show set in Baltimore. Then, the Panthers shared a graphic of a panther standing over a Ravens helmet with the caption: "Charming," a reference to Baltimore's nickname as the "Charm City." They also wrote "nevermore" on the bottom in a nod to Edgar Allen Poe's "The Raven" poem where the raven featured repeats: "nevermore."

 

 
 Dallas Cowboys 50, Tennessee Titans 31 
 A 50-burger wasn't enough for the Dallas Cowboys , who rubbed salt in the Tennessee Titans ' wounds postgame.

 Dallas scored a touchdown on its first six possessions, the first time that has happened in its franchise history since at least 1978, according to ESPN Research. Cowboys quarterback Dak Prescott provided five of the team's seven touchdowns -- four in the air and one on the ground.

 Texas and Tennessee are known for their rich histories in country music, but the Cowboys claimed superiority over the Titans by captioning their post: "Texas Country," which has its unique sound.

 

 
 Philadelphia Eagles 19, Pittsburgh Steelers 16 
 The Philadelphia Eagles held on to defeat the Pittsburgh Steelers at home, ending a seven-game winless streak.

 Philadelphia put up 13 points in the first quarter, pacing it the rest of the game as Pittsburgh's offense struggled. The Steelers finally found the end zone with 1:20 left in the fourth, but it was too little, too late. They couldn't stop the Eagles on their ensuing drive and Philadelphia survived to win.

 Held at Lincoln Financial Field, it was an in-state matchup between Pennsylvania's two squads. The Eagles claimed Pennsylvania with a postgame caption that read: "Our State" in all-caps with an image of linebacker Jalyx Hunt  on his knees pointing to the sky and Steelers quarterback Aaron Rodgers in the background.

title: Bengals-Commanders odds, best bets: Tips, analysis and top plays
summary: Odds, analysis and recommended plays to help you bet the Bengals-Commanders matchup on Monday night.
full_text:
Cincinnati Bengals quarterback Joe Burrow enters "Monday Night Football" as the leading contender for MVP. He gets a chance to further his case for the award with another primetime win, and he's set up for success. The Washington Commanders blitz at a heavy rate (42%), and Burrow has been better when blitzed (86 QBR) than when not. And even though the Commanders blitz so much, they still entered Week 11 only 24th in pass rush win rate. This is all to say that Burrow should have plenty of time to throw and do damage.

 On the other sideline, Commanders quarterback  Jayden Daniels has had a decent season thus far, ranking 14th in QBR entering Sunday. But the Bengals present some challenges against opponents' passing games: Boye Mafe entered Week 10 ranked third in pass rush win rate at edge, Dexter Lawrence II has added 5.0 sacks from the interior, and cornerback  DJ Turner II  has allowed just 0.5 yards per coverage snap.

 

 

 

 Betting outlook 

 

 My inclination would be to bet Bengals -6 and under 54.5 if I were to bet the spread and the total. However, I might prefer to combine those in a way and just take the Commanders' team total under 23.5 (+100) .

 But that's all just vibes. As always, my inclination is to lean on statistical analysis and bet props. Let's look at those, instead.

 

 Notable player props, bets 
 

 Note: Odds by DraftKings   and subject to change. 

 Dexter Lawrence II sacks UNDER 0.25 (-210) 

 Walder: Lawrence has been playing well and has 5.0 sacks, but his pass rush win rate ranks in the 63rd percentile -- good but not otherworldly. Similarly, Daniels has taken sacks at a 6.6% clip this year, just a shade higher than average. When we consider those facts and the low base rate for any individual defensive tackle to record a sack in a game, my model makes the fair price on Lawrence's under -358.

 Jordan Battle tackles + assists UNDER 6.5 (-150) 

 

 Walder: Entering Week 11, there had been 598 games started by safeties this season. In 410 of those games (68.6%), that safety has recorded six or fewer combined tackles. Even if we filter that down to games in which the safety went on to play 90% of the defensive snaps (which is conservative, because it rules out an injury), that rate still drops to only 62.2%. There are plenty of reasons a safety might be expected to record more tackles than that, but I don't see them here. Battle's tackle rate is in the 48th percentile, and he doesn't have big run/pass tackle splits, as he recorded a tackle on 9.5% of pass plays and 10.8% of run plays, so I don't think game script is a big factor here. The odds are in our favor on the under.

 Bengals to NOT allow a first-drive sack (-416), Commanders to NOT allow a first-drive sack (-338) 

 Walder: These two (separate) bets just happen to be in the same game, but each are a value according to my first possession sack model. While the Commanders do bring extra heat frequently -- they have the third-highest blitz rate in the NFL -- they have a below-average pass rush win rate, and Joe Burrow has become awfully good at sack avoidance. That's my favorite bet of the two, but the other side looks pretty appealing, too. It's scarier because Boye Mafe and Dexter Lawrence II are playing well, but the price is too good to pass up.

 

 Jayden Daniels rushing yards OVER 39.5 (+107) 

 Ben Solak: The Bengals had the worst defense against the QB rush entering Week 11. They have allowed 6.7 yards per rush -- almost a yard more than the Arizona Cardinals , who are in second place (5.9) -- and their 3.8 carries per game allowed is above league average as well. Cincinnati hasn't even faced a particularly staunch group of mobile quarterbacks. Malik Willis had a huge day in Week 5, but Baker Mayfield got the Bengals for 30 yards in Week 1, and C.J. Stroud had 29 yards on just three carries in Week 2. Cincinnati didn't see Lamar Jackson this season and has played Aaron Rodgers twice, for goodness sake!

 

 The Commanders need more from their running game if they're to keep Burrow on the sideline. Running back Jacory Croskey-Merritt should be back, but that isn't enough. I expect Daniels to get a little more involved with the running game here as the Commanders look to get the ball on the boundary and away from Lawrence. Daniels had three designed runs (kneels excluded) last week against the New York Giants -- his most in any game so far this season -- and he scrambled another five times as well.

 I'll take this pre-flop but watch live to see whether the Commanders' under-center handoff game falls dead (as expected) over the first couple of drives and consider hitting a live over as they integrate Daniels to get the ground game working again.

title: Inside the gymnastics lore of Bengals star Ja'Marr Chase
summary: Ja'Marr Chase's skill set suggests formal gymnastics training, but the reality isn't quite that simple.
full_text:
CINCINNATI -- It was a move that looked so improbable that the majority of the 70,747 in attendance inside NRG Stadium didn't seem to process it in real time.

 When the Cincinnati Bengals visited the Houston Texans in Week 2, quarterback Joe Burrow heaved a deep ball toward wide receiver  Ja'Marr Chase  ( "F--- it, Ja'Marr's down there somewhere" ). As Chase stumbled toward the near right corner of the end zone, he twisted his body, somehow located the ball to make the catch and then dragged both of his feet inbounds to complete a touchdown.

 While the crowd in Houston reacted in disbelief as the replay on the videoboards confirmed it was a catch, TV announcer Kevin Harlan extolled the All-Pro receiver while watching the catch in slow motion.

 "Oh, the contortion!," Harlan exclaimed. "The body control! The concentration!"

 It was almost as if Harlan was talking about a gymnast. Instead, he was talking about a 6-foot, 205-pound dynamic route runner who is one of the best wide receivers in the NFL.

 Over the years, Chase has spoken about how he took up gymnastics as a kid, once adding that it was something that never leaves his spirit. Given how well he controls his body and can still backflip from a standstill position, it could seem as if those skills might have helped him become an All-Pro player. But with a bit more digging, the reality isn't that linear.

 

 "In gymnastics, you got to stick the landing," Bengals wide receivers coach Troy Walters told ESPN. "And in football, the more times you stick the landing and not go to the ground and fall down, probably the more successful you're going to be.

 "I could definitely see that [connection]."

 Chase was a child with energy that needed to be expended. Sometimes, that manifested in activities outside of football, such as skateboarding. But that also meant leaping off things such as a house, garage or garbage can.

 Toleah Chase decided that if her son, who was around 9 at the time, was doing all that, it would be done correctly. Chase's older brother, Terell Smith, spearheaded the mission.

 "My brother knew somebody [who had access to a gym], and we met there when it was closed, and he taught me how to backflip," Ja'Marr told ESPN earlier this year. "My mom only made me do it so I wouldn't hurt myself."

 After Chase came back from learning the backflips, he would call Toleah into a doorway in their home to showcase his new skill.

 "He was very excited about it," Toleah told ESPN. "And I was a nervous wreck.

 "I always used to tell him, 'Please be careful.' Don't hurt yourself. He was like, 'No, no, I got it, Mom. I know how to do it right.'"

 

 He wasn't exaggerating. In 2019, Chase racked up 1,780 receiving yards in 14 games, and along with Burrow, led the Tigers to a national title. Two years later, Burrow and Chase were reunited in Cincinnati, where Chase has made catches that look straight out of a floor routine.

 Teaching gymnastics concepts to football players isn't new. Jay Clark, who led LSU's women's gymnastics team to an NCAA runner-up finish this year, is a proponent of having athletes do some form of gymnastics at a young age because of the foundational skills that translate to other sports

 "It's control due to the spatial awareness that they have -- the aerial sense, knowing where the ground is and being able to feel that innately," Clark said. "Some people can be born with it, but the reality is that our sport probably combines every part of athleticism better than any other, whether that's strength, power, quickness, spatial awareness, balance, all of it."

 Occasionally, Chase will showcase his "gymnastics" skills in fun ways. The first example was against the San Francisco 49ers  in 2023, when he celebrated a touchdown with a backflip in the end zone.

 "I just wanted to have some fun," Chase said after that game. "I did gymnastics when I was young."

 Two years later, it came up again when asked if he did things to grab his parents' attention while he was growing up.

 "I did gymnastics, y'all," Chase said in September 2025. "It can't leave my spirit."

 This year, those incredible catches have highlighted another strong season. Along with his catch against Houston, he had a leaping, twisting touchdown grab against the Miami Dolphins when he secured the ball with his shoulder pad before landing back on the field.

 After a slow start, Chase is on pace for one of his best seasons. He's coming off a game in which he had 11 catches for 231 yards against the Pittsburgh Steelers  in the Bengals' fifth straight win. It was Chase's third consecutive game with at least 225 receiving yards, tying Jerry Rice, Calvin Johnson and Julio Jones for the most in NFL history.

 Chase will lead the Bengals against the Washington Commanders on "Monday Night Football" (8:15, ET, ESPN), and it should be no surprise that he excels in primetime. He has 110.5 receiving yards per game in 17 primetime games, the NFL's highest mark since the 1970 merger.

 

 "The way Ja'Marr is able to track the ball down the field and just catch it way off his body -- the hand strength, the tracking ability -- it's pretty special," said Bengals offensive coordinator Dan Pitcher.

 Chase's body composition is one of the things that make him unique. Since he entered the league in 2021 as the fifth pick, coaches and teammates noted how Chase had all the tools of a wide receiver but was built similar to a running back. That enabled him to break tackles and pick up yards after the catch.

 But as this year has displayed, one of Chase's greatest strengths is his ability to control his frame while making catches.

 "A lot of times, guys go up, and when they come down, they're all out of whack," said Walters, who has been Chase's position coach since he entered the league. "They hit the ground hard, the ball bounces out.

 "But he comes down where he's able to control his body or contort his body in the air to make an acrobatic catch."

 Similar to Walters, Higgins can understand the comparisons to a gymnast, but Higgins sees something more basic: "Just a freak athlete at the end of the day [who] has God-given talents."
