title: NFL Thanksgiving games: Traditions, best moments, team records, 2026 schedule
summary: NFL games on Thanksgiving Day date back to 1934, and the Lions and Cowboys are always in action. We revisit top performers, the best moments and more.
full_text:
Thanksgiving Day to sports fans is as much about football as it is about the traditional turkey dinner. From high school football in the morning to watching the afternoon game on TV as dinner starts, this tradition is as old as time. Well, almost as old as time.

 The  Detroit Lions  have played at home on Thanksgiving every year since 1934 -- except when games were paused from 1939 to 1944 during World War II. The annual holiday tradition expanded to add a home game for the Dallas Cowboys  in the 1960s. In 2006, the NFL added a third game with no specific host team to the prime-time window.

 Here's the 2026  Thanksgiving Day schedule : 

 
 Chicago Bears at Detroit Lions: 1 p.m. ET, CBS 
 Philadelphia Eagles at Dallas Cowboys: 4:30 p.m. ET, Fox 
 Kansas City Chiefs at Buffalo Bills : 8:20 p.m. ET, NBC 
 
 Each of these games has a halftime performance. Wu-Tang Clan will perform in Detroit, Miranda Lambert will take the stage in Arlington, Texas, and the Goo Goo Dolls will perform in Buffalo.

 So why do the Lions and Cowboys always play at home on Thanksgiving? What does the day look like for the coaches, players, families and fans who put their holiday celebrations on pause to take part? And how many thousands of pounds of food is served at the stadiums? We asked NFL Nation reporters Todd Archer and Eric Woodyard to explain the history. We have also laid out the Thanksgiving stats and numbers you should know, and even took a journey back in time to explore the biggest and best moments on the turkey day stage.

 Note: This story was originally posted in November 2021 and has been updated for 2026. 

 
 Jump to a section: 
 Thanksgiving records  |  By the numbers 
 Best moments in Thanksgiving history 

 
 

 How the Thanksgiving tradition began 
 The Lions were first up to host games every year: In 1934, Lions owner G.A. Richards scheduled a holiday matchup between the Lions and the Bears. Earlier that year Richards had purchased the Portsmouth (Ohio) Spartans football team and moved it to the Motor City, renaming it the Detroit Lions. The defending back-to-back world champion Bears beat the Lions 19-16 in front of 26,000 at the University of Detroit Stadium on Nov. 29, 1934.

 Now, nine decades later, Thanksgiving football has become a staple in Detroit, with the Lions going 37-45-2 in the annual holiday classic. -- Woodyard 

 Thirty-two years later, the Cowboys joined as a home team:  The Cowboys first played on Thanksgiving in 1966, beating the Cleveland Browns  26-14 at the Cotton Bowl. General manager Tex Schramm wanted more national publicity for the Cowboys -- this was before they were known as America's Team -- and thought the holiday game made perfect sense. The NFL was a bit worried, however, and guaranteed the Cowboys a certain amount of gate revenue. A crowd of 80,259 showed up and a tradition was born. The Cowboys have played on every Thanksgiving Day since -- except in 1975 and 1977.

 

 Why didn't the Cowboys play on Thanksgiving those two years?  Prior to the 1975 season, then-commissioner Pete Rozelle wanted to see if the St. Louis Cardinals could build their popularity under coach Don Coryell, whose teams were nicknamed the Cardiac Kids because of their exciting finishes. So he scheduled them to host Thanksgiving games in 1975 and 1977. The Cardinals lost both games decidedly, and Rozelle went back to Schramm to ask whether the Cowboys would take the Thanksgiving game back.

 "It was a dud in St. Louis," Schramm said in 1988 to the Chicago Tribune. "Pete asked if we'd take it back. I said only if we get it permanently. It's something you have to build as a tradition. He said, 'It's yours forever.'" -- Archer 

 
 Thanksgiving records 
 

 Given how long the series has lasted, it's not a surprise that the Lions have the most wins and losses on Thanksgiving Day. But two other teams that frequent the holiday tradition are the Bears and Packers. 

 

 Detroit Lions : 38-46-2 
 

 Dallas Cowboys : 35-22-1 
 

 Chicago Bears : 20-16-2 
 

 Green Bay Packers : 17-20-2 
 
 What's it like to play on Thanksgiving?  
 Pro Bowl left guard Tyler Smith grew up in Fort Worth, Texas, so he knew all about the Thanksgiving tradition when he was drafted by the Cowboys in the first round in 2022.

 Though he might have seen Tony Romo throw five touchdown passes against the Buccaneers in 2006 and  Dak Prescott beat Washington in 2018 with Amari Cooper catching two touchdowns on 180 yards, it was Lions defensive tackle Ndamukong Suh's stomping on Packers offensive lineman Evan Dietrich-Smith in 2011 that he remembers most.

 "All of America was like, 'Wow, did he really just do that?'" Smith said. "I've never seen anybody do that before."

 Now that he is playing on Thanksgiving, he called it an honor.

 "It's a privilege for me each and every opportunity, I think, just to be able to play on Thanksgiving, to be able to have my people gather around, just enjoy the day and see me get to live out my dreams," Smith said. "That's really big for me."

 Growing up, Smith would head to see family in Shreveport, Louisiana, for the holiday. The games were on TV whether he was at his great aunt's house or an uncle's house. There would be more than 20 people in the house, most of them watching football.

 These days, Smith has dinner after the game.

 "That's kind of been my routine," Smith said. "For my game days, I like to be alone [the night before]. I don't like to have that many people around me, so definitely no Thanksgiving festivities before the game, but afterwards, after we handle our business and do what we need to do, definitely get together with family."

 His mother will cook a ham and cabbage greens.

 

 "Stuff that she knows I like," Smith said.

 What does he bring?

 "My appetite," Smith said. -- Archer 

 Lions wide receiver Amon-Ra St. Brown is gearing up to play in his sixth NFL Thanksgiving game with the team, though to him the experience is not so unusual because he would always have at least a practice on the holiday in high school.

 Still, playing on Thanksgiving in the NFL is a big tradition -- and one he has embraced.

 "We always play on Thanksgiving, but I think it's kind of nice because if you have a game on Sunday, you've got to practice on Thursdays, which kind of runs until 5 o'clock, but if you have a game, we have a game at 12:30, we play and then after that we're free and we can hang out with family the rest of the day. You don't have to worry about getting up the next day, so I like the tradition," St. Brown told ESPN.

 "It's fun, and everyone's tuned in on Thanksgiving. Everyone is watching football. I remember as a kid watching Thanksgiving football because you're out eating with friends and then you just throw football on."  -- Woodyard 

 
 How do players celebrate Thanksgiving? 
 Lions: Celebrations generally don't happen until the next day, when Lions players can celebrate with their families. Lomas Brown, former Lions Pro Bowl OT (1985-95), says he "couldn't wait until after the game was over, man." 

 "Because look, it wasn't just that Thursday night, at least for me, I went on an eating binge Thursday, Friday, Saturday and Sunday. I would put on weight over the holiday because a brother would throw down because you didn't have no more responsibility after that game until next week. So, it was almost like another little open week, and that's the way we kind of looked at it, too." -- Woodyard 

 Cowboys: For the Cowboys, most players with families will also celebrate on Friday. With a late-afternoon kickoff, most of the time players will not get back to their homes until later in the evening, far too late for such a heavy meal.  -- Archer 

 
 Teams give back to community 
 Cowboys: The Cowboys open the Salvation Army's Red Kettle Campaign kickoff at halftime of every Thanksgiving game. Since 1997, nearly $3 billion has been raised and aiding the Salvation Army is a long-standing priority for Cowboys owner Jerry…

title: Tracking Jaguars CB/WR Travis Hunter's 2026 season: Snaps on offense, defense
summary: Every week, we will look at how many snaps the two-way corner/receiver plays on offense and defense. Is there a trend in his usage?
full_text:
The Jacksonville Jaguars were emphatic in the offseason that cornerback/wide receiver  Travis Hunter was going to play on both sides of the ball in 2026. The Jaguars have followed through on that, making the 2025 No. 2 overall pick a starter on defense and mixing him in where designed on offense. 

 He has started every game at cornerback and has played at least four snaps on offense in all but one game (Week 4 at Cincinnati). He has made big plays on both sides of the ball and had the best game of his career in Week 6, when he clearly showed what kind of threat he can be. Head coach Liam Coen has been consistent in saying that Hunter's offensive usage is fluid.

 "You want to continue to do what we think is going to give us the best chance at winning throughout the course of the week," he said. "And so, if that's Travis getting more touches, then absolutely will."

 How has Hunter's usage evolved this season? Each week we'll track his stats and evaluate the impact he had on the game.

 

 

 

 Week 11 at New York Giants 

 Hunter played a season-high 73 total snaps (his previous high was 71 in Week 4 against Cincinnati) and a career-high six special teams snaps against the Giants. He played 61 snaps on defense and six on offense, where he touched the ball twice. He had one catch for 3 yards and one rush on an end around that gained 9 yards. It was a quiet day on defense, too, with just six tackles. Hunter has been returning punts in practice, but the Jaguars used Ameer Abdullah in that role against the Giants instead of Parker Washington .

 

 

 Week 10 at Tennessee Titans 
 Hunter came up with his highlight play of the season so far with a diving interception of a Cam Ward pass in the first quarter. Ward scrambled to his right on third-and-8 from the Jacksonville 35-yard line and threw back toward the left side of the field for receiver Elic Ayomanor near the sideline, but Hunter snagged the ball and cradled it to his body with his left hand as he hit the ground.

 "It was an unbelievable catch, unbelievable play," head coach Liam Coen said. "... Such a special play by obviously a special player."

 The Jaguars turned that into an eventual field goal and 10-3 lead early in the second quarter. Hunter, who is tied with cornerback Jourdan Lewis with a team-high three interceptions, played 56 snaps on defense, five on special teams, and five on offense against the Titans. He touched the ball on three of those offensive snaps: An end around that gained 3 yards and two catches for 16 yards.

 

 

 Week 9 at Baltimore Ravens 
 It was a quiet night for Hunter on defense -- five tackles on 44 snaps -- but a bad one on offense. Hunter played six snaps on offense and fumbled the only time he touched the ball. Hunter caught a receiver screen from Trevor Lawrence , and Ravens safety Malaki Starks knocked the ball loose 1 yard behind the line of scrimmage. Linebacker Teddye Buchanan recovered the ball at midfield, and the Ravens took over with 5:10 to play in the third quarter with the Jaguars ahead 20-3.

 The turnover didn't hurt the Jaguars, though, because the Ravens then turned the ball over on downs four plays later, with tight end Mark Andrews fumbling the snap on fourth-and-1. Hunter was officially credited with one catch for minus-1 yard.

 

 

 Week 8 vs. Indianapolis Colts 

 Coming off a Week 7 bye week, it was a relatively quiet day from Hunter -- in terms of stats, anyway. Hunter played 49 of the 60 total snaps on defense tallying four tackles. He played six snaps on offense with one rush for 5 yards and no catches on one target. A new wrinkle this week is that he played a season-high four snaps on special teams -- returning a punt for 1 yard and securing a fair catch on another.

 

 

 Week 6 vs. Houston Texans in London 
 Hunter had the best game of his career against the Texans at Wembley Stadium, catching four passes for 59 yards and a touchdown and also intercepting C.J. Stroud in the end zone. He's just the fourth player since the 1970 AFL/NFL merger with a receiving touchdown and interception in the same game and the first to do it since Philadelphia's Brian Dawkins in 2002. The touchdown and interception came on consecutive drives.

 Per NFL Next Gen Stats, Hunter had 34 coverage snaps and limited the Texans to two catches on five targets. However, he also was hit with a questionable pass interference penalty in the end zone against Nico Collins that gave the Texans the ball at the 1-yard line late in the first half. Despite that, this was the first time Hunter has made a significant impact on both sides of the ball -- 58 snaps on defense and 9 on offense (season high) -- in the same game in his 13 career games. 

 

 

 Week 5 vs. Philadelphia Eagles in London 
 Hunter played every defensive snap (59) for the second week in a row and had six tackles (second-most on the team) and a pass breakup. He was penalized for defensive pass interference that wiped out a third-and-17 incompletion in the second quarter. It gave the Eagles the ball at the Jaguars' 3-yard line and Philadelphia running back Will Shipley scored two plays later.

 On offense, Hunter played five snaps and touched the ball for the first time since Week 1, catching a 9-yard pass on second-and-7 from the Jaguars' 40-yard line. Parker Washington scored on a 51-yard catch-and-run on the next play.

 

 

 Week 4 at  Cincinnati Bengals 
 Hunter played every defensive snap (71) in a 22-17 win against the Bengals and had four tackles and two pass breakups. It's the first time in his career he's played every defensive snap and it was necessary because the Jaguars were down cornerbacks Montaric Brown (hamstring) and Christian Braswell (knee) because of injury.

 "He played his ass off today," head coach Liam Coen said.

 Hunter, however, called his play "decent" and was disappointed that his interception got erased by a roughing the passer penalty on defensive tackle Arik Armstead .

 "I like to criticize myself a lot harder," Hunter said. "My wife does, too. I still give up a catch today, so she's going to be on me about that when I get home."

 Hunter didn't play at all on offense, the first time in his career that has happened. Coen said he didn't want to risk him getting hurt on that side of the ball because that would leave them down three cornerbacks. Hunter said he wasn't mad at that decision.

 

 

 Week 3 vs. New England Patriots 
 In a 35-6 win against the Patriots, Hunter saw an increase in snaps with 42 on defense (70%) and a decrease on offense with four snaps (6.7% of all offensive snaps). He recorded four tackles and his first career interception, picking off New England quarterback Drake Maye in the back of the end zone late in the first half to preserve the Jaguars' 14-3 lead. Maye was trying to hit receiver Efton Chism III on third-and-goal from the 2-yard line, but Hunter out-jumped Chism for the ball. Hunter didn't touch the ball on offense for the second consecutive game, leaving him with only two touches so far this season.

 
 

 Week 2 at Denver Broncos 
 Hunter played 43 total snaps in the loss against the Broncos: 35 on defense (59.3% of all defensive snaps), seven on offense (12.7% of all offensive snaps) and one on special teams. He had one pass breakup and four tackles, and he was penalized for pass interference on a Bo Nix sideline pass to receiver Courtland Sutton . The 22-yard penalty -- plus Coen's unsportsmanlike conduct penalty for arguing the call -- gave the Broncos the ball at the Jaguars' 3-yard line. The Broncos scored what turned out to be the game-winning touchdown on the next play. Hunter was not targeted on offense.

 After Week 2, Coen explained that his cornerbacks are handling drives with a planned rotation -- which is why Hunter was in for only 59.3% of defensive plays.

 "We did it for the most part of the last season as well, before Travis got hurt," Coen said. "It's something that we got to continue to do. We have corners…

title: Who are the winningest NFL coaches of all time?
summary: From Belichick to Reid, there are many iconic coaches in NFL history. Who has the best career record? Check out the stat breakdown now.
full_text:
Only four head coaches in NFL history have won 300 career games across the regular season and postseason. Kansas City Chiefs  coach Andy Reid was the last to cross the 300-win plateau.

 Reid recorded his 300th career victory on Jan. 18, 2025, when his Chiefs defeated the Houston Texans 23-14 in the AFC divisional round.

 Reid, who signed a five-year, $100 million extension with the Chiefs in April 2024, entered the 2026 season looking to add to his career win total and close the gap between him and the NFL's all-time winningest head coach, Hall of Famer Don Shula.

 Let's take a look at which head coaches have the most career victories in NFL history (including both regular-season and postseason play):

 *Active NFL head coach 

 5. Tom Landry, 270 wins 

 Landry was the Dallas Cowboys' head coach for an NFL-record 29 years in a row and the team had 20 consecutive winning seasons, which is also a league record. Landry led Dallas to two Super Bowl wins, defeating the Miami Dolphins in Super Bowl VI and the Denver Broncos in Super Bowl XII. He was named the NFL's Coach of the Year in 1966 and the UPI NFL Coach of the Year in 1975. Landry was an innovator, with the 4-3 defense among his creations. He was named to the NFL's 100th Anniversary All-Time Team.

 *4. Andy Reid, 315 wins 

 Reid is the only head coach in NFL history who has won 100 games with two franchises: the Philadelphia Eagles (coaching the team from 1999 through 2012) and the Chiefs (he has coached Kansas City since 2013). He led the Eagles on multiple deep playoff runs, including a Super Bowl in 2004 and three straight conference finals from 2001 to 2003. However, he wasn't able to hoist the Lombardi Trophy until he arrived in Kansas City. He has turned the Chiefs into a juggernaut, winning three Super Bowls. Reid is an offensive mastermind and quarterback whisperer. He'll likely continue to rack up wins moving forward with Patrick Mahomes , Travis Kelce & Co.

 

 3. George Halas, 324 wins 

 Halas was a co-founder of the NFL and creator of the Bears. For 10 years, he served as player-coach-executive for the Bears (which is how he earned the nickname "Mr. Everything"). In 1930, he retired as a player and focused on ownership, but he would later return to coach the Bears several times. Halas led the Bears to eight NFL championships, tying Belichick's number of titles. Halas coached the team for 40 years and had just six losing seasons. He helped create the T-formation system and used it to set an NFL record for the biggest blowout in league history: a 73-0 win over the Washington team in the 1940 NFL Championship Game. Halas was selected as the AP's NFL Coach of the Year in 1963 and 1965, and he was named to the NFL's 100th Anniversary All-Time Team.

 2. Bill Belichick, 333 wins 

 Belichick is considered by some as the greatest coach in all of professional sports, as he has won an NFL-record eight Super Bowls (six as a head coach with the Patriots and two as an assistant coach with the Giants). He also ranks first among all NFL coaches in playoff wins with 31. Belichick was named the AP's NFL Coach of the Year in 2003, 2007 and 2010. Many franchises have hired away Belichick's assistants and tried to replicate his "Patriot Way," but it hasn't been the same without him. If Belichick returns to NFL coaching, he is just 26 regular-season wins from surpassing Don Shula as the winningest regular-season coach of all time. 

 1. Don Shula, 347 wins 

 After playing in the NFL as a defensive back for seven seasons, Shula decided to retire and become a coach. He got his first head-coaching opportunity in 1963 with the Baltimore Colts, whom he led to the NFL championship in 1968. From 1970 through 1995, Shula had a legendary run as head coach of the Dolphins. Shula led the Dolphins to a pair of Super Bowl victories (in Super Bowl VII and Super Bowl VIII). Miami had a perfect season in 1972, making Shula the only coach in NFL history to go undefeated. He was named the AP's NFL Coach of the Year in 1964, 1967, 1968 and 1972. Whether you're just counting regular-season wins (328) or including playoff wins (347), Shula is the winningest coach in NFL history.

title: Another year of Geno Smith? Jets pleased with the QB's play
summary: New York's QB is coming off his best game of the season against the Chargers.
full_text:
INGLEWOOD, Calf. --  New York Jets quarterback Geno Smith left last week's game on a golf cart, saving him from having to walk to his car on his injured left ankle. A few days later, he was limping around the locker room, undergoing early-morning and late-night treatments. This didn't look like a player on the verge of his best game of the season.

 "I always felt like I was going to play," Smith said Sunday night at SoFi Stadium, "but you have to manage the pain."

 He managed nicely. This week, he left the stadium on cloud nine, walking on air after beating the Los Angeles Chargers , 27-24, to snap a five-game losing streak for the Jets.

 Showing no ill effects from the injury, Smith was nearly flawless, completing 17 of 21 passes for 176 yards and three touchdowns -- a season-high 91.4 QBR. He directed five scoring drives on the first five possessions, as the Jets ended their two-game touchdown drought and resembled the balanced attack they always wanted to be.

 

 "Geno was slicing and dicing," said coach Aaron Glenn, usually not prone to rhyming.

 Smith has accomplished something that didn't seem possible only eight months ago: He's playing his way into their future -- well, 2027 anyway. When the Jets acquired him in a trade from the Las Vegas Raiders , the fanbase groaned, as if to say, "Oh, no, not again."

 His first stint with the Jets (2013 to 2016) conjures up mainly bad memories and, even though he reinvented himself during some good years with the Seattle Seahawks , it's a "What have you done for me lately?" league. And Smith didn't do much last season with the moribund Raiders, throwing a league-high 17 interceptions on a team that landed the No. 1 pick in the draft.

 So, no, there wasn't a whole lot of optimism when the Jets signed up for Geno 2.0. Evidently, what happened in Vegas stayed in Vegas. Look at him now.

 Smith has 15 touchdown passes, only three interceptions. His completion rate (68.1%) is slightly above his career average. He has passed for 2,402 yards -- a 3,700-yard pace -- and his QBR is a very respectable 56.5. The Jets haven't had a quarterback play this well since Ryan Fitzpatrick in 2015.

 The Jets don't have a veteran quarterback under contract for 2027, and they will need a bridge to help with the transition to the quarterback they presumably will draft in the spring. Smith, 36, can be that guy. He won't come cheaply. You can bet he will seek more than the $19.5 million he's making this season from the Jets and Raiders, who are paying $16.2 million of his salary, but it might be a worthwhile investment for the Jets.

 They're only 3-8, facing a likely coaching change -- which would introduce new variables into the equation. But the Jets know better than most teams that finding a competent veteran isn't easy. Smith certainly would be one of the more viable veterans on the open market.

 "No one is surprised; that's Geno," wide receiver Garrett Wilson said of Smith's season. "He's productive as hell. He can put the ball in any spot. When I watched him play at West Virginia, that's what it looked like. There were some throws that he got into tight windows [Sunday]. I'm like, 'Man, what a baller.' I'm happy he's having the season he's having."

 Facing the struggling Chargers (1-9), ranked 25th in points allowed per game (26.6), Smith completed 14 straight passes at one point. He hit running back  Breece Hall out of the backfield for a 7-yard touchdown, then found graybeard wide receiver Sterling Shepard  -- elevated Saturday from the practice squad -- for a pair of touchdowns.

 Two of those scoring passes came outside the pocket, one on a designed rollout, the other when he was flushed by pressure -- impressive stuff, considering his achy wheel.

 

 "Adrenaline," said Glenn, explaining how Smith was able to play effectively through the ankle injury.

 Counting his first go-round with New York, this was Smith's fourth game with three touchdown passes and 80% completion rate. All other Jets quarterbacks have combined for three such games in franchise history -- Mike White , Chad Pennington and Ken O'Brien.

 You may want to reread that paragraph again. Stunning, isn't it?

 "I feel like I can play a whole lot better," Smith said.

 He was coming off back-to-back mediocre performances, so it's not like this is an extended heater. Also, Smith has taken some untimely sacks and the offense has struggled in the red zone. But let's be realistic: He's giving them bang for their buck, considering they got him for a late-round pick swap and are paying him only $3.3 million.

 "Listen, he's a hell of a dude now," Glenn said. "You're talking about someone that understands the game, commands the huddle -- a bona fide leader, vocally and by his actions too. I'm glad we have him."

title: Inside Commanders DC Daronte Jones' unusual coaching journey
summary: From living in his car to various college offices, Washington defensive coordinator Daronte Jones has paid his dues.
full_text:
ASHBURN, Va. -- The gale-force Chicago wind shook Daronte Jones' car and rattled his nerves. It did not blow the future Washington Commanders defensive coordinator off his path, but it made him question his life choices.

 It was March 2002, nearly three weeks after Jones landed a job at Division III North Park University on the city's northwest side, and he was sleeping in his red 1988 Honda Prelude.

 At around 11 p.m., with winds reaching as high 50 mph, he called his aunt Lisa Simmons in Maryland.

 

 "She picked up thinking it was an emergency, which it really wasn't, but it could have been, mentally," Jones said. "The car was rocking side to side.

 "I remember calling home and naturally the family was like, 'Just come home. What are we doing?' That was a moment where you really had to think about how much you're willing to sacrifice, and is it worth it?"

 Jones didn't go home.

 That was the first decision in a long list of sacrifices the first-time NFL defensive coordinator made early in his coaching career. He lived out of his car for two months in Chicago. Then, in 2010, while a grad assistant at UCLA, he slept in the cornerbacks' meeting room for most of his year with the Bruins. Two years later, as a University of Hawaii assistant, he slept in his office for a year before moving into an alumnus' pool house.

 Along his journey -- often with his pet python, Goldie Gambino, living in his book bag -- he also coached high school for two years and nearly left the profession twice -- attending law school at one point, and applying to the U.S. Capitol Police at another in hopes of becoming a Federal Air Marshal. However, like on that frigid night in the Windy City, he always resolved to stick it out.

 "It was like, 'Is it ever going to end?'" Jones told ESPN. "I was like, 'Maybe it's not for me.'"

 A turbulent start to his career helped him develop a deep appreciation for future opportunities -- and for finally reaching this point in his career. It taught him patience; it taught him humility.

 The big breaks finally came, which have led Jones, who is a native of Anne Arundel County in Maryland, to Washington and Monday night's matchup with the Cincinnati Bengals and their high-powered offense (8:15 p.m. ET, on ESPN).

 Jones may have been leaning on the perseverance he forged early in his career to weather Washington's sluggish start on defense this season. After seven weeks, his unit ranked 31st in scoring and 25th in yards. Since, it's seventh in scoring and 19th in yards.

 "It can't get any worse than what it was," Jones said. "I'm not sleeping in my car. I have a home to go to. I have a great family. ... It helps put things in perspective. When you're in the storm and you're in the moment, you've got to take a step back and be like, compared to this isn't not as bad. You've got to compartmentalize the storms."

 

 

 BEFORE ARRIVING IN Washington, Jones had held 14 different coaching jobs, from Division II to Division I-AA, high school, the Canadian Football League to multiple Division I stops and stints with three NFL teams.

 But one of the most formative roles isn't included on his résumé: North Park University.

 Jones spent six months at the tiny school in 2002, but left before coaching a game.

 When he arrived at North Park as a defensive assistant, Jones, fresh off a graduate assistant role at Lenoir-Rhyne University in Hickory, North Carolina, was told he could sleep on a couch in an apartment with other coaches. Jones didn't trust the couch, which, he said, had looked like it had been pulled off the street -- so he slept in his Prelude.

 He kept a suitcase in his locker but other clothes in the Honda -- along with his nearly 3-foot pet Albino Burmese python. Jones said he would park his car near the facility in a different spot each night. On cold nights, he said he'd crack the windows for airflow, turn on the heat and try to stay warm.

 

 Simmons often lent him money when she could. But she said Jones told her, "'I'll just work it out; I'll stay in the car.' He said, 'All I need you to do is call me and wake me up.' So I would get up early and call him, 'Daronte, it's time to get up.' We really wanted things to work out for him, and he was willing to make the sacrifice. We would support him the best we could."

 Simmons never wavered. Every morning at 4 a.m., Jones would receive a call from his aunt, then head to the facility to shower before others arrived.

 Throughout this time, Jones said he had been telling the other coaches on staff he was living in a hotel. When some found out he wasn't, they offered him the pantry in their apartment, which was on the porch and attached to the kitchen with screens that needed fixing. Jones said the room was full of boxes and was so narrow, his double mattress couldn't lie flat -- it was curled on the outside because it wouldn't fit.

 His grandfather told him how to fix and seal the screens, and Jones bought a space heater to keep him and Goldie Gambino comfortable. "I'd sleep in jeans, sweats, a hoodie, leather jacket to stay warm," Jones said. "But it was better than the car."

 Four months later, he accepted a restricted earnings job at Nicholls State. Though the opportunity at North Park might have seemed to be a waste, having never coached a game for the Vikings, the sacrifices Jones made in Chicago became a key theme throughout the rest of his journey.

 

 

 JONES NEARLY DROPPED out of coaching -- twice.

 The first time occurred in 2004 when he was 25 and coaching defense at Jeanerette High School in New Iberia, Louisiana. It was his first year at Jeanerette but second year coaching high school in Louisiana. Jones had given himself a deadline: become a college Division 1 position coach by age 26 or quit.

 He took the LSAT with plans to attend Southern University's law school with an Omega Psi Phi fraternity brother. Then, Mike Lynn, who was Jones' former position coach at Morgan State, where he played offensive line, became the head coach at Bowie State. Their connection led to a job offer. But Jones wasn't sure that he wanted to accept. He could continue teaching in high school, then attend law school classes at night.

 Zeb Simon, Jones' boss at Jeanerette, told him it was a no-brainer and issued him an ultimatum.

 "I'm going to give you a choice," Simon said. "Either you go or I'm going to fire you.'"

 Jones went.

 "It took me about a couple weeks to make that decision," he said.

 

 Five seasons into his stint with the Bulldogs as assistant head coach and defensive coordinator -- the last of which saw his defense ranked No. 1 in Division II -- Jones reached another crossroads. The move to Division I wasn't happening. So, after the 2009 season, he applied for a job with the U.S. Capitol Police, hoping to become a Federal Air Marshal. He had received an offer, and they were in the process of doing a background check when UCLA called. "Maybe it's time for me to look at something else because now I'm in my 30s, and I was like: 'I've got to do something,'" Jones said he was thinking at the time.

 The Bruins offered him a graduate assistant's job. It meant going from a salary of $64,000 a year to $1,000 per month while living in the Los Angeles area. He first consulted Damon Wilson, his boss in 2009 at Bowie State, about the UCLA opportunity. But it was longtime advisor Lional Vital, who spent part of four seasons in the NFL and also served as a scout and executive for 30 years, who convinced him.

 "You've already been homeless," Vital told him.

 Unable to afford the cost of living in Southern California, Jones made his "home" in the UCLA cornerbacks' meeting room, where he spent most of the year sleeping on an air mattress alongside another graduate assistant, Chris Polizzi -- now Iowa's special teams coordinator -- who slept on a futon. The arrangement disappointed Wilson.

 "He felt like I shouldn't have to do that," Jones said of his UCLA living conditions.…
